Obituary: Ruth Ann (Bridges) Ayers
text:
GORHAM – Ruth Ann Bridges Ayers, of Gorham, Maine, passed away surrounded by family on Nov. 4, 2026 at the age of 95.
Ruth Ann was born on July 22, 1931 in Newfield, the oldest of six children of Cecil F. and Ellen L. Hannaford Bridges.
Ruth Ann lived in Newfield in the house where she was born, attending local schools, until she finished eighth grade, when her family moved to Gorham. She graduated from Gorham High School and attended the University of Maine at Orono. She had always been called Ruth Ann until her new friends at the University of Maine decided Ruth was a long enough name to remember.
At the University of Maine she was an honor student and member of honorary societies Phi Kappa Phi, Neai Mathetai, and Phi Beta Kappa. While there, she lived in a cooperative dorm called The Elms where they took turns preparing communal meals and she made many lifelong friends.
On June 22, 1952 she married George H. Ayers, Jr. of Camden, whom she met on her first day of classes at University of Maine. She cherished their three children, nine grandchildren, and seven great-grandchildren.
Ruth enjoyed reading and gardening, filling much of their backyard with perennials. After 30 years of research, Ruth wrote a nonfiction book titled “Early Families of Newfield Maine”, which was over 900 pages. She made good progress in writing a second book titled “The History of Newfield, Maine” but because of being involved in many other activities, then loss of her eyesight, that book was not completed.
Ruth was a life member of the Newfield Historical Society, serving as president for two years, then as corresponding secretary for many years, writing their newsletters. She also gave Newfield History talks at many public meetings. She was a board member of Willowbrook Museum in Newfield, and was active at Camp Mechuwana as a counselor and on the governing board.
While in Newfield she joined the Methodist Church, transferring her membership to Gorham when her family moved there. She was a Sunday school teacher, board member, and officer for the United Methodist Women, serving as treasurer for many years. She was a member of the handbell choir at the School Street United Methodist Church, which later moved to Cressey Road. For many years she was chair of the huge rummage sales held at the church twice a year. She baked many rolls for church suppers, and made tea rings for the church Christmas fairs. She was even briefly a waitress who spilled a bowl of soup on someone’s lap.
Ruth was a member of the Cosmopolitan Club, the Gorham Historical Society and the Maine Historical Society.
Ruth Ann wrote the above obituary herself. Her family would like to add that her love of Newfield included time with her husband George, family and friends spent at their little cabin in the woods where they would observe nature from their screened in porch, or walk down to the brook where they kept a little green rowboat.
She made an enormous difference in her community through her volunteerism, and her efficiency and level of organization frequently magnified her impact. A friend once wrote that when she stepped down from leading a local service organization it took nine people to replace her.
An additional love of Ruth’s was reading, and one of her former volunteer roles was creating recordings of herself reading books for community members whose eyesight had deteriorated. As she lost her own sight in later years, she enjoyed listening to books from the Maine State Library’s digital library.
She is survived by her daughter, Pamela Damon and husband Duane of Gorham, son, Mark Ayers and wife Cindy of Scarborough, son, John Ayers and wife Kim of Ashford, Conn.; grandchildren Alan Damon and wife Christy, Kelly Caiazzo and husband Greg, Elizabeth Damon Mathis and husband Nick, Geoff Ayers, Ryan Ayers, Julianne Ayers, Jacob Ayers, Sarah Ayers and Rachel Ayers; and great-grandchildren Will Caiazzo, Andrew Caiazzo, Eleanor Damon, Fiona Damon, George Damon, Dashiell Mathis, and Hawthorne Mathis. In addition, she leaves behind a large and supportive extended family including her siblings Deborah Desautel and Sherb Bridges.
A graveside committal service will be held at 11 a.m. on Saturday, Nov. 14 at Oak Hill South Cemetery, Hosmer Pond Road, Camden, followed by refreshments at Union Hall, 24 Central St., Rockport.
To express condolences or to participate in Ruth’s online tribute, please visit http://www.DolbyBlaisSegee.com
Donations may be made in Ruth’s name to The Newfield Historical Society or the Gorham Food Pantry.

title: Kyle Larson becomes first back-to-back NASCAR Cup Series champion since 2010
text:
Kyle Larson becomes first back-to-back NASCAR Cup Series champion since 2010
Kyle Larson is now a three-time NASCAR champion.
Larson clinched his third Cup Series title in six years early in the 400-mile season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway on Sunday.
Larson became the first back-to-back champion since Jimmie Johnson in 2010; Johnson won five in a row beginning in 2006.
The 34-year-old Larson became the 11th driver in NASCAR history with three Cup titles, joining a list that includes seven-time champs Richard Petty, Dale Earnhardt and Johnson. Jeff Gordon has four. Lee Petty, David Pearson, Cale Yarborough, Darrell Waltrip, Tony Stewart and Joey Logano have three.
Larson was the overwhelming favorite to hoist the Bill France Cup in Homestead long before the green flag dropped.
He entered the weekend with a 67-point lead over Christopher Bell and needed only nine points to wrap up the title. He got one point for starting the race and earned seven more by finishing fourth in the opening stage. But because Bell didn't win the stage, there was no way for him to catch him the rest of the day.
Larson put himself in position for his latest title with a historic postseason, dubbed NASCAR’s Chase for the championship. He ended a 51-race winless skid by winning three of the previous nine playoff events and finished in the top 10 in eight of them.
He enjoyed a similar finish while winning it all in 2021, his first season at powerhouse Hendrick Motorsports. He won four of the last five races — including the finale at Phoenix Raceway — while still dealing with questions about how his time ended at Chip Ganassi Racing.
His second title came in stunning fashion last year at Phoenix. He took advantage of a late caution — his crew put on two new tires instead of four — and leaped sentimental favorite Denny Hamlin on pit road with two laps to go. Hamlin didn’t have enough time to catch Larson.
Larson’s third title was far less shocking. Securing the title was so much of a slam dunk that Larson was the only Cup driver invited to NASCAR’s championship media day Thursday, leading to a parade event that Larson called awkward.
The biggest question was how Larson and his No. 5 Hendrick Motorsports team would handle the pressure. Larson put that to rest during qualifying Saturday.
“They were debating on if a hot dog is a sandwich and if cereal is a soup,” Larson said. “So I would say they were pretty relaxed. I was surprised by all that.”
Where did Larson weigh in on the discussion?
“The hot dog is not a sandwich and absolutely cereal is not a soup,” he said.
A better question: How does Larson compare to the best drivers in motorsports history?
Parnelli Jones, Mario Andretti, A.J. Foyt and Tony Stewart are widely regarded as the best of the best, guys who proved their worth by winning across varying racing series.
Jones won in sprint cars and stock cars around the same time he won the 1963 Indianapolis 500. Andretti won four IndyCar titles, the 1967 Daytona 500 and the 1969 Indianapolis 500. Foyt won four Indy 500s and the 1972 Daytona 500. Stewart won the 1997 IndyCar championship, three Cup Series titles and is currently racing dragsters at the top level, the NHRA.
Larson raced twice at the Indy 500 and has won dirt-racing events around the world.
He’s already in elite company with three Cup titles.
“He wins in everything he does, and they’re all completely different cars and tracks,” retired driver and current NBC Sports race analyst Jeff Burton said. “And he’s racing against the best in every discipline.”

title: Drake Maye throws 3 interceptions as Patriots get blasted by Packers
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — If Jordan Love has played a better game than he did on Sunday, he can’t remember it.
“It’s definitely up there. It felt great,” the Packers quarterback said.
Because of it, Green Bay looks like a team capable of staying in the mix in the formidable NFC North.
Love threw for 372 yards and three touchdowns and ran for a score, and the Packers scored 21 points off four New England Patriots turnovers to roll to a 45-27 win.
Green Bay’s receivers had a huge day, with Christian Watson catching seven passes for 171 yards and a TD and Matthew Golden finishing with 10 catches for 164 yards and a score. Kaleb Johnson ran for a touchdown and Savion Williams had a TD catch as Green Bay finished with 478 total yards.
“It’s crazy, because I know there’s probably a lot more in there,” Golden said. “We’ve still got so many more plays out there to make.”
The Packers hadn’t scored 45 or more points and had 450 or more yards since Nov. 11, 1962 at Philadelphia.
“We got our (butts) kicked. There’s no two ways around it,” Patriots coach Mike Vrabel said.
Late in the game, “MVP!” chants for Love could be heard from visiting Packers fans.
“It’s a surreal feeling,” Love said.
Love completed three passes of at least 43 yards, and seven of 28 or more.
“Those are low-percentage throws in theory, but he’s making them look high-percentage,” Packers coach Matt LeFleur said. “They’re right on the money.”
Packers safety Xavier McKinney had a pair of interceptions and Evan Williams also had a pick.
Green Bay entered the day last in the NFL in rushing, averaging 60.6 yards per game, but finished with 129 yards on the ground.
The Packers (6-3) got plenty of help from the Patriots (5-4) as they built a 24-7 lead en route to their fifth win in six games.
New England’s Drake Maye took a step backward after weeks of steady play, throwing three interceptions while completing 21 of 38 passes for 299 yards and three touchdowns. Maye had thrown just one pick in his previous four games. He’s now tied with Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert with an NFL-worst 11 INTs.
“We haven’t had a clean, a turnover-free game yet,” Maye said. “It’s starting with me. It’s one of the biggest differences between winning and losing football games.”
The Patriots set a franchise record for points allowed at Gillette Stadium, which opened in 2002. New England hadn’t given up 45 points in the regular season since a 45-7 loss to the New York Jets on Sept. 26, 1993.
Maye made questionable decisions on all three of his turnovers in the first half. Two of them set up Packers touchdowns. Rhamondre Stevenson, Efton Chism and Mack Hollins all had TD catches for the Patriots. Stevenson also had a fumble that set up Watson’s score before leaving with a knee injury late third quarter.
DeMario Douglas caught five passes for 102 yards.
The Packers led 24-14 at halftime, then drove down the field on the opening possession of the second half. Love punctuated the seven-play, 70-yard drive with a 10-yard TD pass to Williams.
New England rookie Karon Prunty was in coverage on the score after Carlton Davis III suffered a knee injury in the second quarter.
Gillette Stadium was full of energy before the game as the Patriots celebrated members of their 2016 team — including an appearance by Tom Brady in the Fox broadcast booth — to commemorate the 10th anniversary of their record comeback win over the Atlanta Falcons in Super Bowl 51.
It quickly dissipated after the Patriots opened with a penalty, followed on the next play by Maye throwing the ball into traffic and being intercepted by McKinney at the New England 14.
Two plays later, Love easily found the end zone on a scramble and the Packers jumped in front 7-0.
Green Bay never trailed.
Injuries
Packers: Linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper left early in the first quarter with a chest injury. Running back Josh Jacobs left later in the quarter with a broken finger, LaFleur said. … Wide receiver Bo Melton was evaluated for a concussion.
Patriots: Left guard Ben Brown (knee) limped off a few plays after Davis late in the second quarter. … Special teamer Brenden Schooler exited with a hamstring injury. … Left tackle Will Campbell walked off with a knee injury in the fourth quarter.
Packers’ receiving duo has rare achievement
Watson and Golden became the first Packers teammates to have 150 or more receiving yards and a touchdown catch since Don Hutson and Andy Uram did it in 1942.
Up next
Packers: Host Minnesota next Sunday.
Patriots: Travel to Germany to play Detroit next Sunday in Munich.

title: There’s no need to feel bad for Susan Collins
text:
On election night last week, I went to bed at 10 p.m. (I have a baby). Even by that time, the sky was looking blue, if you know what I mean.
I woke up again at around 3 a.m. and was up for an hour rocking the baby back to sleep — he’s teething — and I didn’t even mind that much because I just kept scrolling through Democratic win after Democratic win.
The biggest congrats of the night must go to Troy Jackson, who not only beat a 30 year incumbent, but who did it with a campaign lasting less than four months, a fraction of his opponent’s funding and, as he himself has pointed out, a funny accent.
(Hey, if a successful campaign can happen in under four months, maybe it’s time to legally set time limits on when campaigns can start advertising. Imagine the peace in our mailboxes.)
I have been waiting years for Sen. Susan Collins to lose. Years.
Specifically, I have been waiting eight years. Eight years since 2018 and her vote for Brett Kavanaugh which, along with her vote for Neil Gorsuch, led directly to the end of a nationwide right to abortion (as well as a ton of other terrible Supreme Court decisions, such as “anything the president does while President isn’t a crime ever.”)
I honestly thought Collins would die in office or retire on her own terms, and while I would have been satisfied to not have her in the Senate anymore under almost any circumstances, it’s so much nicer to have her definitively lose a race, to be rejected by Maine voters.
After the Jan. 6 Capitol insurrection, I wrote of Sen. Collins that I would “use my meager talents to make sure her legacy is remembered the way she deserves it to be remembered – as a failure.” I still intend to do that.
Don’t feel bad for Susan Collins. She can head to a comfortable retirement with a nicely padded bank account. The worst that will happen is she’ll be haunted by the ghosts of the American women who died because they couldn’t get abortion care in time.
After Tuesday’s Democratic shellacking — and at the time of writing — Paul LePage might be the only Republican in the entire country to have flipped a seat in the House of Representatives. If Paul LePage is your upside, things aren’t going well for you.
If LePage is my congressional delegate, I will quite obviously not be thrilled. LePage supports terrible policies and I just plain don’t like him. His campaign leaned into homophobia in its mailings (of which I received several), repeatedly reusing an image of his electoral rival, Matt Dunlap, with an LGBT Pride flag. That’s it. That’s the whole attack. That a guy held a Pride flag because I guess LePage and his voters think supporting gay people is an inherently negative thing.
On the other hand, I almost feel bad for LePage. (Almost.) First of all, he’s at risk of having me as a constituent, and we all know I’m extremely annoying. Second, he’s 78 years old and not a particularly vigorous 78, either. He’ll be the oldest freshman congressman in American history. He barely looked like he wanted to run his campaign in the first place.
You can say a lot about LePage’s governorship of Maine, but at least the man looked like he was having a good time.
As of Thursday morning, he was clinging on by fewer than 2,700 votes in a district that Trump won by nine points in 2024. LePage could be relaxing on a beach in Florida right now. Instead, he has to keep pretending to live in an apartment above a barbershop in Augusta.
Also. While a couple dozen congressional races remain uncalled, at the time of this column’s submission, the count is at least 237 Democrats to 147 Republicans in the House of Representatives. (218 seats are needed for control.)
Not only will Paul LePage be in a minority — surely a terrifying prospect for the man who once expressed fear of the menace of “D-Money, Smoothie and Shifty” — but it promises to be a tiny, reviled minority, bound inextricably to a president who pretty much every average person dislikes.
It’s like LePage found a magical cursed monkey’s paw at Marden’s, wished to be a congressman, and the paw may grant his wish in a terrible way.

title: Pope wraps up Uruguay visit and heads to most fraught stop of his tour in Milei's Argentina
text:
Pope wraps up Uruguay visit and heads to most fraught stop of his tour in Milei's Argentina
Pope Leo XIV is wrapping up his visit to Uruguay on Sunday by marking an important Catholic feast day that is tied to the country’s independence, capping his effort to draw attention to the role the church has played in Latin America’s most secular country.
Leo was traveling to the city of Florida, north of Montevideo, before heading to Argentina for the second leg of his three-nation tour of South America. It's expected to be the most politically delicate, given the Catholic Church's sharp criticisms of the austerity program of libertarian President Javier Milei.
For his final event in Uruguay, Leo was commemorating the feast of the Virgin of the Thirty-three. Every year, thousands of pilgrims flock to the city to pray before the small wooden icon of the Virgin Mary.
Related video: Notre Dame coaches reflect on meeting Pope Leo while in Rome
According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the Guaraní statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in Florida on Aug. 25, 1825.
Leo became the first pope in nearly four decades to visit Uruguay, in hopes of reminding its people that the Catholic Church is part of their very identity as a nation — even if in subsequent decades the country went on a deeply secular, and at times anticlerical, route.
An assessment after the first leg of the trip
Leo was hoping to leave a final parting message before opening the second leg of his South American trip, which he went ahead with despite having undergone surgery Oct. 13 to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung. The final stop is in Peru, his second homeland.
Leo, 71, has appeared in fine form at his events, singing loudly, bounding up stairs and gamely greeting the crowds in his popemobile. He has not cut any events short, including those that have kept him out until past midnight Rome time.
“This visit will also serve to reinforce the image of Leo as a leader, not merely in a spiritual sense, but in a much broader capacity as a political leader and a widely recognized figure who, far from shying away from conflict or tension, offers a powerful perspective and commands a highly respected voice,” said Luis Bahamondes, a professor at the Center for Judaic Studies at the University of Chile.
A potentially delicate meeting with Milei
Milei is due to meet Leo at the Buenos Aires airport and then the two will appear together for the traditional welcome ceremony and exchange of speeches. The encounter could be tense, given Milei’s austerity measures that have slashed social spending, and his embrace of artificial intelligence.
Milei’s sweeping spending cuts have greatly strained relations with Argentine church leaders, who have criticized his government for putting economic orthodoxy ahead of the needs of the poor.
Since taking office in December 2023, for example, Milei has slashed Argentina’s health care budget by 48% in real terms. Planned cuts to the public university system, which represents a near-universal point of pride in the crisis-prone country, sent students into the streets.
Much like its allies in the Trump administration, Milei's government has portrayed the cuts as part of a necessary reform process to remake Argentina’s troubled economy and eliminate fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy.
According to official data, poverty in Argentina reached 32.3% of the population during the first half of 2026, representing about 15 million people.
Milei has also courted AI investment and data centers with promises of limited regulation. Leo has warned about the threats to humanity and the environment of the AI race and called for strict, internationally policed safeguards on its development.
A trip to complete Francis’ unfinished business
In Argentina, Leo is very much completing unfinished business left by his predecessor, Pope Francis. The Argentine Jesuit, the former archbishop of Buenos Aires, never returned home during his 12-year pontificate, confounding friends and foes alike.
“There’s a lot of disagreement over Francis and his legacy in Argentina,” said David Lantigua, a theology professor and faculty fellow at the University of Notre Dame’s Kellogg Institute, which focuses especially on Latin American affairs.
Much of the polemics stems from his tenure in Buenos Aires, when the former Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio was a sometimes divisive partisan figure in a politically polarized country. Bergoglio was a slum priest, who advocated for the poorest and most marginalized — the sector of Argentines who have been feeling Milei’s social spending cuts the most.
“I think we’ll see that kind of tension with Leo — that’s the ministry Francis left behind,” Lantigua said.
Leo, who spent two decades as a missionary priest in Peru ministering to poor people, is very much a pastor in Francis' image and owes his pontificate to the late pope.

title: Obituary: Ian McKibbin White
text:
CUMBERLAND FORESIDE – Ian McKibbin White, former director of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, Calif., died on Oct. 3, 2026, after a brief illness. He was 97 years old, the son of Osborne White of Salem, Mass. and Aileen Dowsett White of Honolulu, Hawaii.
Ian was born in Honolulu, Hawaii but his family moved to a working ranch in Healdsburg, Calif. in 1931. His mother raised Great Danes and his father raised Percherons. Ian’s early years were spent riding horses to check fence lines, except when he was 8 years old, he painted his first painting. That was the beginning of a lifelong passion for art.
Education began for him at the Cate School in Carpinteria, Calif. There, he was allowed to bring his colt to train, fancy pigeons he raised, and to take his first art lessons. During those years, he also discovered taxidermy, creating display cases with painted backgrounds and local birds for his room. He excelled in anything equestrian but did not like baseball! Ian earned his BA in Architecture at Harvard and returned for a year in Industrial Design. In 1952, it was the Korean War, and he signed up for four years in the Navy, serving as a minesweeper.
In 1956, he went back to study at the UCLA School of Design. In New York, he was hired to design the Brooklyn Botanic Garden Golden Jubilee Exhibitions, where he was discovered by Tom Buechner, the Brooklyn Museum Director, who became his mentor and lifelong friends. Buechner hired him to be an exhibition designer for the Brooklyn Museum-Now he was in the art world. While at Brooklyn, he created the Freida Schiff Warburg Memorial Sculpture Garden and several exhibitions which caught the attention of Tom Howe, the Director at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco. Ian accepted the position of assistant director there in 1967. He had another challenge that wouldn’t allow him to go to the west coast until June of that year. In the summer of 1951, Ian had been privileged to sail the schooner “Bowdoin” into the Arctic with Capt. Donald B. MacMillan. He was a senior at Harvard, sailing with classmates and crew, two of whom were to become his future brothers-in-law. That summer opened his eyes to the beauty and wilderness of the Arctic. He responded with his camera and notebook of sketches. In 1967, he was asked by Bowdoin College to create an Arctic museum for the college, and he had six months to do it before landing in San Francisco. It was successfully completed, and it earned him an Honorary Doctor of Fine Arts degree from the college. By this time, he had met and married Florence “Floppy” Hildreth from Maine, and they has sons Peter and Daniel, and daughter, Susanna. They settled in Ross, Calif. where they lived for over 20 years.
Ian became Director of the Legion of Honor in 1970 and soon was called upon to guide its joining with the DeYoung Museum to form the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. It was an era of blockbuster traveling shows, developing his curatorial staff, and expanding the collections with major acquisitions and gifts. Ian was always painting during vacations, sometimes at Fallen Leaf Lake near Tahoe with his family, or trips to Montana, Italy, Maine, and Hawaii with Tom Buechner and another great artist friend, Clyde Aspevig.
He was a devoted Bohemian Club member for over 50 years. He was retired in 1987, after 20 years of demanding museum work. He and Floppy built a new home in Healdsburg, Calif., overlooking the valleys of Sonoma County and spent the next years creating gardens, another love of Ian’s, and a studio for serious painting, at last. Thirteen years brought weddings and triplet grandchildren, plus four more. Ian delighted in sharing their lives. In 2001, the California stakes were pulled and the Whites moved to Maine. In 2018, he published the story of his life and love of art, “The Creative Impulse: Art of Ian McKibbin White.” He painted his last water color at a family reunion in August, surrounded by his entire loving family, overlooking yet one more landscape that inspired him.
Ian leaves his devoted wife, Floppy, together for 67 years; son, Peter Addington-White and wife, Dr. Joan Addington-White of San Francisco, Calif., son, Daniel Hildreth White and wife, Jennifer Akers White of Falmouth, daughter, Susanna McKibbin White and partner, Kathleen Mary Emery of Huntington, Mass. Also surviving are much-loved grandchildren, Alexander and Murielle Addington-White; Ellery and Nichole Addington-White and their daughter Lucy, whom Ian was delighted to meet at the reunion for the first time, his first great-grandchild; India Addington-White, Emma Addington-White; Sam and Martha White, and just arrived Nella Maria (as this was being written); JP and Mary Catherine White who gave us Mia Christine three days after Ian died; and Malia Louise White. Not to be forgotten, Ian is also survived by his beloved, noisy Jack Russell Terrier, MollyMolly.

title: Bruins start fast in win over Panthers
text:
BOSTON — Elias Lindholm, Mikey Eyssimont and Morgan Geekie each scored a goal in an opening period that started out testy, carrying the Boston Bruins past the Florida Panthers 4-1 on Sunday.
Jeremy Swayman made 40 saves, 17 coming in the first period, for the Bruins, who improved to 7-0-0 at home by winning their fourth straight game a day after placing young star James Hagens on injured reserve.
JJ Peterka added a goal for Boston, which owns a plus-21 goal differential at TD Garden. David Pastrnak and Pavel Zacha each added two assists.
Carter Verhaeghe scored a power-play goal for the Panthers, and Jacob Markstrom stopped 32 shots. Florida has lost three of four games.
Boston’s 6-foot-7 defenseman Nikita Zadorov dropped the gloves against 6-foot-1 forward Brady Tkachuk at the opening faceoff, setting the stage for 126 total penalty minutes.
Just over six minutes later, Florida’s Garnet Hathaway squared off against forward Mark Kastelic.
The Panthers swept the three games against Boston last season, winning each by one goal.
Following a lengthy review, Lindholm was credited with a goal that made it 1-0 just 4:50 into the game after his wrister broke off Markstrom and trickled behind him, nearing the goal line as he attempted to pull it back with his glove.
Eyssimont poked a loose puck into the net following his wraparound shot, making it 2-0 less than two minutes later.
Geekie then scored for the fourth straight game, one-timing a shot for a power-play goal at 15:59 with the Bruins on a two-man advantage.
Verhaeghe’s one-timer cut it to 3-1.
The Bruins, who entered with the NHL’s second-best goal differential behind Carolina, were off since rolling to a 6-2 victory at Pittsburgh on Thursday.
Up next
Panthers: Close their three-game road trip Tuesday at Columbus.
Bruins: Play the second of four straight at home Thursday, facing longtime rival Montreal.

title: Susan Collins could confront Trump
text:
I have urged Sen. Susan Collins to confront President Donald Trump.
Pardoning the Jan. 6 insurrectionists; supporting the creation of DOGE; covering up the Epstein files; launching the war against Iran; putting ICE in our streets; pursuing vendettas via lawsuits; rounds of tariffs; bombing fishermen; backing Putin and Netanyahu—Trump has degraded the presidency and the United States.
Collins (or an aide) made a reply that told me she was prevented, procedurally, from doing anything. The reply schooled me about impeachment (yes, I learned). If representatives initiated the process, and representatives and then senators moved it along, up to a Senate vote — then, following deliberation, she would be counted, Nay or Yea.
Collins can do more; confronting Trump would be an on-the-ground, human thing. Being with, listening to, persuading fellow congresspeople — these are the essential steps.
I have suggested that I accompany Susan, even do the speaking.
Susan Collins does, in fact, have agency enough to confront Donald Trump.
Michael Hatem, Ph.D.
Portland

title: 31st ‘Art for Art’s Sake’ Show & Sale Aug. 21-23
text:
The Lincoln Arts Festival (LAF) Art Show has been held since 1995, and almost always at a shipyard. For many years now, Hodgdon Yacht Services, at 100 Ebenecook Road, Southport has generously provided the perfect space for this show, Art for Art’s Sake.
This year’s opening reception/sale is Friday, Aug. 21, 5-7 p.m. Saturday, Aug. 22 (Art Interaction Day) hours are 10 a.m. - 5 p.m. and the final day, Sunday, Aug. 23, is 10 a.m. - 3 p.m.
There are 23 artists/artisans participating this year, all with links to our region, and four for the first time. Most of the artists will be participating in “Art Interaction Day” on Saturday, with on-going demos and chats between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. Come enjoy the wonderful works of our local talent – and perhaps find a gift or two for a special occasion, or just something you can’t resist!
Here’s the art show’s 2026 lineup: (Bold=new this year, *=not at Art Interaction Day)
Liz Ambrosino – potter with special firings; Christine Thalia Andersen – ceramics, paintings; Alan Bellows – black smith; Wendy Bellows – paintings, handspun + wovens, handmade journals; Margaret Canepa (new) – watercolor paintings; Nancy Custer Carroll (new) – paintings; Cheryl Cayer (new) – paintings; Martha Cowdery and Mike Tomko – seaglass art, floor cloths; Jim Farnan – paintings, decoupage; Clark Griffith – potter; Brittney Honisch – hand carved lino-prints; Don Josephson* – American Expressionist paintings; Nora Lally – jewelry; Jeanne Lally – illustrative art; Jim LaMorder – photography; Cecelia Ludwig – paintings; Susie Porter – paintings; Rimar Reed – paper art constructions; Fran Scannell* – plein air paintings, cards; John M.T. Seitzer – paintings and more; Ursula Smith* – hand-wovens; Annette Stormont – ceramic sculpture.
Set your course for Hodgdon Yacht Services by land or sea: 100 Ebenecook Road, Southport or 43° 49′ 45.768″ N | 69° 40′ 36.6852″ W

title: Death Notice: Candace Hilton Smith
Light snow falls in Rangeley
text:
The first signs of winter appeared early Sunday morning with light snow flurries in Rangeley.
A spokesperson for the National Weather Service couldn’t say how much it snowed, but said western Maine could continue to see bouts of winter weather throughout the week.
There’s also potential for a more widespread system headed into the weekend, most likely Friday or Saturday, that would bring light snow and heavier rain to coastal areas.

title: Gender identity has no place in election headlines
text:
Do we really need the news highlighting a person’s gender identity, seemingly validating their worthiness of their job or success? Why do we care what someone’s gender identity is? Can they do the job or not?
Now, according to this paper, Maine has its “first openly nonbinary” state lawmaker (Nov. 4).
I don’t care.
If you feel it “news” to share that, how about sharing every legislator’s gender identity? Just make it a blanket practice in every news article.
Or, wait. Are you consciously discriminating against cisgender people because they are not hip, cool or woke? Now I worry that nonbinary lawmakers will focus only on nonbinary issues and not be “for the people” but only for their people.
Once we in Maine voted in legal gay marriage, didn’t it reflect that “we” accept everyone? Just stop already. It’s not news, it’s irritating and discriminatory.
Elza Allen
Arundel

title: Amoeba infections leave 5 with permanent vision loss, 1 dead in this state
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - The Louisiana Department of Health has identified 10 Acanthamoeba infections since 2024, including one fatal brain infection this year. The state epidemiologist said contact lens wearers should remove their lenses before showering, swimming or using a hot tub
Theresa Sokol, state epidemiologist for the Louisiana Department of Health, said Acanthamoeba is found in many environments.
What Acanthamoeba is
“Acanthamoeba are what are referred to as a free-living amoeba,” Sokol said. “These are single-celled organisms that live in the environment. They’re in soil, they’re in dust, and they’re in fresh and salt water.”
Sokol said the organisms also can be found in swimming pools, drinking water systems, and HVAC systems.
“Pretty much everyone is going to be exposed to Acanthamoeba during their lifetime,” Sokol said. “The good news is that most people exposed to Acanthamoeba aren’t going to get sick, but for a few people it can cause serious infections of the sinuses, of the brain, and sometimes of the skin and the eyes as well.”
Cases reported in Louisiana
Sokol said eight of the 10 infections since 2024 were eye infections. Seven of those eight people wore contact lenses, and five cases resulted in permanent vision loss.
“It’s a severe infection, even though it typically doesn’t spread to other parts of the body or result in death,” Sokol said.
The other two patients were reported this year, Sokol said. One had a sinus infection and the other had a brain infection. The patient with the brain infection died. Sokol said both patients had underlying medical conditions.
Sokol said the department is not releasing further details about the patients, including where they lived.
“We want to protect the privacy of the patients that have been infected,” Sokol said. “So we don’t share any more detailed information than that.”
She said the patients were located throughout the state. Sokol said the amoeba can live in tap water in any drinking water system in Louisiana.
“The amoeba can live in tap water anywhere in Louisiana or in the United States because it really takes a very, very high level of chlorination in order to kill these amoeba,” Sokol said. “It’s not a level that would be practical for use in drinking water systems.”
What contact lens wearers should do
Sokol said eye infections linked to contact lens use often occur in people who are healthy. She said some of those people did not follow the best contact lens hygiene or wore their lenses while swimming or showering.
“Contact lenses can absorb and hold water,” Sokol said. “If the lenses come into contact with tap water or swimming pools or some other water where the amoeba live, then those amoeba can sort of latch onto or get trapped beneath the lens, which is directly against the cornea. That’s where the infection happens.”
Sokol said contact lens wearers should:
- Wash their hands with soap and water and dry them thoroughly before handling lenses.
- Remove lenses before showering, using a hot tub or swimming.
- Clean and rinse lenses with the proper solution every time they are removed.
- Store lenses properly.
“You need to dry them thoroughly,” Sokol said of hands. “You don’t want to have your hands wet while you are handling them.”
She said leftover water on the hands can get into a lens.
“That’s the water that can then get into your contact lens perhaps and be absorbed or latch onto it and then just remain there,” Sokol said. “That’s what we’re trying to avoid.”
Sokol said getting water in the eyes while not wearing contact lenses has not been shown to be a risk for infection. She said a person who has had trauma to the eye or recent eye surgery might potentially have an opening. She said most infections are identified among people who wear contact lenses.
Symptoms, diagnosis and treatment
Sokol said symptoms of Acanthamoeba eye infections can look like those of other common eye infections. They include eye pain, redness, blurred vision, sensitivity to light, and excessive watering.
“It’s really best anytime you get any of those symptoms to just check with your healthcare provider,” Sokol said. “There are prescription treatments that are available.”
“The earlier you seek care, the more likely to have a positive outcome,” she said.
Sokol said symptoms could appear “several days or up to several weeks after exposure.” She said it can be hard to know when someone was exposed.
Sokol said the amoeba sometimes can be seen under a microscope. She said reference laboratories can run tests that identify the amoeba’s genetic material. The specimen depends on the type of infection, she said. A brain infection might require a brain biopsy, and an eye infection might be tested with fluid from the eye.
She said skin and sinus infections caused by Acanthamoeba often are treatable but can spread to other parts of the body, which makes them harder to treat.
“The brain infection that is caused by Acanthamoeba is oftentimes difficult to diagnose,” Sokol said. “If the diagnosis happens at a later stage, then sometimes that increases the risk that a patient may not survive that infection. However, several patients with that infection have been successfully treated in the past.”
Nasal rinsing, medical devices and tap water
Sokol said using tap water for nasal irrigation, or cleaning nasal irrigation devices with tap water, is a known risk factor for sinus and brain infections caused by Acanthamoeba.
“Tap water should not be used for nasal or sinus irrigation,” Sokol said. “It really can pose a risk of severe disease.”
Sokol said nasal irrigation devices can be used safely with water that is labeled sterile or distilled. Boiled and cooled tap water also can be used, she said.
She said people who use other medical devices that use water, such as a CPAP machine, should follow the manufacturer’s instructions and use safe water.
Sokol said sinus and brain infections occur mostly among people with weakened immune systems. She said those conditions include HIV, AIDS, a history of an organ transplant, cancer, and diabetes, among others.
“People who have a condition that weakens their immune system need to be especially aware of using the safe types of water in nasal irrigation devices or other medical equipment,” Sokol said.
Sokol said people can still shower with tap water. She said infection is not associated with swallowing or drinking tap water.
“There’s no need to be concerned,” Sokol said. “That’s not how Acanthamoeba infections happen.”

title: Police make arrest in a deadly shooting at Winston-Salem State during homecoming weekend
text:
WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. (AP) — Authorities on Sunday arrested a man in a shooting during homecoming weekend at Winston-Salem State University in North Carolina that left one person dead and at least one other person injured.
Winston-Salem police said officers who were on campus for homecoming events heard gunshots around 9:45 p.m. Saturday. They found a 19-year-old man with a gunshot wound. They rendered aid but the man died at the scene.
A 22-year-old woman who had what appeared to be a gunshot wound was taken to a hospital, where she was treated and later released.
Assistant Chief Jason Swaim said at a news conference the investigation led to Ziyaire Spinks, 20, who was arrested and being held without bond on charges of murder, assault with a deadly weapon and possession of a firearm on educational property.
According to police, the shooting stemmed from an argument between two groups of people. They confirmed Spinks was not a student at the university.
A second shooting on campus happened less than an hour later, with police responding when they heard shots. In that case, Swaim said two people were injured when gunfire erupted following an altercation.
Authorities said they were investigating to determine if there was any connection between the two shootings. No arrests have been made in the second case.
Chief William Penn, Jr. of the Winston-Salem Police Department vowed during a news conference that authorities will find all of those responsible for the violence at the school.
“It’s important that the blame of these tragic events go to the right people and that’s the folks who committed these acts,” he said, asking people not to point fingers while the investigation is ongoing.
University officials canceled the remainder of homecoming activities Sunday, saying instead that a local church planned to lead a call for prayers in support of the community.
On social media, community members were sharing their condolences and asking for prayers.
Chancellor Bonita J. Brown called the shootings “senseless violence.” In a statement, she assured students, faculty and parents that the campus was secure and that additional law enforcement would remain while the investigation continues.
The school offered counseling for anyone in need.
“We also recognize the concern and anxiety these events have created among our students, parents, families and broader community,” Brown said. “We take our responsibility for campus safety seriously.”
Forsyth County Sheriff Bobby Kimbrough, Jr. echoed the sentiments of the chancellor and other law enforcement officials during the news conference.
“Right now, the community is in need of your prayers. The community is in need of us coming together,” Kimbrough said.
___
Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Kyle Larson wins 2nd consecutive Cup Series title, becomes the 11th NASCAR driver with 3
text:
HOMESTEAD, Fla. (AP) — With the NASCAR Cup Series championship flag flying from a car window, Kyle Larson’s youngest child stood atop the No. 5 Chevrolet and signaled to everyone what had been known for hours.
Three-year-old Cooper held up a single finger.
Yep, his dad was No. 1 again.
Larson clinched his third Cup Series title in six years early in the 400-mile season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway on Sunday. He became NASCAR’s first back-to-back champion since Jimmie Johnson in 2010; Johnson won five in a row beginning in 2006. Both of them accomplished the feat at powerhouse Hendrick Motorsports.
The 34-year-old Larson also became the 11th driver in NASCAR history with three Cup titles, joining a list that includes seven-time champs Richard Petty, Dale Earnhardt and Johnson. Jeff Gordon has four. Lee Petty, David Pearson, Cale Yarborough, Darrell Waltrip, Tony Stewart and Joey Logano have three.
“He’s going to pass me,” said Gordon, the vice chairman at Hendrick. “I’ve already come to that conclusion. Kind of knew that when he was coming to Hendrick Motorsports. He’s special.”
Ryan Blaney won the season finale, which returned to South Florida for the first time since 2019. The championship event had perfect weather and a star-studded lineup of celebrities, including Johnson, singers Jason Derulo and Cole Swindell, WNBA star Sophie Cunningham and golfer John Daly. Racing legend Mario Andretti also tapped a good luck message for Larson.
They were treated to a drama-filled ending. Blaney passed Tyler Reddick of 23XI Racing with a little more than a lap to go and with NBA legend Michael Jordan watching from pit road. Blaney held a brief celebration in victory lane before clearing the way for Larson.
“Obviously he’s incredibly talented,” Blaney said of Larson. “His natural, God-given talent is off the charts. He is very deserving to win his third championship.”
Reddick finished second, followed by William Byron, Christopher Bell, Bubba Wallace and Denny Hamlin.
The real party awaited Larson, who finished 12th. He immediately stopped near the start-finish line for a smoky burnout and then exchanged high-fives and hugs with his team, his wife and his kids. He climbed atop his car with all three children.
Owen, 11, grabbed the flag and started waving it through the air. Audrey, 8, picked up a handful of confetti and started throwing it at her brothers. Cooper posed for pictures before eventually sliding down the windshield and into a pile of confetti.
It was a family affair for sure.
Larson was the overwhelming favorite to hoist the Bill France Cup in Homestead long before the green flag dropped.
He entered the weekend with a 67-point lead over Bell and needed only nine points to wrap up the title. He got one point for starting the race and seven more by finishing fourth in the opening stage. But because Bell didn’t win the opening stage, he had no path to catch Larson the rest of the day.
Larson responded to crew chief Cliff Daniels dropping the news over the radio by saying, “That was anticlimactic.”
Larson scraped the wall early in the second stage, cut a tire and never challenged for the lead.
“Got the word that we had clinched it, and I started driving like an idiot,” Larson said. “I’m more mad at myself.”
Nonetheless, Larson put himself in position for the title with a historic postseason, dubbed NASCAR’s Chase for the championship. He won three times in the 10 playoff events and finished in the top 10 in eight of them.
“They deserve everything, the spoils of victory,” Hamlin said. “They performed absolutely incredible during these last 10 races.”
Larson enjoyed a similar finish while winning it all in 2021, his first season at Hendrick. He won four of the last five races. His second title came in stunning fashion last year at Phoenix. He took advantage of a late caution and leaped sentimental favorite Hamlin on pit road with two laps to go.
Larson’s latest one was far less shocking. Securing the title was so much of a slam dunk that Larson was the only Cup driver invited to NASCAR’s championship media day Thursday and it led to a weeklong conversation about his position in motorsports history.
Larson no doubt belongs in the same conversation as Parnelli Jones, Mario Andretti, A.J. Foyt and Tony Stewart — guys who gained recognition for winning across varying racing series.
Larson raced twice at the Indy 500 and has won the Rolex 24 at Daytona, three Chili Bowls and four Knoxville Nationals.
“I think he’s got to be looked at as one of the all-time greats,” said Hendrick, who won his 16th Cup championship.
Added Gordon: “It’s hard to pick the most impressive thing that he does because he gets in an IndyCar, he goes fast, Sprint car. ... That’s rare air, very rare. There’s just so few guys that are capable of doing that.”

title: Luigi Mangione’s cousin wins election in Baltimore
text:
BALTIMORE, Md. (Gray News) - Republican Nino Mangione won the Baltimore County Council’s District 5 seat on Tuesday, defeating Democrat Shawn McIntosh. Nino Mangione campaigned on promises to crack down on violent crime and support law enforcement.
Family connection
Nino Mangione is a cousin of Luigi Mangione, who pleaded guilty in August in connection with the 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.
Nino Mangione and Luigi Mangione share a grandfather, Nick Mangione Sr., who built a business empire in the Baltimore area.
Statement after arrest
After Luigi Mangione’s arrest, Nino Mangione released a statement.
“Our family is shocked and devastated by Luigi’s arrest,” he said. “We offer our prayers to the family of Brian Thompson, and we ask people to pray for all involved.”
Council service
Nino Mangione has held a Baltimore County Council seat in District 3 since June 1. He was appointed to replace a council member who was resigning.

title: Body cam shows Massachusetts police chief found in unmarked cruiser with vodka
text:
Body cam shows police chief found in unmarked cruiser with bottles of vodka
Police body camera footage obtained by Hearst sister station WCVB shows officers discovering the chief of a nearby department in an unmarked cruiser with two bottles of vodka last month.
Westborough, Massachusetts, Police Chief Todd Minardi was placed on leave following the incident in Shrewsbury on Oct. 23. The town also announced that it was taking steps to retain an outside investigator.
A report written by a lieutenant of the Shrewsbury Police Department indicates that Minardi was found sleeping in a vehicle in the area of 507 Boston Turnpike. The report states that Minardi was dressed in street clothes in his unmarked police cruiser.
Body camera footage from Shrewsbury police shows officers approaching the vehicle just before 12:30 p.m. on Oct. 23. Officer Tyler Vlass opened the door and said, "What's going on?"
Minardi, who was off duty, was holding a bottle of liquor in his right hand.
"We got a call for your well-being. The car's been here for a while, they said. We want to make sure you're okay," Vlass said.
"Yeah," Minardi replied.
The 911 call that prompted the welfare check came from a man who works nearby.
"It just looks like he's passed out in the car and I just want somebody to check on him," the caller said.
When asked by Shrewsbury Officer Kevin Warwick if he had made the call, the man confirmed, saying, "Yeah. I was worried because I saw that car there yesterday. He was here since yesterday."
A Westborough police lieutenant arrived at the scene, and Minardi repeatedly apologized.
"I'm sorry," Minardi said.
"What's that?" Lt. Kevin Caviston asked.
"I'm sorry," Minardi repeated.
"Nothing to be sorry about," Caviston said.
"I'm sorry to put you in this position," Minardi added.
An ambulance arrived, and Minardi eventually agreed to go to the hospital.
Minardi was cited for having an open container of alcohol in the vehicle. Officers noted they could not charge him with operating under the influence since the car was not on when they arrived.

title: Pets of the Week
Rain moves out by mid afternoon, then placid weather returns
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The wet weather will likely continue at least through the first half of the day today before clearing to the east by 5 pm or so. Temps will stick mainly in the 40s today. Once it clears lingering cloudiness will stick around overnight into Monday with the chance for a shower especially to the north and along the coast. This week will be much calmer than last week for the most part with seasonable temps and mainly sunny skies. We are keeping an eye on next weekend for our next system potentially.
Sunday: Some rain early, then clearing and cooler in the afternoon
The rain will continue in the morning with the chance for some wintry mix across colder spots in the west and the far north on Sunday but will begin to move east as the day goes on. The showers should be out of the state by 4 or 5 pm except for maybe extreme eastern Washington county. Temps will be cool once again with highs only reaching the mid to upper 40s for most.
Sunday night: Rain finally fully departs
After a soggy few days things settle down and a seasonably cool night arrives with some lingering cloudiness. Temps will be in the upper 30s for most.
Monday: A drier day
Things dry out and Monday looks to be a somewhat cloudy day but otherwise typical November weather with highs in the upper 40s and low 50s. There may be a few isolated showers in the morning but otherwise a more placid day.
Tuesday and beyond: A more settled week then watching the weekend
After last week was more active this week looks quieter with few chances of active weather besides the weekend. Highs will mostly be in the upper 40s and low 50s. With lows mainly staying in the upper 20s and 30s. However, we are watching a system for late in the week towards next weekend that could provide some early season snow especially for inland and northern regions. It’s a long way off and there are lots of details to work out but it is something we are watching.
Sunday: Showers early, clearing late. Highs in the upper 40s and low 50s. Winds NE at 10-15 mph.
Sunday night: Rain ends clouds stick around. Lows in the upper 30s and low 40s. Winds NE 5-10 mph then going calm.
Monday: Mostly cloudy but dry. Highs in the upper 40s and low 50s. Winds W 5-10 mph.
Monday night: Still mainly cloudy. Lows in the 30s. Light wind.

title: Damariscotta and Newcastle Approve Interlocal Public Works Agreement
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Damariscotta and Newcastle residents approved an interlocal agreement between the towns for a potential shared public work department at the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
Damariscotta passed the article 1,018-285 and Newcastle passed it 989-308.
In addition to the acceptance of the interlocal agreement, voters also approved the following article requesting $75,000 from each town to go toward engineering and searching for a potential property for the department.
Damariscotta Town Manager Andy Dorr said the town had a nearly 70% turnout of registered voters. With the approval, the select board will be discussing the results at its Wednesday, Nov. 4 meeting. (Editor’s note: The Lincoln County News prints Wednesday morning.)
Dorr said the next steps are working with Newcastle to determine a plan for the next phase of the effort.
“There is still a lot of work to be done and we look forward to bringing the community along on that journey,” Dorr said. “Please stay engaged and ask questions.”
Conversation around the possibility of a joint public works department began in May 2025. Preliminary findings were shared at a meeting in March of this year.
In a letter to residents signed by both select boards explaining the proposal, officials said a group has worked together since May 2025 to study historical costs, analyze local road networks, and draft a proposed interlocal agreement.
The select boards said in the letter there are four main reasons the towns came together for the possibility of a joint public works department: direct local control, year-round proactive care, fair cost sharing, and long-term pay off.
Damariscotta and Newcastle would direct daily schedules, priorities, and emergency responses, keeping local staff members accountable instead of contracting third-party vendors, according to the draft of the interlocal agreement.
Year-round proactive care would replace the current contracts the towns use for public works services. The letter said contracting services could sometimes restrict the work done during active snowfall and a local department would provide an “in-house” crew instead that also handle preventative maintenance such as ditching, clearing culverts, and tree trimming.
According to the letter, initial costs will be higher to cover equipment and a garage, and operational savings are projected to pay back set up costs within 10-15 years.
The final revised agreement also outlines what would happen if voters in the future didn’t approve a fiscal year’s budget. If either town fails to appropriate the funds to support its share of the department, the town manager and public works joint oversight board will meet to discuss the failed appropriation and develop a revised budget to bring back to voters in the town it failed in.
The joint oversight board will consist of six voting members, with three appointed by each town. No more than two select board members from each town may serve on the oversight board.
The oversight board will be responsible for policy, planning, and monitoring of the department. It would not be responsible for supervising employees, intervening in daily operations, or hiring.
The board would also be charged with selecting a public works director, who will handle work previously done by a road commissioner, manage daily operations, supervise staff, develop policies for board approval, prepare draft budgets, and more.
The proposed agreement will not merge the towns, create an imbalance, or erase voter authority over spending, Newcastle Town Manager Kevin Sutherland said at the introductory meeting in March.
While working on the interlocal agreement, town officials created a project proposal explorer site, which presents projected costs and comparisons based on different scenarios. The website can be found at ledgehillcrossing.com/public_works.html.

title: Replica firearm recovered after suspects flee stolen vehicle in Lewiston
Advice for learning the mother tongue of your ancestors
text:
Advice for learning the mother tongue of your ancestors
Whether through the death of an older relative, the sale of a property passed down for generations gets sold or the destruction a handful of surviving heirlooms, losing a tangible connection to your family’s ancestral homeland can bring unexpected sorrow.
Learning a language spoken by their parents, grandparents or great-grandparents is a way some English-speaking children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren of immigrants choose to reinforce ties to the old country and nurture their cultural identity.
Knowing the mother tongue of one's ancestors could unlock a stack of letters that clarify hazy chapters of family history. Basic speaking skills may lead to meeting cousins in another country. Listening to stories and songs in the original language conveys nuances and meaning that often are lost in translation, experts say.
Imparting an ancestral language to their children also is important to some parents. Adults who grew up speaking a language other than English, perhaps because they had immigrant parents or they were born abroad themselves, may see the language as a way to foster intergenerational bonds, preserve family traditions and expand future career options.
Whether you’re a parent who wants a child to know their roots or someone eager to acquire an ancestral language yourself, here are tips for claiming a legacy through language.
Don’t let a fear of making mistakes derail you
Linguists and educators generally categorize foreign language students into two broad groups, each with different starting points and perhaps motivations. Most children and adults are second-language learners, who begin formal instruction with little or no prior knowledge.
Most heritage language learners, by contrast, organically acquired some familiarity with a language other than English as young children, said Tanya Ivanova-Sullivan, associate director of the National Heritage Language Resource Center at the University of California, Los Angeles. They typically heard the language spoken at home and understand or speak it themselves to varying degrees.
“Heritage language speakers are home chefs,” Ivanova-Sullivan said. “They learned the language in the family kitchen from parents and grandparents rather than in the classroom.”
Repeated early exposure tends to give heritage language students an advantage over second-language learners, but they may be reluctant to speak up in class if they aren't confident in their grammar or relatives teased them for not being fluent, experts say.
Many people are embarrassed about making mistakes when conversing in a language they don't know very well, said Arturo Diaz, executive director of the UCLA Center for World Languages. He encouraged students to use what they already know, saying perfection doesn't have to be the goal.
"So just remove any apprehension you may have in learning language and then just have fun with the experience," Diaz said.
Look for opportunities to learn and practice
Some scholars and educators say that someone with a cultural or familial relationship to a language also could be considered a heritage language student even if they are starting pretty much from scratch, according to the Center for Applied Linguistics, a nonprofit research and teacher education organization that promotes language learning and linguistic diversity.
Listening to relatives whose first language isn't English is an effective way to learn a heritage language, Yang Xiao-Desai, a professor of Chinese at San Francisco State University, said.
“Ask your grandparents for stories,” she said. “Ask them to share a story of a dish, a story of a recipe, a piece of furniture. Whatever you can.”
Podcasts, music and subtitled movies and videos in a target language also may help learners pick up words and phrases.
Ivanova-Sullivan recommends expanding the circle of people with whom you practice. Some communities have programs that pair an English speaker learning a foreign language with a native speaker who wants to learn English.
“When you’re expanding your network, you’re expanding the opportunities to use the language in different ways, and that’s how your vocabulary (grows)," she said.
Book a trip to the place your people are from
Visiting your family's country of origin can be a valuable experience for people who can afford the trip, Ivanova-Sullivan said. She takes her 12-year-old to her native Bulgaria for two months every summer.
Organized tours overseas for people who want to visit their ancestral homelands have multiplied in the last decade, in part due to at-home DNA test kits.
If you're interested in learning a language while traveling but have limited time off from work, check out intensive programs like EF Language Abroad, which has campuses in Spain, France, Korea, Italy, Germany, Japan and the United Arab Emirates.
Before or after traveling, connect with members of your extended family on social media platforms like Facebook and Instagram. Even beginner students can pick up phrases and customs from their relatives.
Consider a local heritage language school
Parents who want their children to learn a family language and embrace their heritage can consider community language schools, which integrate language lessons with cultural traditions. Volunteers and parents from local immigrant communities often operate such schools as nonprofit organizations.
Classes typically are held after school or on weekends. Most are designed for children learning or maintaining a language spoken at home, but some serve adult learners as well, said Joy Peyton, president of the Coalition of Community-Based Heritage Language Schools.
“They use their languages with their parents, with their friends,” Peyton said. “They recognize that their language has value.”
The coalition, a nationwide initiative that connects and advocates for these schools, has documented nearly 1,000 programs teaching 62 languages in 44 states, she said. Korean is the most-taught language, according to Peyton.
Ana Lúcia Lico, a co-founder and board member of the organization, came to the U.S. from São Paulo, Brazil, at age 35. She made sure her two sons, now 20 and 23, learned Portuguese and were immersed in Brazilian culture while growing up in Northern Virginia.
Her older son, Gabriel Lico Bickham, attended a local heritage language school for two hours every Saturday for about a decade, starting at age 4. He remembers learning grammar but also being immersed in games like “Corre cotia,” similar to the American duck, duck, goose.
Classes aren't the only way for children to learn a family language
Lico, whose husband was born in the U.S., said she also exposed her boys to Brazilian Portuguese through music, dance and playing sports.
“Soccer is huge in Brazil,” she said. "Through soccer, my kids developed a whole amazing set of vocabulary, words that I never had to teach them."
Hiring childcare providers who are native speakers or shopping in neighborhoods where a heritage language is spoken are additional ways for children to learn the ancestral tongue, said Richard Brecht, co-director of the American Councils Research Center, a nonprofit group devoted to the improvement of language learning worldwide.
Comic books about a group of children living in a fictitious neighborhood in Brazil helped Bickham learn Portuguese, a skill he says is helping shape his future. Also fluent in Spanish, he recently graduated from the University of Virginia. In January, he leaves for Mozambique, where Portuguese is the official language, for an English teaching assistant position through the Fulbright program.
“Growing up today, I feel very close to my Brazilian identity,” Bickham said. “And the language is probably the most important aspect out of that because the language is what unlocks all these cultural aspects.”

title: Lost class ring returned 47 years later
text:
PAWTUCKET, R.I. (WJAR) - A class ring lost nearly 50 years ago on a beach near Seattle has been returned to its owner after turning up in Washington state.
“The ring means a lot to me because it brings back great memories of my mother,” Paul Benson said.
Ring lost at beach near Seattle
Benson graduated from St. Raphael Academy in Pawtucket nearly 50 years ago. One summer, his brother, Eric Benson, borrowed the ring and took it out West, eventually to a beach near Seattle, where he was wrestling with friends.
“I just took the ring off, put it down on the rock,” Eric Benson said.
As the tide rolled in, the ring was gone. Eric Benson said he thought, “My brother is going to kill me.”
Asked by reporter Jake Baum what his reaction was when he learned his brother had borrowed and lost the ring, Paul Benson said Eric never told him.
Found with a metal detector
The ring stayed on the beach off Puget Sound for nearly 50 years. In November 2025, Seattle native Lucas Thrun found it with a metal detector.
Thrun said parts of the beach were exposed that normally are not. He said there is a video of him finding the ring.
Thrun has hunted for items on Seattle beaches for years.
“This is the stuff that people in my hobby dream about,” Thrun said.
Returned in person
Thrun contacted the school, but the school had no way to reach Benson. Through friends, Thrun and others found Benson’s address and went to his door.
“I was napping,” Benson said.
Benson said he was stunned. After initial disbelief, he was eager to meet the man who would return his ring.
“If it wasn’t for him, it would just be a lost memory,” Benson said.
Thrun flew to Rhode Island, nearly 3,000 miles from where he found the ring, to hand it back in person. Eric Benson, who now lives in Israel, made it a priority to be there.
“Little did I know it would be a 47-year history. He forgave me. But trust me, he never forgot,” Eric Benson said.
Eric Benson also said, “Next time I take the ring, I’m gonna ask him.”
Baum asked Paul Benson whether the experience showed that there are still good people in the world. Benson answered, “Yes.”
“It’s about life in general and how pieces fall into place, and Lucas kind of brought that all together for me,” Benson said.

title: Obituary: Elvira J. Del Camp
text:
PORTLAND – Elvira J. Del Camp, a beloved mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, sister, aunt, and friend, passed away peacefully at her home in Portland, Maine, on Oct. 24, 2026, at the age of 99, surrounded by her loving family and caregivers.
Born in 1927 to Italian immigrants, Elvira Rossi grew up of humble beginnings during the Great Depression in Melrose Park, Ill., as the youngest of three sisters and one brother. After World War II, she met Mike Del Camp, who immediately became the love of her life. They married in 1950 and soon began raising their family of five boys, Michael, Thomas, David, Brian, and John, who became the center of Elvira and Mike’s universe. In 1972, the couple moved their family from Chicago to Portland, Maine, where Elvira made many dear friends over the years. The memories of her love and her life of complete dedication to her family will always be cherished by those who survive her.
She loved each of her sons, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren equally, despite their different personalities and paths. When people learned she had five boys, the common reaction was often “…your poor mother…”
Yet Elvira never saw it that way.
She considered herself blessed, and each son brought her great joy: Michael earning his Eagle Scout Award, Tom being the first to give Elvira her first grandchild, David and Brian competing as teammates on the college gridiron, and John returning home safely as a decorated combat veteran.
Whether she was cheering her sons on at athletic events, working as a secretary to the plant manager at General Electric in South Portland, participating in women’s golf and bowling leagues, boating on Sebago Lake, or trying to keep up with her boys on the ski slopes, she made wonderful friends and memories wherever she went. True to her Italian roots, any friends her boys brought home were always offered snacks, a home-cooked meal, or both. She was known for planning menus weeks in advance for large holiday gatherings or even hosting parties for other team parents at David and Brian’s Maine Maritime Academy football games—long before tailgating was common.
Elvira lost Mike, her best friend and lifelong love, in 1985 after 35 years of marriage. She remained in their home for the next 41 years as a widow. An avid animal lover, she deeply appreciated the unconditional love her dogs gave her.
Her inner strength was forged as a Gold Star family member when her only brother, Ben, was killed in action in 1944 during World War II. She rarely spoke of it, but she always held him close in her heart. Anyone who knew Elvira knew she was a proud, patriotic citizen with a fierce love for her country. A voracious reader, she stayed well-informed on current events and was never afraid to share her opinions. Family gatherings often featured lively discussions—and sometimes good-natured yelling—but she could disagree spiritedly at one moment, and share laughs while breaking bread the next. Over the years, she opened her home and heart to girlfriends, wives, and the blended families of her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, always generous to a fault. Her love for each of them was unmistakable.
Elvira was among the last of the Greatest Generation. A devout Catholic, she will be fondly remembered for her integrity, loyalty, love of family, patriotism, welcoming spirit toward friends and strangers alike, and keen sense of humor. While her family has lost their beloved matriarch, they take comfort in knowing she lived a wonderfully blessed and full life.
In addition to her brother, Ben, she was predeceased by her parents, Frank C. and Michalena Rossi; her sisters Ann, (husband Hartzel) and Rose, (husband Warren); and her husband, Mike Del Camp.
She is survived by her sons Michael, Thomas and wife Cynthia, David and wife Barbie, Brian and wife Maureen, and John and wife Debra. She is also survived by her grandchildren Christine and husband Patrick, Laura and husband Kyle, Yana and wife Talya, Tracy and husband Roger, Nate and wife Chanel, Rachel and husband Ryan, Tara and fiancé Derek, Dakota, Katarina and husband Berk; and her great-grandchildren Arthur, Luke, Penelope, Nikko, Carter, and Giovani.
Elvira and her family extend their heartfelt thanks and humble gratitude to her dedicated caregivers, Rose Ricci and Lucia Igani, as well as Nurse Tracy Rickards, Katie, Lynn, Wanda, Ellen, Michelle, and Rebecca on staff at Beacon Hospice. Their professional care, attention to detail, and dependability allowed Elvira to remain comfortably in her home during the past three years.
A Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated at St. Joseph’s Church, Stevens Avenue, Portland, on Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 11 a.m., followed by a reception at Bruno’s restaurant, 33 Allen Ave., Portland.
Arrangements are in the care of Advantage Funeral and Cremation Services, 199 Forest Ave., Portland, ME 04103. Please visit http://www.advantageportland.com to view Elvira’s online memorial.
In lieu of flowers, please make a donation in Elvira’s name to:
Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland
217 Landing Rd.
Westbrook, ME 04092

Eastern Maine shoppers donate food for cancer patients
text:
Maine (WABI) - For people going through cancer treatment, getting nutritious food can be a challenge. One local nonprofit got a helping hand from shoppers across eastern Maine on Sunday.
The Christine B. Foundation held regional food drives at four Hannaford locations in Brewer, Bucksport, Machias and Dexter.
“We’re giving them a little wish list of items that we’d like to have to be able to provide healthy food to cancer patients. All of the food is going to benefit cancer patients in those communities,” said Board Member Michelle Allen.
“We are really trying to focus on fresh produce as much as we can. But we are really trying to get as much as high nutritious quality as much as we can, beans, peanut butter, pasta, proteins, chicken, ground beef all of those things,” said Program Coordinator Ben Wyman.
Volunteers pick up food packages at the distribution center in Bangor, before delivering them to patients’ homes. Allen says that good nutrition plays a key role in supporting cancer patients.
“Cancer patients in our area nutrition really are medicine for these people. Research has shown that the healthier food and the more nutrition that we can provide cancer patients, the better off they’re going to be during their treatment and afterwards,” said Allen.
Organizers say that support would not be possible without the generosity of community members.
“Everyone that’s brought us out something after grocery shopping today has had a smile on their face. They feel good about doing something special for the community and for people that are going through a hard time,” said Allen.
“Even with it being tight for everybody, you’re still finding a way to be generous and help support their neighbors who are going through this and may not have access otherwise,” said Wyman.

title: An 11-month-old girl weighed just 4 pounds when she died. Now, her mom is facing charges
text:
NORTH CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) - A South Carolina mother is facing charges after her 11-month-old daughter was found dead and emaciated in an insect-infested apartment.
Janette Clayton, 27, has been charged with homicide by child abuse after her 11-month-old daughter, Nomai Weathers, was found dead in June at an insect-infested apartment in North Charleston.
The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division, which is leading the case, made the announcement about the new charge Friday. Clayton was initially charged with three counts of unlawful conduct toward a child.
Documents show Nomai was born prematurely and diagnosed with sickle cell disease, which required medically necessary appointments. Clayton allegedly failed to take her daughter to these appointments.
Nomai was found dead June 17 near the front doorway of her family’s apartment, partially wrapped in a blanket. She was emaciated, weighing only 4 pounds, 13 ounces.
The apartment was reportedly in “deplorable” conditions, infested with cockroaches and flies. Officials say no food or child care supplies were found.
An autopsy revealed Nomai’s cause of death to be starvation with acute bronchopneumonia due to neglect. The manner of her death was ruled a homicide.
The case also led to two North Charleston Police Department officers, who had previously responded to the apartment, being placed on leave. One was later fired and charged, while the other was reinstated.
