title: Death Notice: Randy M. Wimert
Patriots take a step back offensively in loss to Packers
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Members of New England’s 2016 Super Bowl-winning team reunited at Gillette Stadium on Sunday for Rob Gronkowski’s induction into the Patriots Hall of Fame.
The current Patriots could have used Gronkowski’s playmaking abilities against Green Bay. The defending AFC champions would also have benefited from having a quarterback who placed a premium on ball security. Alas, Tom Brady was calling the game from the Fox television booth.
From Drake Maye throwing three interceptions in a game for the second time this season, to Rhamondre Stevenson fumbling the ball on a four-turnover day for the Patriots, the signs of regression were everywhere in a 45-27 loss to the Packers.
“I wasn’t good today,” Maye said.
It’s been an up-and-down season for Maye, who was named the AFC Offensive Player of the Month for October after a rough opening month. The 2025 MVP runner-up kicked off the season with a three-interception game against defending Super Bowl champion Seattle.
Maye now has 11 picks, tied with Justin Herbert of the winless Chargers for the most in the NFL.
Maye’s first interception came two plays into the first series of the game. The bad throw gave the Packers a short field, and they needed just two plays to cover 14 yards for a touchdown.
“You can’t put the team in the hole straight off the bat, first possession,” Maye said.
Green Bay made New England pay for the turnovers, scoring 21 points after takeaways. Coach Mike Vrabel said his team became predictable after the Packers took a 17-0 lead.
“It’s tough to spot good teams any sort of lead, and we’ve done that,” Vrabel said.
Once again, the Patriots were without their top two offseason acquisitions at wide receiver, A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs. Running back TreVeyon Henderson remains sidelined indefinitely after revealing last week that he had spent several days in a hospital undergoing tests to determine the cause of unexplained neurological symptoms that have affected his strength and coordination.
Having a healthy complement of offensive options might solve some of the problems currently plaguing the Patriots. Taking care of the ball is another important area to shore up after Stevenson committed his second fumble of the season and the 19th of his career, 11 of which he lost. Stevenson left the game in the fourth quarter after suffering a knee injury.
“We’ve been through a lot, and we’ve got a lot of bumps and bruises. Got some big wins, got some bad losses. We’ve got to find a way to be consistent. Coach (Vrabel) preaches being consistent,” Maye said. “We won the AFC, played in the Super Bowl. Everybody’s coming after us, and we’ve got to respond.”

title: Football Sees Big Win Against Bowdoin
text:
After seven consecutive losses, the Bobcats finally found the win column in the last home game of the season, outlasting rival Bowdoin 10-7 in a defensive slugfest at Garcelon Field on Saturday. The Bobcat’s defense recorded six sacks, and the offense delivered when it mattered, taking a 10-7 lead with 1:07 remaining.
Neither team found rhythm early. Bates opened with the ball at its own 25-yard line and went three-and-out, and Bowdoin answered with a three-and-out of its own. The Bobcats first real threat came on a 46-yard gain from Quin Carver’28, but the Polar Bear’s defense came up with an interception at the 10:38 mark to halt the drive. After another Bates stop, a roughing the punter extended the Bowdoin drive, but the drive was stopped by a penalty and two sacks.
Bates then put together an eight-minute drive that ended in a field goal for a 3-0 lead. Bowdoin responded quickly, starting a drive off at the 35 yard line with a touchdown to go up 7-3.
After halftime, the Bobcats appeared to have a chance to swing momentum when they came up with another interception, but a pass interference call wiped it out and gave the Polar Bears new life. Bates held firm anyway. The defense racked up sacks on back-to-back possessions, including a stretch where it forced a punt and then stopped Bowdoin again after an offensive turnover.
With about five minutes left, Bowdoin intercepted Bates. However, a set of sacks and a punt gave the Bobcats good field position. Then came the game’s decisive stretch: Two big plays by Jeff Vidou ’28 set up and scored the go-ahead touchdown, putting Bates up 10-7 with 1:07 to play. The defense closed it out with a final stop.
After the final whistle, first-year Miles Lesser ‘30 was pleased with the result but wanted more from a rivalry game. “They really showed resilience finally for the first time this year,” Lesser said. “There wasn’t really the intensity I was looking for from the team, though. It’s a rivalry game.”
Postgame, Vidou described the winning catch. “We ran a hitch again, got a little open and put it in my hands,” he said. In addition, Vidou credited the offensive line for their necessary protection. After the final whistle, he said, “That feeling was euphoric.”
In regard to what the win meant for senior night, Vidou said, “It means everything. That’s my family, those are my boys.”
The Bobcats close the last home game of the season 1-7 and look to get another win in their final game at Hamilton.

title: How to keep your game meat from spoiling, starting the moment you pull the trigger
text:
Editors note: This story was originally published in November 2021.
A silent November morning is suddenly interrupted by the distinct sound of deer quickly moving in your direction. A doe enters the clearing, zig-zagging with its tail out and head down. It’s being chased and you know it.
It passes by your stand and seconds later, a huge buck enters the clearing. Steam blows from his nostrils and its gait slows while it searches for a date.
Your crosshairs find their way to the buck’s shoulder and your finger to the trigger. The shot feels good and the deer disappears back into the woods. A crimson trail leads you a short distance and soon, you’re standing over your dream buck.
Now what?
Now, so they say, “the work begins.” No matter the species, once a big game animal is dead, it must be taken care of properly.
This process starts with timely recovery. This is especially true during warm weather, which is becoming increasingly more typical here during Maine’s hunting seasons.
Bears are particularly susceptible to spoilage during the early baiting season, as temperatures are regularly in the 70s and often 80s. As soon as oxygen and blood flow stop inside an animal, bacteria begin to take over. At 40 degrees, a field dressed bear has roughly 12 hours before it begins to spoil, six hours at 50 degrees and three hours at 60 degrees.
Cooler temperatures are your best friend when it comes to caring for your game animal but, regardless of temperature, the first step after photos and celebration, is to field dress or “gut” the animal.
Most hunters are familiar with this process but for those who aren’t, it’s pretty basic. Without getting too technical, using a sharp knife, the animal is cut open from the breast bone to pelvic bone, with great care being taken not to puncture the stomach lining or other organs.
The organs are then removed from the animal, leaving a “dressed” carcass. This allows the carcass to begin cooling properly and quickly, as well as liberating it from harmful bacteria found in the entrails.
After the animal is dressed, the carcass should be cleaned, if necessary, removing any dirt or undesirable substances such as urine or stomach contents which may have come in contact with the meat. Though it seems fairly simple and straightforward, for those not familiar with the process, it is advisable to have an experienced hunter aid in teaching proper technique or, at the very least, research how-to tutorials or videos online.
After the animal is dressed and removed from the field, it needs to be cooled. Cooling the meat slows bacteria growth and spoilage. Here in Maine, game animals are commonly suspended from a tree, or in a garage or barn with their hide on, for a few days.
This is especially common with deer and is acceptable practice, provided temperatures are cool enough, preferably 34 to 37 degrees. Animals can be “aged” in these temperatures for several days or even up to two weeks.
Aging enhances the quality of flavor as well as texture, resulting from a controlled breakdown of connective tissue and removal of moisture from the meat. Leaving the hide on protects the meat from insects and other contaminants.
Bears must be cared for a bit differently, as their hide and fat act as insulative barriers which prevent meat from cooling properly and must be removed soon after harvest. I prefer to quarter my bears and hang them in a neighbor’s walk-in cooler for several days.
A walk-in cooler is a luxury, but if warm temperatures prevent proper aging outside, animals can be quartered and aged in a refrigerator on a low setting or even a cooler, with the quarters and meat placed over blocks of ice. Just make sure the meat does not come in contact with water from the ice inside the cooler.
After the animal is properly cooled and aged, it may be butchered as desired in your preferred method. Care should be taken during this time to ensure the meat is safe and clean.
Butchering should be done in a very clean environment with clean instruments. It should take place in a cool area, which will prevent the meat from spoilage while it waits to be packaged and frozen.
Meat should then be properly packaged, preferably in vacuum-sealed bags, which remove nearly all the air from around the meat. That ensures minimal freezer burn and lengthens its shelf life. As soon as it’s packaged, meat should be placed into the freezer without delay.
Hunting offers us many things: Recreation, conservation, sport, fresh air, time with family and friends, satisfies a primal need within us and fulfills a natural drive and desire to provide food and ensure survival.
Sure, there’s the occasional animal we deem a “trophy” and put on the wall, but the real trophy will always be high-quality, delicious, healthy meat. From the second the trigger is pulled, proper care must be taken to ensure we get the most out of the animal we harvest and utilize it to its fullest potential.
Best of luck to all this season. Be still, be quiet and be patient. Remember why we hunt and do it right.

title: ‘Atlas Shrugged’? No thanks.
text:
A recent letter asks readers to “Please stop vilifying the rich” (Oct. 4). And to read Ayn Rand’s “Atlas Shrugged.” This “Billionaire’s Bible” urges peasants to allow the rich to run the world without rules.

title: Luigi Mangione’s cousin wins election in Baltimore
text:
BALTIMORE, Md. (Gray News) - Republican Nino Mangione won the Baltimore County Council’s District 5 seat on Tuesday, defeating Democrat Shawn McIntosh. Nino Mangione campaigned on promises to crack down on violent crime and support law enforcement.
Family connection
Nino Mangione is a cousin of Luigi Mangione, who pleaded guilty in August in connection with the 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.
Nino Mangione and Luigi Mangione share a grandfather, Nick Mangione Sr., who built a business empire in the Baltimore area.
Statement after arrest
After Luigi Mangione’s arrest, Nino Mangione released a statement.
“Our family is shocked and devastated by Luigi’s arrest,” he said. “We offer our prayers to the family of Brian Thompson, and we ask people to pray for all involved.”
Council service
Nino Mangione has held a Baltimore County Council seat in District 3 since June 1. He was appointed to replace a council member who was resigning.

title: Late week storm may bring rain or wet snow to Maine
text:
Late week storm may bring rain or wet snow to Maine
A November gale may bring the first flakes for some later this week
Late week storm may bring rain or wet snow to Maine
A November gale may bring the first flakes for some later this week
Maine's Total Weather is tracking a storm that could arrive in Maine at the end of the week or this weekend (November 13-14).
A colder air mass is expected to move into Maine this week, with Friday highs possibly limited to the 30s and low 40s. Higher-level temperatures will also be dropping, opening the door for snow to develop.
The big question is where the storm tracks. A path near or over Maine would bring in warmer air, increasing the chance for rain. A track farther south of the state would put snow in play, while a storm that tracks too far south could leave us with little or no precipitation.
It's still too early to determine what, if anything, will fall across Maine. The forecast should become clearer during the week. We'll be watching closely and keeping you updated!

title: Kyle Larson wins 2nd consecutive Cup Series title, becomes the 11th NASCAR driver with 3
text:
HOMESTEAD, Fla. (AP) — With the NASCAR Cup Series championship flag flying from a car window, Kyle Larson’s youngest child stood atop the No. 5 Chevrolet and signaled to everyone what had been known for hours.
Three-year-old Cooper held up a single finger.
Yep, his dad was No. 1 again.
Larson clinched his third Cup Series title in six years early in the 400-mile season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway on Sunday. He became NASCAR’s first back-to-back champion since Jimmie Johnson in 2010; Johnson won five in a row beginning in 2006. Both of them accomplished the feat at powerhouse Hendrick Motorsports.
The 34-year-old Larson also became the 11th driver in NASCAR history with three Cup titles, joining a list that includes seven-time champs Richard Petty, Dale Earnhardt and Johnson. Jeff Gordon has four. Lee Petty, David Pearson, Cale Yarborough, Darrell Waltrip, Tony Stewart and Joey Logano have three.
“He’s going to pass me,” said Gordon, the vice chairman at Hendrick. “I’ve already come to that conclusion. Kind of knew that when he was coming to Hendrick Motorsports. He’s special.”
Ryan Blaney won the season finale, which returned to South Florida for the first time since 2019. The championship event had perfect weather and a star-studded lineup of celebrities, including Johnson, singers Jason Derulo and Cole Swindell, WNBA star Sophie Cunningham and golfer John Daly. Racing legend Mario Andretti also tapped a good luck message for Larson.
They were treated to a drama-filled ending. Blaney passed Tyler Reddick of 23XI Racing with a little more than a lap to go and with NBA legend Michael Jordan watching from pit road. Blaney held a brief celebration in victory lane before clearing the way for Larson.
“Obviously he’s incredibly talented,” Blaney said of Larson. “His natural, God-given talent is off the charts. He is very deserving to win his third championship.”
Reddick finished second, followed by William Byron, Christopher Bell, Bubba Wallace and Denny Hamlin.
The real party awaited Larson, who finished 12th. He immediately stopped near the start-finish line for a smoky burnout and then exchanged high-fives and hugs with his team, his wife and his kids. He climbed atop his car with all three children.
Owen, 11, grabbed the flag and started waving it through the air. Audrey, 8, picked up a handful of confetti and started throwing it at her brothers. Cooper posed for pictures before eventually sliding down the windshield and into a pile of confetti.
It was a family affair for sure.
Larson was the overwhelming favorite to hoist the Bill France Cup in Homestead long before the green flag dropped.
He entered the weekend with a 67-point lead over Bell and needed only nine points to wrap up the title. He got one point for starting the race and seven more by finishing fourth in the opening stage. But because Bell didn’t win the opening stage, he had no path to catch Larson the rest of the day.
Larson responded to crew chief Cliff Daniels dropping the news over the radio by saying, “That was anticlimactic.”
Larson scraped the wall early in the second stage, cut a tire and never challenged for the lead.
“Got the word that we had clinched it, and I started driving like an idiot,” Larson said. “I’m more mad at myself.”
Nonetheless, Larson put himself in position for the title with a historic postseason, dubbed NASCAR’s Chase for the championship. He won three times in the 10 playoff events and finished in the top 10 in eight of them.
“They deserve everything, the spoils of victory,” Hamlin said. “They performed absolutely incredible during these last 10 races.”
Larson enjoyed a similar finish while winning it all in 2021, his first season at Hendrick. He won four of the last five races. His second title came in stunning fashion last year at Phoenix. He took advantage of a late caution and leaped sentimental favorite Hamlin on pit road with two laps to go.
Larson’s latest one was far less shocking. Securing the title was so much of a slam dunk that Larson was the only Cup driver invited to NASCAR’s championship media day Thursday and it led to a weeklong conversation about his position in motorsports history.
Larson no doubt belongs in the same conversation as Parnelli Jones, Mario Andretti, A.J. Foyt and Tony Stewart — guys who gained recognition for winning across varying racing series.
Larson raced twice at the Indy 500 and has won the Rolex 24 at Daytona, three Chili Bowls and four Knoxville Nationals.
“I think he’s got to be looked at as one of the all-time greats,” said Hendrick, who won his 16th Cup championship.
Added Gordon: “It’s hard to pick the most impressive thing that he does because he gets in an IndyCar, he goes fast, Sprint car. ... That’s rare air, very rare. There’s just so few guys that are capable of doing that.”

title: Wisdom Lady Pioneers Make History With First State Soccer Championship
text:
Wisdom Girls Make History With First State Soccer Title as Five County Teams Finish Championship Saturday
Five Aroostook County soccer teams entered Saturday with state championships on the line, and one made school history.
The Wisdom Lady Pioneers rallied from a halftime deficit to defeat Bangor Christian 3-1 in Presque Isle, capturing the program's first girls soccer state championship and bringing a Gold Ball home to St. Agatha.
It was a fitting finish to a remarkable postseason for the St. John Valley, which had five teams representing three schools in Saturday's state championship games.
Fort Kent's boys and girls, Madawaska's boys and Wisdom's boys all finished as state runners-up, bringing an end to seasons that included Northern Maine regional championships.
Here's how Championship Saturday unfolded for the County.
Girls Soccer
Eight-Player: Wisdom Makes History With First State Championship
Wisdom 3, Bangor Christian 1
For the Wisdom Lady Pioneers, Saturday was about more than winning one final game.
It was about making history.
After previous state championship appearances in 1997, 2021 and 2025, Wisdom finally brought home its first girls soccer Gold Ball, defeating Bangor Christian 3-1 in the Eight-Player state championship at Skyway Elementary School in Presque Isle.
And the Lady Pioneers had to come from behind to do it.
Bangor Christian struck first when Rivers Bradford scored with 16:45 remaining in the opening half, giving the Patriots a 1-0 advantage that held through halftime.
Wisdom needed a response, and Emma Soucy provided it.
With 18:25 remaining in regulation, Soucy sent a long free kick toward the Bangor Christian goal. The ball bounced inside the penalty area and found its way into the net, tying the game at 1-1.
Then Ellie Cyr took over.
With fewer than 11 minutes remaining, Cyr converted a free kick from just outside the penalty area to give Wisdom its first lead of the afternoon.
And with 1:13 left, Cyr scored again, sending the ball into an open net to put the finishing touches on a 3-1 victory.
Wisdom goalkeeper Mikayl Michaud finished with eight saves.
It was a remarkable turnaround against a Bangor Christian team that had defeated Wisdom twice during the regular season and beaten the Lady Pioneers 3-0 in last year's state championship.
The victory also ended a long wait for the program.
Wisdom had previously reached the girls state championship game in 1997 and again in 2021, when the Lady Pioneers fell to North Yarmouth Academy 3-0 in the Class D final.
After another runner-up finish in 2025, the Lady Pioneers returned determined to finish the job.
They earned their opportunity with an impressive Northern Maine tournament run, shutting out previously unbeaten Sumner 5-0 in the semifinals before defeating top-seeded Dexter 3-1 in the regional championship.
Cyr scored all three goals against Dexter, then added two more in Saturday's state final.
For a team whose huddles have ended with the familiar chant of “1, 2, 3, FAMILY,” Saturday provided another word worth celebrating.
Champions.
And for the first time in program history, the Wisdom Lady Pioneers can call themselves state soccer champions.
Class C: Maranacook Defeats Fort Kent for State Championship
Maranacook 2, Fort Kent 0
Fort Kent's girls returned to the Class C state championship after capturing their fourth consecutive Northern Maine regional title.
But Maranacook came away with a 2-0 victory Saturday afternoon at Lewiston High School, winning its second straight Class C championship.
Evelyn Stevenson scored both goals for the Black Bears.
Stevenson opened the scoring just over two minutes into the game, giving Maranacook an early advantage.
Fort Kent continued to battle and increased its offensive pressure in the second half, but Maranacook's defense kept the Lady Warriors off the scoreboard.
Stevenson added the second goal with 9:06 remaining to secure the victory.
Fort Kent finished its season at 14-2-2, another impressive year for a program that has become a consistent presence in Northern Maine championship soccer.
The Lady Warriors earned their fourth consecutive regional title with a 3-0 victory over Orono earlier in the week.
Although Saturday didn't bring the result they wanted, four straight Northern Maine championships are an accomplishment worth celebrating.
Boys Soccer
Class C: Hall-Dale Edges Fort Kent in Defensive Battle
Hall-Dale 1, Fort Kent 0
Fort Kent's boys were involved in one of Saturday's closest state championship games, but a second-half goal proved to be the difference.
Greyson Cary scored with 19:44 remaining in regulation to lift Hall-Dale to a 1-0 victory at Lewiston High School.
Fort Kent goalkeeper Kyle Paradis turned in a strong performance, finishing with seven saves, including several important stops in the opening half.
The Warriors had opportunities of their own, but Hall-Dale goalkeeper Landon Gilbert preserved the shutout with three saves.
The Bulldogs captured their third consecutive Class C state championship, with all three title-game victories coming by 1-0 scores.
Fort Kent had earned its spot in Saturday's final with a dramatic 2-1 overtime victory over Orono in the Northern Maine championship, with Dominic Cyr scoring both goals.
The Warriors finished their season as Class C North champions, joining the Fort Kent girls in representing their school at the state finals.
Class D: Monmouth Takes State Title Over Madawaska
Monmouth 8, Madawaska 0
Madawaska's postseason run ended Saturday at Messalonskee High School, where Monmouth defeated the Owls 8-0 in the Class D boys state championship.
The Owls entered the game following a strong Northern Maine tournament, capped by a 2-0 victory over Fort Fairfield in Wednesday's regional final.
Aiden Gagnon opened the scoring in the 13th minute of that game, Josh Querze added another in the 25th, and Aleck Gendreau recorded the shutout.
Saturday's matchup against Monmouth proved to be a difficult one for Madawaska, but the result doesn't take away from what the Owls accomplished this season.
Madawaska finished as Class D North champion, earning its opportunity to compete for a Gold Ball.
Eight-Player: Telstar Defeats Wisdom in Boys Final
Telstar 4, Wisdom 1
Wisdom's boys were hoping to join the Lady Pioneers as state champions, but Telstar came away with a 4-1 victory in Saturday's Eight-Player championship in Presque Isle.
The Pioneers had battled through a challenging Northern Maine tournament to reach the state final.
Wisdom survived a penalty-kick shootout against Calais in the semifinals before defeating Piscataquis 5-4 for the regional championship.
That victory gave the Pioneers an opportunity to compete for a state title close to home.
Although Telstar took the Gold Ball, Wisdom's boys finished their season as Eight-Player North champions.
A Fall Worth Remembering Across the St. John Valley
Five state championship appearances from three St. John Valley schools is an accomplishment worth recognizing.
Fort Kent sent both its boys and girls teams to the Class C finals, with the Lady Warriors capturing their fourth consecutive Northern Maine championship.
Madawaska brought home the Class D North boys title, while Wisdom swept the Eight-Player North championships.
And on Saturday, Wisdom's girls completed their season with a historic victory.
After coming up short in previous state championship appearances, the Lady Pioneers rallied from a halftime deficit to bring home the program's first girls soccer Gold Ball.
There were plenty of moments worth remembering this fall, from overtime winners and penalty-kick finishes to regional championship celebrations and one final state championship.
Congratulations to all five teams, their coaches, families and communities for representing Aroostook County throughout the postseason.
And a special congratulations to the Wisdom Lady Pioneers, your 2026 Eight-Player girls soccer state champions!
The 2026 MPA Soccer Championships on 101.9 The Rock are proudly presented by Pineland Farms in Mars Hill.

title: Police make arrest in a deadly shooting at Winston-Salem State during homecoming weekend
text:
Authorities on Sunday arrested a man in a shooting during homecoming weekend at Winston-Salem State University in North Carolina that left one person dead and at least one other person injured.
Winston-Salem police said officers who were on campus for homecoming events heard gunshots around 9:45 p.m. Saturday. They found a 19-year-old man with a gunshot wound. They rendered aid but the man died at the scene.
A 22-year-old woman who had what appeared to be a gunshot wound was taken to a hospital, where she was treated and later released.
Assistant Chief Jason Swaim said at a news conference the investigation led to Ziyaire Spinks, 20, who was arrested and being held without bond on charges of murder, assault with a deadly weapon and possession of a firearm on educational property.
According to police, the shooting stemmed from an argument between two groups of people. They confirmed Spinks was not a student at the university.
A second shooting on campus happened less than an hour later, with police responding when they heard shots. In that case, Swaim said two people were injured when gunfire erupted following an altercation.
Authorities said they were investigating to determine if there was any connection between the two shootings. No arrests have been made in the second case.
Chief William Penn, Jr. of the Winston-Salem Police Department vowed during a news conference that authorities will find all of those responsible for the violence at the school.
“It’s important that the blame of these tragic events go to the right people and that’s the folks who committed these acts,” he said, asking people not to point fingers while the investigation is ongoing.
University officials canceled the remainder of homecoming activities Sunday, saying instead that a local church planned to lead a call for prayers in support of the community.
On social media, community members were sharing their condolences and asking for prayers.
Chancellor Bonita J. Brown called the shootings “senseless violence.” In a statement, she assured students, faculty and parents that the campus was secure and that additional law enforcement would remain while the investigation continues.
The school offered counseling for anyone in need.
“We also recognize the concern and anxiety these events have created among our students, parents, families and broader community,” Brown said. “We take our responsibility for campus safety seriously.”
Forsyth County Sheriff Bobby Kimbrough, Jr. echoed the sentiments of the chancellor and other law enforcement officials during the news conference.
“Right now, the community is in need of your prayers. The community is in need of us coming together,” Kimbrough said.
___
Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: PVSC hosts annual used gear “Ski Sale” at Hermon Mountain
text:
HERMON, Maine (WABI) - Winter is coming, and so is ski season!
Before you hit the slopes, be sure to check out your gear.
Those in need of some new pieces are in luck Sunday at Hermon Mountain as they partnered with Penobscot Valley Ski Club to host their annual used gear “ski sale”.
A variety of gently used items were available for sale at a heavy discount, including snowboards, downhill skis, poles, and winter accessories.
Members of PVSC were also at the event to mingle with the skiing community and connect them with local programs.
“You can pick up a pair of skis just that they would be usable for as inexpensive as 20 bucks or something like that. And then poles and boots as well. So, it’s an opportunity to get some equipment, use equipment, some of its pretty good shape. So, it’s a good chance to get a pair that you can, use and try out, and if you really like it, then you can, go up to something more expensive,” said Dan Baumert, President of the Penobscot Valley Ski Club.
Organizers say consignment sales like this help to reduce waste and give skiers a great price on their favorite pieces of gear- while also providing a low-cost option for those looking to try the sport out.
The sale runs from noon to 4 p.m. Sunday.

title: Potato people, this one’s for you: GFFC’s Annual Fundraiser is back
Novel Jazz Septet at the Opera House
text:
An evening with the Novel Jazz Septet is so much more than a musical show. Steeped in the stories and the history surrounding both Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn, the band brings the audience into a time and place that informed some of the most iconic and influential music of the 20th century and helps listeners understand the forces that shaped Ellington’s and Strayhorn’s contributions to the jazz world. The septet will bring their compelling program to the Opera House at Boothbay Harbor on Friday, Aug. 21, at 7:30 p.m. And, the show will be recorded for a new CD, so the enthusiasm and engagement of the room will be captured as an added element of the experience.
Band member Barney Balch finds the experience as mesmerizing today as he did 22 years ago when the group first assembled. “It all started in a performance that we were doing an informal thing, and someone called out an Ellington tune that none of us had ever heard of before. And I said, ‘Sheesh, you know, between the seven of us playing here, there’s about two centuries of collective jazz knowledge, and none of us have ever heard of this tune. I wonder how many tunes Duke Ellington wrote?’ and the answer to that is, thousands.”
Balch’s fascination is sustained by the extraordinary access that he has had to precious, and rarely seen, compositions. “Ellington started writing in the mid-20s and, and he died in ‘74 and he was just writing constantly. So I thought, ‘I wonder where all these are?’ And I found out about what's called the Ellington Archives, at the Smithsonian Museum of American History, where they have the originals, the penciled manuscripts–lead sheets, they're called; there are 400 book boxes of these that had been in a garage someplace, and had sustained some water damage. So that's when they consulted with the Smithsonian, and the Smithsonian said, ‘Well, we'll take it!’” Balch reflects on the momentous experience of being in the presence of archival gems: “The first time I held the penciled copy of Mood Indigo, my hands were shaking. There's nothing like it and it's really fun.”
Balch shares that Strayhorn, who was quite a bit younger than Ellington, and tragically died very young, also composing at that time, and “There are lots of backstories about how those guys met, and our shows basically deal with both the tunes and the stories. There's a story behind every piece and it's my jazz iceberg, I call it. We've been chipping away at this, as I said, for 22 years and haven't even made a dent.”
Asked about how the collaboration process works with the septet, Balch says, “We start by looking through the collection of tunes that we've been thinking of doing. They have to be down ranged from typically being written for 18-piece orchestras, down to seven pieces. So that's a challenge. After we do a first arrangement, we all get together, and it's probably one of the most fun sessions of the year. We play these things, try them out, and then we sit around and say, ‘Geez, you know, this would sound really cool as a samba. And let's pick up the tempo.’ So we're not necessarily reproducing these songs exactly as they were written in 1928 or 1936. We're dusting them off and bringing them up harmonically and rhythmically. And there will be times where we make a change to one of these tunes and we all just go, ‘Whoa!’”
With regard to the storytelling that places this music squarely in its tumultuous history of absent civil rights, Balch says, “There are a lot of stories tied up in that, and I really try to bring both of those out in our shows–the song as well as the backstory. Because it's just so compelling and we have a lot we can learn. There’s a lot the audience can still learn about music; how it has responded to social issues has never been more relevant than right now in so many ways.”
Advance discounted tickets, $20, are available from the box office at 86 Townsend Ave., Boothbay Harbor or by calling 207-633-5159. title: Support the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
There’s a new bill being considered in Congress, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, that deserves support. As we see the climate changing around us — storms strengthening and pollution increasing due to the burning of fossil fuels — we could speed the change to renewables by asking Sens. King and Collins and Reps. Pingree and Golden to support this bill.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) has a reasonable chance of passage if we support it. This bill would expand and improve electrical transmission lines, engage the community early in the environmental approval process and speed up the building of needed electrical infrastructure.
Being a bipartisan bill, no one is entirely happy with it. Thankfully, experts agree it could significantly reduce carbon emissions. There are many energy generation projects on hold because the developers cannot get permission to connect them to the grid. This is the case for both renewable projects and fossil fuel projects, but a majority of such projects are renewable.
Moving to renewables, as well as decreasing the pollution in the air and slowing the warming of our planet, will gradually decrease the cost of electricity in America. The blanket of CO2 surrounding and heating our planet is getting worse daily. We have no time to waste.
Email your legislators and ask them to support BAAJA. Our electricity will be more dependable — and eventually cheaper — if this passes.
Nancy Hasenfus
Brunswick

title: Dad of 20-year-old co-pilot in Florida Learjet crash says her final radio calls showed ‘she’s tough’
text:
(AP) - The father of the 20-year-old co-pilot killed alongside eight others in a Florida Learjet crash said Friday he has repeatedly listened to her final radio transmissions, searching for answers and finding pride in how she handled the crisis.
Allan Filgueiras, a pilot who helped teach Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras to fly, said he marveled at how “she’s tough” even as the plane plunged straight toward the ground Sunday.
“I wanted to be by her side. Inside the plane, to help,” he said at a news conference, often holding back tears.
“She showed me what it is to be a hero,” he said, “because once you see that coming, a lot of the big boys — military or whatever — they can’t handle. And she was the one over there to the last minute fighting.”
Nathalia Filgueiras can first be heard calmly telling air traffic control about ice buildup on the plane as it flew into a thunderstorm. Turbulence tossed it up and down by 700 feet (200 meters), but the situation quickly escalated as the aircraft fell at breathtaking speed. “Declare an emergency 722-Bravo-Delta. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute!” she said.
Her father and aviation safety experts have praised her composure as she called out updates while knowing the plane’s fate was sealed. The captain, 55-year-old Jeff Gregory, is believed to have been at the controls.
“For the family — it’s like having the heart torn from my chest,” Allan Filgueiras said in Spanish. “I have to find a way to go on living.”
Young co-pilot’s family and instructor say she earned her job on merit
The family has challenged online criticism questioning whether she had enough experience to be in the cockpit of a high-performance business jet. She had more than 1,300 hours of experience and completed extensive training to earn her commercial pilot’s license and Learjet certification.
Her father’s attorney, Stuart Grossman, said the news conference aimed to “preserve not just her memory, but her reputation.”
“She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years,” Grossman said, noting there were no immediate plans for any lawsuit.
The National Transportation Safety Board has not yet determined what caused the crash. The Learjet accelerated beyond its design limits as it fell, and pieces of its tail were found miles away from the crash site, which is a deep crater on the edge of a road. Investigators were still searching the area Friday after finding part of an engine a day earlier. The cockpit recorder remains missing.
Allan Filgueiras said he helped teach her how to fly after taking her aloft for the first time at age 12. Once she got a job as a pilot, she told him she couldn’t believe she was getting paid to do something she loved.
“It was her happiest moment, to fly,” he said.
Mentor says her professionalism showed in final calls
Her mentor and instructor, Chris Kirk, said she earned her position through dedication and perseverance by putting in hard work and long hours.
During her Learjet 60 check ride in March, the examiner was so impressed he thought she had more than 5,000 hours of experience — nearly four times the amount of flight time she had logged.
Kirk said her professionalism was evident in those final radio transmissions, which gave the NTSB important information. Many members of the military special forces who Kirk worked with probably couldn’t keep their wits in a similar situation.
“This was an incredible human being,” Kirk said, “who did a job that very few people would have been able to do under a duress that’s unimaginable.”
Retired airline pilot John Cox said earlier this week that his career began similarly to Nathalia Filgueiras’, as he started flying professionally at age 19. He said she had done well to earn a Learjet co-pilot’s seat.
“To be in the right seat of a Lear 60, she had to impress somebody, because that’s a good ride. I mean, that’s great. I know she loved it,” said Cox, who now runs Safety Operating Systems, an aviation consulting company.
The other crash victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children, relatives said. The family’s nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed. The other two victims were Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, who owned the Arca Boutique Hotel in Honduras.

title: Drake Maye throws 3 interceptions as Patriots get blasted by Packers
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — If Jordan Love has played a better game than he did on Sunday, he can’t remember it.
“It’s definitely up there. It felt great,” the Packers quarterback said.
Because of it, Green Bay looks like a team capable of staying in the mix in the formidable NFC North.
Love threw for 372 yards and three touchdowns and ran for a score, and the Packers scored 21 points off four New England Patriots turnovers to roll to a 45-27 win.
Green Bay’s receivers had a huge day, with Christian Watson catching seven passes for 171 yards and a TD and Matthew Golden finishing with 10 catches for 164 yards and a score. Kaleb Johnson ran for a touchdown and Savion Williams had a TD catch as Green Bay finished with 478 total yards.
“It’s crazy, because I know there’s probably a lot more in there,” Golden said. “We’ve still got so many more plays out there to make.”
The Packers hadn’t scored 45 or more points and had 450 or more yards since Nov. 11, 1962 at Philadelphia.
“We got our (butts) kicked. There’s no two ways around it,” Patriots coach Mike Vrabel said.
Late in the game, “MVP!” chants for Love could be heard from visiting Packers fans.
“It’s a surreal feeling,” Love said.
Love completed three passes of at least 43 yards, and seven of 28 or more.
“Those are low-percentage throws in theory, but he’s making them look high-percentage,” Packers coach Matt LeFleur said. “They’re right on the money.”
Packers safety Xavier McKinney had a pair of interceptions and Evan Williams also had a pick.
Green Bay entered the day last in the NFL in rushing, averaging 60.6 yards per game, but finished with 129 yards on the ground.
The Packers (6-3) got plenty of help from the Patriots (5-4) as they built a 24-7 lead en route to their fifth win in six games.
New England’s Drake Maye took a step backward after weeks of steady play, throwing three interceptions while completing 21 of 38 passes for 299 yards and three touchdowns. Maye had thrown just one pick in his previous four games. He’s now tied with Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert with an NFL-worst 11 INTs.
“We haven’t had a clean, a turnover-free game yet,” Maye said. “It’s starting with me. It’s one of the biggest differences between winning and losing football games.”
The Patriots set a franchise record for points allowed at Gillette Stadium, which opened in 2002. New England hadn’t given up 45 points in the regular season since a 45-7 loss to the New York Jets on Sept. 26, 1993.
Maye made questionable decisions on all three of his turnovers in the first half. Two of them set up Packers touchdowns. Rhamondre Stevenson, Efton Chism and Mack Hollins all had TD catches for the Patriots. Stevenson also had a fumble that set up Watson’s score before leaving with a knee injury late third quarter.
DeMario Douglas caught five passes for 102 yards.
The Packers led 24-14 at halftime, then drove down the field on the opening possession of the second half. Love punctuated the seven-play, 70-yard drive with a 10-yard TD pass to Williams.
New England rookie Karon Prunty was in coverage on the score after Carlton Davis III suffered a knee injury in the second quarter.
Gillette Stadium was full of energy before the game as the Patriots celebrated members of their 2016 team — including an appearance by Tom Brady in the Fox broadcast booth — to commemorate the 10th anniversary of their record comeback win over the Atlanta Falcons in Super Bowl 51.
It quickly dissipated after the Patriots opened with a penalty, followed on the next play by Maye throwing the ball into traffic and being intercepted by McKinney at the New England 14.
Two plays later, Love easily found the end zone on a scramble and the Packers jumped in front 7-0.
Green Bay never trailed.
Injuries
Packers: Linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper left early in the first quarter with a chest injury. Running back Josh Jacobs left later in the quarter with a broken finger, LaFleur said. … Wide receiver Bo Melton was evaluated for a concussion.
Patriots: Left guard Ben Brown (knee) limped off a few plays after Davis late in the second quarter. … Special teamer Brenden Schooler exited with a hamstring injury. … Left tackle Will Campbell walked off with a knee injury in the fourth quarter.
Packers’ receiving duo has rare achievement
Watson and Golden became the first Packers teammates to have 150 or more receiving yards and a touchdown catch since Don Hutson and Andy Uram did it in 1942.
Up next
Packers: Host Minnesota next Sunday.
Patriots: Travel to Germany to play Detroit next Sunday in Munich.

title: Susan Collins’ loss carries a particular sadness
text:
Rev. Steve Edington is minister emeritus of the Unitarian Universalist Church of Nashua, New Hampshire, and a former minister of the First Universalist Church of Rockland.
I began my career in the Unitarian Universalist parish ministry in 1979 when I was called to serve the congregation at the First Universalist Church of Rockland, Maine.
The chair of the search committee was State Sen. Samuel W. Collins, a prominent member of that church. He was also the Republican majority leader of the Maine State Senate. Collins went on to become an associate justice on the Maine State Supreme Court.
Sam Collins, who passed away in 2012, was one of the most decent and honorable politicians —and human beings — I have known. Despite being a longtime Democrat, I was pleased to vote for him when he ran for, and won, reelection in 1982. Although he and I did not always see eye to eye on various issues, his bedrock integrity gained him my vote.
I had concluded my ministry in Rockland and moved on to another ministerial assignment when Sam’s niece, the now departing U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, began her political career.
The last time I saw Sam was when I returned to Rockland to take part in a memorial service at the Universalist Church. Susan had just been elected to her first term in the United States Senate. In the brief conversation we had, Sam spoke of how proud he was of his niece, Sen. Susan Collins.
I thought on these things as I watched Maine’s U.S. Senator-elect, Troy Jackson, celebrate his victory over Collins this past election night. I was pleased with Troy Jackson’s win. Had I been a resident of Maine (for now, I live in New Hampshire), Jackson would have had my vote.
At the same time, I could not help but feel sadness for Susan Collins.
She comes from a well-established Yankee Republican family of good and honorable people. She did much good for the people of Maine in her 30-year Senate career, often working across the aisle for legislation she felt served the greater common good and going beyond partisan politics. I believe she entered the Senate with the idea of being Maine’s next Sen. Margaret Chase Smith.
Many years in, Collins found herself engulfed in the age of Donald Trump.
When Trump became the Republican presidential nominee in the summer of 2016, Sen. Collins — by then in her fourth term in the Senate — announced that she would not support him, saying she felt he lacked the character and integrity to hold the office of president.
During Trump’s first, and now second, terms as president, Collins did vote to oppose several of his major initiatives, including Trump’s effort to overturn the Affordable Care Act and his so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
Following Trump’s second impeachment in the wake of the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection, an insurrection he instigated, Collins voted to convict and remove the president from office.
But when it came to her dealings with Trump, Sen. Collins also often found herself playing two ends against the middle. Analysis tells us that she reliably voted in line with his initiatives and appointments.
Perhaps Collins’ most telling move in this regard was her casting her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court. Kavanaugh, in turn, cast the deciding vote to overturn the 1973 Roe v. Wade decision that had established a constitutional right to abortion.
It was Collins’ approach/avoid dance with the Trump presidency that finally caught up to her in last week’s midterm election.
Collins had arguably managed to bring herself around to accommodating Trump more often than she did standing up to him. Most of the senator’s moves to oppose him were taken when she knew Trump would still get the outcome he wanted, allowing her to demonstrate a kind of independence while remaining in Trump’s good graces.
I daresay this was the kind of game Sen. Margaret Chase Smith never would have played, whatever the political consequences. At this point, though, it no longer matters.
Ms. Collins has had her Senate career. She did good in numerous ways, while making decisions that finally cost her the office she held for three decades.
A few months from now, my wife and I will once again become residents of Maine when we move to Kennebunk to be near our son, daughter-in-law and two granddaughters. I look forward to having Troy Jackson and Angus King as my United States senators.
And I wish Susan Collins the best, wherever her life may take her from here.

title: Gorham artists, shoppers kick off holiday season at local maker’s market
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GORHAM – Sydney Hobart watched potential customers scan her bright red greeting cards at the Cherry Hill Place Maker’s Market on Sunday. They chuckled, reading the quippy, festive quotes on the front.
“Three wise men? Be serious,” one read. Next to it, “Peace on Earth? Let’s start with the family and see how it goes.”
Hobart, who owns a small craft business called Salty Handmade Goods, was one of a few dozen vendors selling goods at the market as hundreds of visitors got an early jump on their holiday shopping.
Hosted by Cherry Hill Place and local market coordinator, PL&H Makers, the event boasted more than 40 local vendors, food trucks and a bar to keep shoppers warm as the holiday chill sets in. Until Dec. 20, a rotating cast of local artists will sell their wares every Sunday, including a two-day event after Thanksgiving.
A live musician sat in the corner, serenading shoppers in the market’s second weekend ever as they perused the booths. Not all her fellow vendors have leaned into the holiday season quite yet, but Hobart said getting an early start has already made her a big hit in her second year selling her crochet goods.
“This is the first time I’ve done cards and ornaments and stickers, and it really has changed my business. “I’m just having so much fun with it.” Hobart said, pointing to a small pink Christmas tree bearing ornaments filled with scrap yarn. Those, and her squishy crochet pickles, were her bestsellers on Sunday.
Some shoppers visited the market just to browse, but Standish resident Christine Van Voorhis said she normally hits local craft fairs to shop for gifts. She was pleased to have found a few good ones already: a pair of earrings and a couple of Hobart’s cards. She also enjoys maker’s markets as an opportunity to support local artists.
“It’s just all about the community and supporting everybody. And I’m really excited,” Van Voorhis said of her locally made holiday gift finds.
The event’s organizer, Samantha Dyer, is also excited so many people are turning out to support local business owners. In the market’s first weekend, nearly 2,000 visitors spent their Sundays exploring the venue. Some stood in a line wrapped around the entire building waiting to get in.
Dyer says that enthusiasm will only ramp up as the holidays approach. Soon, the venue will be decked out with festive decorations, and the rotary club will be selling Christmas trees.
Artist Karen Dubbs Fisher said by 11:30, just an hour and a half into the market, she’d already sold a couple dozen of her colorful, Maine-themed cards and calendars.
“At one time I got so busy that I lost my money bag,” she laughed, tucking a $5 bill into a bag with the rest of her sales. She’s excited to be even busier as the season picks up.

title: After historic rout, Maine Republicans chart course out of the political wilderness
text:
Maine Republicans were largely repudiated up and down the ballot on Tuesday.
The party’s figurehead, Sen. Susan Collins, lost her U.S. Senate seat after 30 years. Their gubernatorial candidate, Bobby Charles, earned only 37% of the vote. And they lost seats in both the state Senate and House of Representatives, after coming tantalizingly close to winning the lower chamber two years ago.
Republicans now have the smallest state Senate caucus (at 11 members) since 1984 and the smallest House caucus (at 61 members) since 2018. That means state Democrats will maintain a governing trifecta it’s held since 2018.
The party’s lone bright spot, former Gov. Paul LePage’s victory in the 2nd District congressional race, came via a razor-thin margin in an overwhelmingly Republican-leaning area.
The electoral disaster has left Maine Republicans trying to decide whether it was a one-off national wave, or a signal that the party needs to fundamentally recalibrate its approach to certain issues.
Some believe that Republicans up and down the ballot were simply the victims of a nationalized election cycle, one that produced a so-called “blue tsunami” in opposition to President Donald Trump.
But others believe the party needs new leadership and a fundamental realignment, one that steers clear of xenophobia and culture wars and focuses more on the economic and pocketbook issues that voters said in poll after poll was their top concern.
“The Republicans are going to be in the wilderness until they drop this culture war stuff and start understanding that they need to acquire power for the right reasons: to make economic change in Maine, to make life less hard for Mainers,” said Lance Dutson, a Republican consultant and former Collins staffer. “I don’t foresee the forces at play in the current Republican Party as having any clue that that’s the case for quite a long time.”
When asked in an interview Friday if Republicans need to change their priorities, Maine GOP Chairman James Deyermond focused on what he viewed as positive results for the party.
Deyermond hailed LePage’s 2nd District win, observing that he was the only Republican in the country to reclaim a Democratic-held seat in Congress without being helped by redistricting. And he noted that the party did not see as big of a backlash at the state level as other states.
“We helped save Maine from the calamity that happened to the rest of the country,” Deyermond said. “We stuck with it, and I think we ran a good program.”
But the election results showed it was likely the moderate Collins who helped her party stave off total annihilation here. While LePage crawled to victory in his district, Collins won the area by double digits. At a time when her party has been defined by Trump, Collins, aided by tens of millions in outside spending, proved once again more popular with voters than the president.
Republican state legislative leaders did not respond to interview requests on Thursday. Incoming Republican lawmakers chose Sen. Trey Stewart, R-Presque Isle, and Rep. Kenneth Fredette, R-Newport, to lead their respective chambers’ minorities on Friday.
But Rep. Amy Arata, a former assistant House Republican leader from New Gloucester who is termed out office, said in a Facebook post that her party needs to be more tolerant of people with differing viewpoints. She went on to criticize Trump’s broad, aggressive — and at at times violent — crackdown on immigrants and his punitive tariffs.
Arata lamented that “at least a dozen” of her colleagues were “swept away in a blue wave caused by a president who has some very unpopular policies, along with some good ones.”
“My colleagues didn’t do anything wrong and they didn’t deserve to lose,” Arata wrote. “We need to be free to disagree with (Trump) when he’s wrong, just as we celebrate when he’s right. Otherwise, we will continue to lose wonderful Republican leaders in our state.”
UNABLE TO SURVIVE THE WAVE?
Former state Rep. Laurel Libby, who runs a conservative nonprofit and super PAC, made a national name for herself by opposing transgender athletes in girls’ sports. She believes that Maine Republicans fell victim to a national backlash from Trump not keeping his campaign promises to fix the economy.
“This was not a Maine-specific issue,” Libby said in an 18-minute Facebook video posted Thursday. “This was a blue wave — a blue tsunami — around the country.”
But Republicans would be making a mistake to attribute the losses to Trump alone, said Nicholas Jacobs, a political science professor at Colby College who has studied rural voters.
“I’d be cautious about assuming their problems disappear when Trump leaves office,” Jacobs said. “The party has increasingly become a Trump party in a state that isn’t a Trump state. And that’s part of a much larger national trend in which state and local politics have become almost indistinguishable from national partisan politics.”
Perhaps no Maine Republican embodied the embrace of Trump as did Charles, who won the primary against more moderate and mainstream opponents by leaning into the anti-immigrant and culture war rhetoric. Early in the race, the Leeds lawyer openly embraced Trump, at one point inviting federal agents to patrol polling locations.
This Trumpification has been fueled by the conservative media ecosystem in the state, led by the Maine Wire website, which has largely trained its fire on nonwhite Mainers alleged of fraud or wrongdoing. The Maine Wire is the media arm of the conservative Maine Policy Institute.
“They amplify a hard-right message,” Kevin Raye, a former chief of staff for former Republican Sen. Olympia Snowe, said of the Maine Wire. “And it resonates with the hardcore base. But the base is shrinking and that amplification doesn’t resonate well with the broader electorate.”
Raye, who was the state Senate president from 2010 to 2012, said he disenrolled from the Republican Party back in 2024 when Trump locked up the presidential nomination for the third straight cycle.
“I think that the co-opting of the party by Donald Trump and the MAGA movement have basically driven the party into virtual extinction in New England,” he said.
LIFE WITHOUT COLLINS
Over the last decade, the rightward shift squeezed Collins into an untenable position. To many in her own party, she was never loyal enough to Trump. And to her opponents, she was never doing enough to stand up to him.
“Everybody ignores the fact that I voted to convict him in the second impeachment trial,” a candid Collins told The New York Times after her defeat this week. “What bigger break could there be? It is never enough. I want results and they want angry rhetoric.”
But Collins’ defeat means more than losing a powerful seat in the U.S. Senate in a Democratic-leaning state. The party is also losing a key cog in its fundraising and organizing machine.
“Many people don’t realize the amount that the Collins team does for the Republican Party here in Maine,” Lauren LePage, a GOP strategist and daughter of Paul LePage, said in a social media post. “They’re quiet, they don’t seek credit for it, but they have given enormous amounts of resources to the party. This loss is devastating for our party, but more importantly, for the people of Maine.”
Maine Republicans also have lost their best statewide candidate. And it’s difficult to imagine who will take up the mantle next. Since 2018, Collins was the only Republican member of Congress from Maine.
With Collins not on the ballot, the party has essentially punted statewide races in recent years. Republicans fielded a former state party chairwoman against Sen. Angus King, the independent who caucuses with the Democrats, in 2024. But she got little financial support and lost in a rout. Charles, the Republican who ran for governor this cycle, also lost in a blowout after getting no help from national Republicans, who saw the writing on the wall.
Even Libby, the rising star who was not on the ballot Tuesday, saw her former legislative district flip blue.
THE PATH FORWARD
Lauren LePage said she hopes — and expects — the national and state parties will take a close look at what went wrong.
Dutson, the Republican consultant, pointed to the 2010 cycle as a model path forward. That year, Dutson contended, Republicans focused on pocketbook issues and largely avoided culture wars. And as a result, Republicans won the Blaine House and majorities in both chambers of the state Legislature.
But Duston said Paul LePage, who won with only 38% of the vote in a three-way race, “squandered” that coalition by focusing on culture war issues once elected — and on fighting with leaders and members of his own party.
LePage made national headlines when he told the NAACP to “kiss my butt” when he refused to attend a Martin Luther King Day event. He also removed a pro-labor mural from a state office and frequently warred with the Legislature and press corps.
The Republican consultant said he doesn’t expect the party to change in the near-term, because lawmakers in more competitive districts are the ones getting swept out of office, while those in safe, deep-red districts are getting reelected.
“The extremists survive, so it’s extra hard for the party to heal itself,” Dutson said.
Deyermond said he plans to seek reelection as the party chairman when Republicans hold elections in early January. He said his party will hold Democrats accountable, especially as they contend with a $1.3 billion structural budget deficit.
“We’re going to hold the Democrats’ feet to the fire,” Deyermond said. “They’re going to be here in two years. President Trump won’t be on the ballot in two years, so they’re going to have to find another bogeyman to scare Maine voters.”

title: Coast to coast, part VI: Santa Monica, Las Vegas, Moab to Dodge City
text:
Finishing our Route 66 adventure proved to be almost anti-climactic. After leaving Needles and Barstow, California, on Route 66, we were submersed in all of the bad of California — the unrelenting traffic, the smog, the high prices (on everything) and a homeless issue that erases much of what is good, especially surrounding Santa Monica Pier and the end of Route 66. At least the Griffith Observatory was informative — but packed.
So, it’s on to Vegas, Utah and points east, quickly.
Our weather has been spectacular, with only four days of intermittent rain. Yet, 100-degree temps in Vegas and at Hoover Dam, where Ellsworth residents Brian Saunders and wife picked us out of the crowd, wrecked our camper’s refrigerator and forced us to take some R&R in the Oasis RV park pool.
Our Super Duty didn’t notice the heat as it climbed I-15 north to Mesquite, Arizona, where the highway swiftly rises up from the high plains through the mountain pass for the Virgin River. Steep walls and deep canyons on this winding path are the first clue to future driving in Utah.
Forced to give up our Zion National Park plans due to restrictions and trail closures, we headed out Route 14 from Cedar City to Bryce Canyon National Park. This scenic road delivers fascinating views on a twisting, climbing tarmac that often lacks guardrails— an apparent Utah DOT philosophy. We crest The Saddle at 9,900 feet into the high plains, before descending to Route 89 and then onto Scenic Route 12 — a veritable gem of a highway — just before Bryce.
Always a spiritual visit, Bryce has been “found” — it was much too crowded from our previous visit. With more trail closures, the masses were funneled onto the same trails, like a conga line climbing the Beehive in Acadia. We diverted to paths less traveled, meeting another couple from New Hampshire, with roots in New Sweden, Maine, and relatives in Ellsworth. America is very grand and very small at the same time.
Day 24 we leave Bryce Valley RV Ranch — one of our nicer, more peaceful, cleaner camping locations — for more of Route 12 East. The road does not disappoint with you able to see yourself coming and going on some tight 180-degree turns, plus magical vistas that we don’t have in the east. A hike up the Escalante River, crossing it six times, takes us to one of Utah’s highest arches, a wonderful climax to another great day.
Again, the Super Duty proves an excellent chaperone. Its numerous features lending themselves to comfort and convenience, while the Powerstroke engine delivers seamless power to pull not only the camper, but the long grades and steep elevations as we go up and down heading past Tropic, Fruita, Torrey and other old Mormon towns.
Moab is the prize now, an outdoor recreation mecca un-paralleled in the region. If you can think of doing it outdoors, Moab provides the opportunities. Mountain biking, dirt biking, UTVs/ATVs, Jeep rentals, rafting, skydiving, back-country hiking and camping — it’s all here in Moab.
Our most expensive RV park of the trip, at $115 a night, reflects Moab’s popularity. And we were ten miles from town.
Enticed by the visuals and the remote roads in Canyonlands NP, we rent side-by-side Can-Am UTVs in Moab for a 60-mile adventure through Meander Canyon (aptly named) down the Colorado River and across the face of some mesas and buttes on a trail no more than two-tracks wide across some cliff faces, with more than a thousand feet down on the other. Heart-pumping fun — in the heat and the dust, with lots of other adventurers.
Arches National Park was equally stimulating, on a different level. Again, our Ford mingled with the masses, its dually body sometimes making parking snug, but never compromising our mission. I wouldn’t have swapped it for anything else.
Leaving Moab, one of the most engaging and popular parts of our whole trip, provided another driving miracle; Utah’s Scenic #128 Byway. Winding along with the Colorado River north towards Colorado, we trace the walls of massive canyons for over 15 miles, reveling in the constant beauty. A wide valley along the way is populated with ranches, horse farms, VRBOs and even spas. Hiking trails to arches and buttes abound. Moab is worth a week or\ two all by itself.
After a stint on I-70, we exit the highway for Colorado Route 50, connecting to the old Santa Fe Trail — the original commercial pathway across the west from Missouri to then-Spanish-controlled Santa Fe. After crossing the Rockies and the Continental Divide (11,312-feet) at Monarch Pass, a twisting route with huge drop-offs — and NO guardrails — the Ford doesn’t miss a beat descending the other side with its excellent dynamic cruise engaged and the diesel engine providing the braking.
Keeping track at RV parks and other work locations, the Ford Super Duty dominates pulling RVs and work fleets, easily by more than two to one out west. It’s a pattern that emerged in Illinois.
Day 29 finds us along the Arkansas River and on the rural Santa Fe Trail headed east, well over 5,000 miles into our journey. The Plains of Kansas are ahead, with more history and real America.
Next up: The final leg of our journey.

title: Technology from South Korea is helping Maine kelp farmers be more efficient
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Technology from South Korea is helping Maine kelp farmers be more efficient
The Aquaculture Research Institute says this is likely the only machine of its kind in the U.S.
Technology from South Korea is helping Maine kelp farmers be more efficient
The Aquaculture Research Institute says this is likely the only machine of its kind in the U.S.
While the kelp industry is still young in Maine, in other parts of the world it's been farmed on a large-scale for years. Staff at the University of Maine's Aquaculture Research Institute say the technology they use to get it done is unlike anything here in the U.S.
In order to grow kelp, kelp seed is painted onto several feet of string. That string is then tightly wrapped around rope that will eventually be put underwater. Most farmers in Maine do this process manually, by hand.
"Which takes a lot of people and time and boats and fuel and that's all really expensive," said Adam St. Gelais, an Aquaculture Innovation Specialist at the Aquaculture Research Institute.
About two years ago, they acquired a new piece of machinery from South Korea. It doesn't have an official name, but some of the staff endearingly call it the "Korean Unicorn," thanks to it's unicorn-like shape.
The machine is able to take kelp-covered string, and rapidly tie it around the rope it needs to grow on.
"To our knowledge, it's the only one of these machines that's ever left the country," said St. Gelais.
While it costs a couple thousand dollars to buy outright, the real cost comes from shipping it over. For that reason, it's still not realistic for Maine's smaller kelp operations to use, but the Aquaculture Research Institute wanted to test out how effective it is with local farmers.
On Friday afternoon, the team brought it to a boat launch near Ken Sparta's farm. Sparta harvests kelp and oysters, and is also the owner of the Freeport Oyster Bar. For about an hour, they were able to create more than 2,000 feet of grow lines before even stepping on a boat.
Then, they took the grow lines out on the water. The rope gets laid into the water, held down by anchors. Buoys help keep it floating closer to the surface. The entire line is pulled tight so that there are long horizontal lines of growing seaweed.
The Aquaculture Research Institute hopes that by demonstrating its success, it will begin to see more of the technology here.
"The intention really is to make seaweed farming more efficient for growers in Maine," said St. Gelais.

title: Building owned by Saudi oil giant damaged in missile attack on Riyadh's financial district
text:
Building owned by Saudi oil giant damaged in missile attack on Riyadh’s financial district
A building belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the financial district in the capital Riyadh has been damaged in a missile attack.
The strike in King Abdullah Financial District was reported after Saudi Civil Defense issued an early-warning alert of a potential threat to the city.
Video circulating on social media and verified by CNN shows damage to upper floors of the Aramco building, with windows seen blown out. But Saudi authorities said the impact was minimal.
"An administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was subjected to an attempted attack" on Sunday, according to the official Saudi news agency, citing a source at the Saudi Energy Ministry.
Related video: Russian missile strikes on former Ukraine school
"The incident resulted in falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building, with no injuries or fatalities reported," the agency reported.
However, one witness said they saw ambulances heading to the area.
CNN has reached out to the Information Ministry by email for further details.
The Houthis, who have fired missiles and drones towards multiple targets across Saudi Arabia over the last three months, have not claimed responsibility.
Multiple loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital Riyadh early Sunday.
The Saudi led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles in Riyadh and the southern region. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote in a post on X that air defenses also "intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh."
Saudi defense challenges
The missile attacks on Riyadh came a day after Yemen's Houthi-run health ministry said Saudi airstrikes had killed at least 33 people near the capital Sanaa, including women and children.
"We will punish the Saudi regime for its crimes against the Yemeni people," said Mahdi al-Mashat, a senior Houthi official, on Saturday.
Last month, 13 people were killed in one missile strike on Riyadh's international airport, and several more died in other strikes on the airport.
The Houthis have said they will continue firing missiles and drones against Saudi Arabia so long as the Kingdom carries out airstrikes against the parts of Yemen they control and enforces a blockade against its territory.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, putting it firmly among the top ten military spenders worldwide. It has acquired US fighter jets as well as Patriot and THAAD air defense systems, and a range of advanced weaponry from France and the United Kingdom.
But the Saudis have a lot to defend: a country roughly one-fifth the size of the US, with threats on three sides - from Iran, Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, and the Houthis.
The Saudis are intercepting many of the missiles and drones fired by the Houthis. But some get through. The defense ministry faces difficult choices in distributing the existing systems with so many installations vulnerable to attack.
The Houthis have learned to combine ballistic and cruise missiles with long-range drones to overwhelm Saudi defenses, according to analysts.
In Yemen, the Saudi-backed coalition is trying to prevent the Houthis from advancing further south towards the port of Aden, which is held by the internationally-recognized government.
The Houthis have frequently targeted Aden's airport with missiles in recent weeks, after taking a stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast in September.
Hostilities between the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, and Saudi Arabia reignited in July, shattering a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire that had largely halted fighting between the two sides.

title: The 10 most expensive homes that sold in Maine in October
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
A 7,000-square-foot oceanfront estate near Nubble Lighthouse off the coast of York was the most expensive home sold in Maine during the month of October.
We found the 10 most expensive residential property sales that took place across the state in October using information from state transfer tax documents, which are available to the public online.
All of the homes are located along Maine’s coast, stretching as far south as York up to Milbridge in Washington County. The properties have a combined sale price of more than $42 million but cost an average of $4.2 million.
