title: Paul George scores 27 in Celtics’ rout of Bucks
text:
MILWAUKEE — Paul George scored 27 points, Jayson Tatum added 21 and the Boston Celtics rolled to a 117-97 victory over the slumping Milwaukee Bucks on Sunday night.
This marked the second matchup between these teams in five nights. The Celtics had beaten the Bucks 109-102 on Wednesday in Boston while resting Tatum.
Boston (8-2) built a big enough lead Sunday to sit Tatum for the entire fourth quarter as the Celtics continued a four-game trip that started with a 119-80 win at Charlotte on Friday. The Celtics next head to Philadelphia and Toronto.
Kyle Kuzma led Milwaukee with 27 points.
Myles Turner scored just three points for the Bucks, though he did have five rebounds and a career-high seven assists. Turner, who has shot 1 of 15 over his last two games, was coming off a scoreless performance in a 121-107 NBA Cup loss to the Toronto Raptors on Frieday.
The Bucks (1-9) are off to their worst start since 1993-94, when they lost 10 of their first 11 games and went on to finish 20-62.
Kuzma scored 14 points in the first five minutes of the game to help Milwaukee grab an early 20-6 lead. Tatum and George sparked an 18-0 run that enabled the Celtics to take control later in the first half.
Tatum scored the final 10 points of the first quarter to cut Milwaukee’s lead to 27-25. George delivered the first eight points of the second period.
George’s 3-pointer in the opening minute of the second quarter gave Boston its first lead at 28-27. George then hit a layup and another 3-pointer to cap the 18-0 spurt.
Boston owned a 58-45 halftime advantage. The Celtics scored the first nine points of the third period to extend their lead to 22, and they stayed in front by at least 15 the rest of the way.
Up next
Celtics: At Philadelphia on Tuesday night.
Bucks: At New York on Tuesday night.

title: Obituary: Cheryl Ann Clark Martin-Hunt
text:
FAIRFIELD – On Oct. 28, 2026, we lost our beloved Cheryl Ann Clark Martin-Hunt after an arduous and fierce battle with appendiceal cancer.
Cheryl was born April 21, 1951, in Augusta. She was the daughter of Gerald “Jack” and Irma O. (Fowles) Clark. Cheryl did not come into this world alone – she was accompanied by her twin, Carol, and they remained close for Carol’s entire life.
Cheryl attended Readfield Elementary School and graduated from Kents Hill School in 1969. She attended the University of Maine at Orono for a time, and after college, Cheryl returned home to pursue various lines of work. These included waitressing and retail, owning her own business, Martin’s Sandwich Shop on Water Street in Augusta, and working in real estate and insurance in New Jersey. She was employed by the state of Maine for 24 years and retired from the Department of Transportation as Executive Assistant to the Commissioner of the DOT. She thoroughly enjoyed her work there and made many friends.
Cheryl was a beloved wife, adored mother, and revered friend to many people, some since her sub-primary years. She was always there when needed and gave generously of her time and attention to both people and causes, such as the homeless program in Bangor and the Veterans of Foreign Wars. Cheryl was a consummate homemaker and enjoyed cooking, reading, travel (unless a plane or cruise ship was involved!), gardening, the Ogunquit Playhouse, and going to the movies. She hosted amazing New Year’s Eve parties for many years and never forgot a birthday.
Cheryl dearly loved her twin sister, Carol, and they had many grand adventures together. Their bond was unbreakable, and Cheryl was shattered by Carol’s passing in 2020. Cheryl was also predeceased by her parents; her sister, Joan Shailer, her brother, Gerald “Jerry” Clark and wife, Francine; nephew Gene Clark, and niece Grace Shailer.
She is survived by her husband of 32 years, Eric Hunt Sr. of Fairfield; daughter April Cameron and husband, Travis, and son Ryan Martin. She is also survived by former spouse Clyde Martin; brother Earnest “Gene” Clark; grandson Austin Cameron and companion, Amber, grandson Logan Cameron and fiancée, Clarrissa Lettre; great-granddaughters Aubree, Hadlee, and Gabriella Cameron; brother-in-law, Bruce McLeod; aunt Jane White; nieces Debra Sue, Stephanie, and Heather, nephews Robert and Jon Shailer; and Michael Clark and wife, Jennifer, and their sons Nathan and Alex; and her bonus children Michelle Kew; Michael Hunt-Dubois and husband, Matt Dubois, and their son Jensen; Tiffany Stewart and husband, Jonathan, and their children, Emma Berkoski and husband Jake, Eli, Lauren, and Tewolde, and Eric Hunt, Jr., and his children Katelyn, Alyssa, and Cole; and many dear cousins and friends.
Cheryl will be sadly missed and lovingly remembered by so many people for a long time to come. She touched many lives.
There will be a celebration of Cheryl’s life on Nov. 21, at The VFW Hall in Winslow, from 1 to 3 p.m. All are welcome to attend. Interment will be in the Niche Wall at the Augusta Veterans’ Memorial Cemetery at a later date.

title: Uplifting sign at Red Barn in Augusta leads to misconception over political message
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When Trever Benedict, co-owner of The Red Barn in Augusta, came in to work Wednesday, the first thing he did was place a new roadside sign in front of his business. He switches the sign to display a new uplifting message every couple of weeks, he said, and this change was overdue.
This sign, reading “Sorry to spoil the ending for you, but everything is gonna end up okay,” was especially meaningful to Benedict because his dad has suffered two strokes this year as his mother’s health also declines. He thought of them as he put it up, he added, thinking nothing else was out of the ordinary.
But when he posted a picture of the sign on Facebook, it was met with hundreds of angry comments, direct messages and later some phone calls from people who thought he was celebrating the overwhelming victory of Democrats in Maine and across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Some people said they would boycott The Red Barn, according to Benedict.
“Naturally it was taken entirely out of context, and it basically created this uproar that we’re in the midst of now,” Benedict said Saturday morning. “For it to come back as this backlash, name-calling from the community, it’s really disheartening, it’s infuriating, and it’s ridiculous, frankly.”
Benedict posted an update on Facebook Thursday that clarified the intent behind the sign, but turned the comments off to avoid negativity. He said people continued to message him directly.
The Red Barn has stirred some controversy in the past under previous owner Laura Benedict, Trever Benedict’s aunt. Laura lashed out at Augusta city officials in 2017 after mistakenly believing that she had been fined for not having a mass gathering permit for a fundraising event, and she publicly removed an employee from the restaurant’s work schedule after he made racists remarks on Instagram.
Trever Benedict said there has never been anything political about the signs the restaurant posts, and that people sometimes stop in just to thank them for how the message improved their day.
“I hope that people can just strive to see the good and not scrutinize everything to the point where they look so hard to find the negative in everything,” Benedict said. “We have never been more divided than we are right now, and this whole example of this sign is exhibit A.”
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Madeleine Kaptein can be reached at mkaptein@metln.org

title: Obituary: Gayle Ruth Briggs
text:
FALMOUTH – Gayle Ruth Briggs passed away peacefully on Oct. 29, 2026, following a long illness. She was 76.
Born on April 28, 1950, in Lincoln, Maine, to Allison and Louise Whitney Briggs, Gayle graduated from Brewer High School, Class of 1968, and went on to attend Westbrook College, where she earned a degree in dental hygiene. She worked in that profession for several years in Boston, Mass., before life’s journey led her in a new and exciting direction.
Gayle embarked on a fascinating career as a flight attendant with Pan American World Airways, traveling the world and enjoying destinations throughout Europe and Africa while based in New York City, N.Y.
Her later endeavors included working with the Maine Tourist Information Bureau and, ultimately, retiring from L.L.Bean, where she served as a customer service specialist.
A passionate advocate for conservation and environmental protection, Gayle believed deeply in preserving the natural world for future generations. Her love of nature and the outdoors inspired a lifelong commitment to leaving the world a better place through her conservation efforts and volunteer work. Alongside her husband, Joe, she volunteered for many years with recycling initiatives in Yarmouth and Freeport, as well as Maine beach cleanups.
Gayle shared more than 40 wonderful years of marriage with her husband and soulmate, Joseph Sukaskas, whom she met while volunteering at an off-Broadway theater. Their life together was filled with shared adventures, a love of the outdoors, and a deep appreciation for the beauty of New England.
She was a loving sister, aunt, and friend, always offering unwavering support to those fortunate enough to have her in their lives. Gayle had a special gift for making others feel cared for. Friends and family were often the grateful recipients of her thoughtful homemade gifts, especially comforting soups and chocolate chip cookies. She proudly considered herself a “chocolate chip cookie connoisseur.”
Gayle was also the biggest supporter and cheerleader of her nephews’ and nieces’ many athletic and artistic pursuits, attending their games, performances, and events whenever possible. She delighted in cheering them on and wholeheartedly encouraging their interests and accomplishments.
Family gatherings and Friday pizza nights held a special place in Gayle’s heart, and those cherished traditions will live on in the memories of all who shared them with her.
Gayle found joy in hiking, long walks, picnics, snowshoeing, and contemplating the wonder of the universe. She felt a profound spiritual connection to nature and found peace and inspiration in the world around her. She and Joe especially enjoyed taking scenic drives throughout New England’s coastal and mountain regions. She held a special affection for Casco Bay, Camden, and, above all, Acadia National Park.
Gayle’s genuine youthful spirit, optimistic outlook, and enduring faith in the goodness of humankind were among her most beautiful qualities. Perhaps these words from Walt Disney’s Bambi best reflect the way she viewed life and the natural world:
“Everything in the forest has its season. Where one thing falls, another grows. Maybe not what was there before, but something new and wonderful all the same.”
May this sentiment live on in her memory.
Gayle was predeceased by her beloved husband, Joseph Sukaskas; her brothers, Daryl and Gary Briggs; her parents, Allison and Louise Briggs; and her feline companions, Snippy and Mesha.
She is survived by her brother, Bryan Briggs, and his wife, Deborah Walls, of Falmouth, her sisters-in-law, Pamela Briggs of Hamden, and Tammy Ruuk-Briggs of Brewer; and her many beloved nieces and nephews – nephews Erik Briggs and his wife, Rena, of Framingham, Mass., Nathan Briggs and his wife, Molly, of Hamden, Wilson Briggs and his wife, Paige, of Highlands, N.J., Brandon Briggs and his wife, Courtney, of Freehold, N.J., Zachary Briggs and his wife, Casey, of Gorham, and Alexander Briggs and his wife, Nicole, of Brunswick, nieces – Alyson Yachanin and her husband, Seth, of Hamden, and Catherine Briggs of Portland. She also leaves behind great-nieces Addison, Makenzie, Avery, Amelia, Emersyn, Ava, and Violet, great-nephew, Wilson; and several cousins.
The family extends its heartfelt gratitude to Gayle’s compassionate caregivers at Cornerstone Companions, as well as Catherine Briggs, Tabby Nyatichi, and Theresa Lehman; the staff at Falmouth House at OceanView and Legacy Memory Care; Compassus Hospice Care; and Dr. Allyson Malloy and Dr. Paul. Your kindness, dedication, and loving care will always be remembered and deeply appreciated.
A Celebration of Life will be held on Saturday, Jan. 16, 2027, from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. at Maine Audubon, L.L.Bean Great Room, 20 Gilsland Farm Rd., Falmouth. Burial will be private.

title: VIDEO: Small plane crashes into truck while making emergency landing
text:
VIDEO: Small plane crashes into truck while making emergency landing
Dash cam video captured the moment a small plane collided with a pickup truck during an emergency landing along a Florida road on Saturday.
The Lee County Sheriff's Office said two pilots aboard the aircraft attempted to land after experiencing a mechanical issue in Fort Myers, Florida.
The incident occurred around noon.
Authorities said during the landing, the plane crashed into the rear of a pickup truck that was traveling eastbound on Bayshore Road.
Watch video of the landing in the playfinder above
No injuries were reported.
According to the sheriff's office, the Federal Aviation Administration is leading an investigation into what led to the incident.
"Thankfully, this incident had a positive outcome, and no one was injured. Given the recent tragic news involving aviation accidents, we are especially grateful that everyone is safe," Sheriff Carmine Marceno said in a post on Facebook. "We will continue working closely with our partners at the FAA as they review the circumstances surrounding this incident. The safety of our community remains our top priority."
The incident comes days after a Learjet traveling from Austin, Texas, crashed along a busy road in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people on board.

title: After 70 years without a grocery store, neighbors build their own
text:
After 70 years without a grocery store, neighbors build their own
The shelves are nearly stocked at the We All Eat Market, and Darlene Battle is ready to shop.
For Battle, who has lived in Birmingham's Fountain Heights neighborhood her entire life, the market opening Saturday means a place to buy groceries closer to home and a chance to see an idea she watched grow become reality.
"This is a market that is birthed in the neighborhood," said Battle, vice president of the Fountain Heights Neighborhood Association.
The market's owners said Fountain Heights has gone about 70 years without a grocery store. Now, they hope We All Eat will make fresh food easier to find and give neighbors a place to connect.
"We deserve the best, and we're not going to wait for anyone else to give it to us," co-owner Dominique Villanueva said. "We're going to build it ourselves."
From a garden to a grocery store
Villanueva and co-owner Chris Gooden live in Fountain Heights, Alabama. They said the idea for the market grew from their own experience and conversations with neighbors who shared the same need. Villanueva said after the COVID-19 pandemic began, a bus line serving the neighborhood was cut. For people who relied on the bus to reach a grocery store, the trip became even harder.
The couple had already begun growing food in the neighborhood. Villanueva said they started farming on a nearby lot in 2017 after outgrowing their front and backyard gardens. Planning and fundraising for the market began around 2021.
Battle remembers the early days. She said the owners shared produce with neighbors through a free market, and sometimes she would come home to find a bag of produce on her steps.
"They didn't just start with the market," Battle said. "They started with reaching out to neighbors and being neighborly."
Gooden said We All Eat plans to offer produce grown on neighborhood lots and by cooperative farmers, along with other locally grown or organic products. Shoppers can also expect bulk herbs and spices. The market has a demonstration kitchen, where Gooden hopes to offer classes and help customers learn how to use ingredients they may not have tried before.
For Battle, convenience matters. She said the grocery store she currently uses is at least a 10-minute drive away. Before that store opened, the trip was longer.
"We were excited once we got that store, because before then it was at least 15 or 20 minutes,” she said. "This is actually a convenient market with healthy options."
Villanueva described We All Eat as a $1 million project supported by community members and outside funders. Gooden said the first $30,000 came from grassroots donations, including small contributions from people who stopped by and learned what they were trying to build. Another $150,000 of support came from the city of Birmingham.
The grand opening is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. The owners said the celebration will include shopping, children's activities, herbal tea blending and door prizes.

title: Democrats plan to push clean energy to lower bills and challenge Trump’s fossil fuel agenda
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.
With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week’s midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle.
Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.
Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump’s clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will “work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors.”
American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy “feels bolstered.”
Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.
“The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they’ll use that power effectively,” said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. “The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them.”
Trump holds veto power but thinks he and Democrats can deal
Trump said after Tuesday’s election that Democrats will send over “things that are insane” and he will veto them, speaking generally about legislation. But in the comments to Fox News, he predicted that “after a couple of months of vetoes,” he and Democrats will find ways to work together.
The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is “committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this.”
Trump promised to lower energy prices. Instead, his war with Iran and other policies increased the price of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.
Trump particularly dislikes offshore wind. Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a large wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has started operating commercially.
Will the president change his tune on green energy? That’s doubtful, said former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff.
“He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy,” Dorgan said in an email.
Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, which cause climate change, because he argues that would give the U.S. the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group, said that as voters have changed the balance of political power in Washington, “the affordability message is unmistakable.”
Sommers said in a statement there is a real opportunity for bipartisan cooperation to reduce costs and strengthen the economy, starting with an energy permitting reform proposal announced in September. The legislation is aimed at shortening the timeline to get big energy projects started.
Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should reject that proposal and use their stronger position to pass legislation that actually builds out much-needed clean energy.
Reversing Trump’s anti-climate policies
The administration has reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency, reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.
Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.
Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats’ more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.
Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats’ list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.
Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.
A potential stalemate seen on clean energy and climate policy
David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.
Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.
“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”
One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.
States could advance clean energy without waiting for Congress
Democrats scored victories in races for governor in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.
Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.
Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.
“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.”
___
Associated Press writers Alexa St. John and Matthew Daly contributed to this report.

title: Cooper Flagg’s 3rd straight double-double leads Mavericks past Nets
text:
DALLAS — Newport native Cooper Flagg had 25 points and a career-high 12 assists for his third consecutive double-double and fourth of the season as the Dallas Mavericks beat the Brooklyn Nets 130-93 on Sunday night.
Kyrie Irving scored 21 points and Daniel Gafford added 18 as the Mavericks played the first of a home back-to-back.
Michael Porter Jr. had 19 points and nine rebounds for the Nets, who were swept in a back-to-back to begin a four-game road trip. Nolan Traore added 14 points.
The Nets didn’t trail until the final two minutes of Saturday’s 124-121 loss at Atlanta but never led against the Mavericks.
Flagg, last season’s Rookie of the Year, had his 16th career 20-point half and first this season after opening hot by hitting 5 of 6 shots in the first period. He had missed 6 of 8 shots and scored four points in the first half on Friday against Utah but finished with 21 points in Dallas’ 112-100 win.
The Mavericks shot a season best 57.1% and scored a season high in points on Sunday. They led 66-46 at halftime, and the 37-point final margin was the largest of the game.
Brooklyn’s Julius Randle grew up in the Dallas area and went into play averaging 23.5 points in his homecoming games but finished with 13 points.
Nets rookie Mikel Brown Jr., who tied his career-high with 18 points on Saturday, sat out, not yet cleared for back-to-backs as he recovers from a back injury that limited him to 21 games last season for Louisville.
Up next
Nets: Visit New Orleans on Wednesday night.
Mavericks: Host Indiana on Monday night.

title: Native American women made history in tribal, state and federal elections
text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — A third-grade field trip to the Navajo Nation Council sparked Crystalyne Curley’s political ambition when she witnessed a fiery debate erupt between two tribal lawmakers.
“I thought to myself at a very young age, that’s where I want to be,” Curley said.
On Election Day, Curley surpassed that childhood dream and broke a barrier she says she never imagined as a nine-year-old: She was elected the first woman president of the Navajo Nation.
This week’s elections brought a wave of milestone victories, from the nation’s first Black female governor to the first openly gay man and first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. It also marked a turning point for Native American women, whose leadership in their families and communities has rarely translated to formal political power.
Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the Senate, Deb Haaland the first to win a state governorship, and Curley the first to lead one of the largest tribes.
“This is a win for all Navajo women,” Curley told The Associated Press.
Jordan James Harvill, a Cherokee Nation citizen and strategist with the advocacy group Advance Native Political Leadership, said decades of political organizing are bearing fruit as more Native women run for and win office.
“This is a seismic shift that is happening in our communities,” he said.
The Navajo Nation elects its first woman president
Lene Bitsui supported Curley in the Navajo Nation election because she felt she was best positioned to restore order to the tribal government after what she sees as a period of dysfunction. But when Bitsui cast her ballot, she felt pessimistic.
“I thought our people weren’t ready for a female president,” Bitsui said. “I was wrong, and I feel so happy to have been wrong.”
The modern, centralized Navajo government has been led by men since its establishment under federal pressure over a century ago. Navajo has the largest land base of any federally recognized tribe, spanning 27,000 square miles (70,000 square kilometers) in Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is second in population to the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma.
Some Navajo people believe traditional teachings prohibit women from holding top government positions. Others say women’s absence from the presidency stands in contrast to the matrilineal structure of Diné society.
“You see the language of tradition used to both deride the possibility of a woman being president and to say that women’s leadership is needed now,” said Jennifer Nez Denetdale, a professor of Diné studies at the University of New Mexico.
Curley, who narrowly defeated attorney Justin Jones, according to unofficial results, told the AP she faced sexist rhetoric while campaigning and expects to be held to a higher standard as the first woman president.
“As women, we have to work twice or triple as hard, especially within Navajo politics,” said Curley, who also was the first female to lead the tribe’s legislative branch as speaker of the tribal council.
After Curley and her running mate Chris Deschene take office in January, they plan to transition the Navajo Nation away from coal development, historically a major economic engine for the tribe, and reassert its leading role in national discussions around federal Indian policy.
The Seneca Nation of Indians in western New York also elected its first woman president, longtime council member Tina Abrams, on Tuesday.
Native women make gains in U.S. Congress
At her Senate victory celebration in St. Paul, Minnesota, Democrat Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Nation and the state’s outgoing lieutenant governor, credited supporters from her community.
“I could not run for the U. S. Senate without Native women. I could not exist in the way that I do without Native women,” Flanagan said.
More than 230 years after the U.S. Senate was established, only four Native people have served in the chamber, all men.
“This is a win that shows we can break every single glass ceiling,” Harvill said.
Flanagan will join Oklahoma Republican Sen. Tom Cole, a citizen of the Chickasaw Nation. A victory for Democrat Mary Peltola, a Yup’ik woman, in Alaska’s still unsettled Senate race, would mark the first time three Native people have served in the chamber simultaneously.
In the House, Kansas Democrat Sharice Davids, Ho-Chunk, and Oklahoma Republican Josh Brecheen, Choctaw, won reelection. New York Democrat Claire Valdez, a citizen of Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, and Michigan Democrat Sean McCann, a citizen of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, became the first Native Americans elected to represent their states in Congress.
Deb Haaland notches another first in New Mexico
Haaland’s political career has been defined by historic milestones. She was one of the first two Native women elected to Congress in 2018 before becoming the first Native American to lead a U.S. Cabinet agency, the Interior Department.
Now, in her home state of New Mexico, the Laguna Pueblo citizen, will break ground as the first female Native governor of a U.S. state.
“I think it’s a long time coming,” said Haaland, who traces her ancestry in what is now New Mexico back 800 years.
She is tasked with making good on campaign promises to make life more affordable for struggling New Mexicans and addressing persistently poor education outcomes in the state.
Haaland, who is affectionately known as “Auntie Deb” in parts of Indian Country, was tearful reflecting on the support she has received from Native voters and other Native women in politics, including Davids and Flanagan.
“It makes me very happy that we’re able to have a presence,” Haaland said. “It’s not just a slogan. It matters that people feel represented.”
___

title: Staff at the US center for AI safety are reporting to the White House, raising independence concerns
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — With public anxiety growing over mounting reports about out-of-control artificial intelligence agents, the tiny U.S. government division charged with assessing the safety of new AI offerings lacks a permanent leader and has stopped publishing its research.
Officials with the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, or CAISSI, an independent division of the Commerce Department, recently were asked to informally report to an office of the White House. That’s according to two former government officials with knowledge of the ongoing conversations who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to avoid repercussions for current staffers.
The new arrangement concerns some critics, who worry that the executive branch might be politicizing decisions that could affect everything from cybersecurity to bioweapons and that the center’s findings could be altered or muted in deference to the tech industry, which has been largely entrusted to police itself.
“These are really powerful institutions that can drastically improve our lives, or the alternative. And the hope is that you can put in nonpartisan or bipartisan technocratic experts to enact policy in a way that best serves the American public,” said Caroline Siegel Singh, an AI and emerging technology program manager for the Federation of American Scientists.
Others argue that bringing AI safety officials closer to the orbit of President Donald Trump, who has taken an outwardly hands-off approach to the issue, could give the division more prominence — and perhaps more funding.
The center, which has experienced departures and until recently was called the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation, is allocated $10 million per year. That’s about one-eighth the annual budget of its counterpart in the United Kingdom, which is far less celebrated for its frontier technologies.
In April, the division’s director was hired and then fired within days. His replacement lasted a few months before he resigned, and the center has been without a permanent leader ever since, although the head of its parent institute doubles as its acting director.
In August, Congress started asking why the center suddenly stopped making public its reports about how safely certain AI systems were performing. San Francisco giant OpenAI also had chimed in by then, asking policymakers to throw more money and support behind the division.
The White House didn’t respond to specific questions about CAISSI. But it said in a statement that Trump had formally established his new Super Intelligence Force — the president’s preferred term for artificial intelligence. Trump has commissioned a report on risks from his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, and will ensure “continued U.S. leadership on SI for the benefit of the American people,” the White House said.
An industry that polices itself
The federal government often takes an active role in deciding what is safe for the public.
Take the automobile industry, for example. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration sits crash test dummies in cars and then runs them into walls to measure how human bodies are affected by vehicle collisions. Government researchers then analyze the crash test data, share it with the public and prescribe national standards to improve vehicle safety, all with the mission of saving lives and lowering economic costs from crashes.
With AI models, safety testing looks very different.
Under then-President Joe Biden, leading AI companies voluntarily agreed to promote “safe, secure, and transparent development” of their models by sharing details with the newly created division of the Commerce Department and following the administration’s guidelines for tests and transparency reports.
In September, following alarming reports of AI systems eluding their makers’ control, Trump asked leading AI companies to undertake “tremendous self-policing” as part of a voluntary safety pact, but his administration hasn’t said how it will monitor the AI companies’ implementation.
The technology is advancing so rapidly that many models are now deployed instead as AI agents that work without human prompting and can plan out myriad steps in real-world environments, such as in a recent case in which an AI agent sent a false tip to Philadelphia police about an unsolved homicide case.
As AI capabilities have grown, the government’s capacity to independently check these systems hasn’t kept pace. There still is no standard process for testing how safely AI agents are acting in the real world, even in simple cases such as when AI agents book a flight, said Sayash Kapoor, an incoming assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley School of Information.
“Our previous methods would just look at the final answer, the final check, whether the flight was correctly booked. And in this case, it might seem as if the task was solved correctly,” said Kapoor, the co-author of a new paper examining agent evaluations. “But unless you’re looking at the entire set of steps that an agent took, you won’t be able to tell that the agent made a huge mistake.”
Trump has prioritized dominance in AI
When Trump started his second term, he initially empowered venture capitalists David Sacks and Sriram Krishnan as his AI czar and senior AI policy advisor, respectively. Their expertise was in leading tech investments, not the technical evaluation of AI models.
Both stepped down earlier this year but Sacks now serves on Trump’s technology advisory council. And after a relatively unknown Anthropic engineer resigned, warning about the dangers of AI development, Trump made a series of policy changes.
Trump empowered National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to lead his new Super Intelligence Force, which the president said would keep the U.S. dominant in AI development.
Clayton’s appointment to the force, along with the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, Emil Michael, shows how the administration is pushing to frame decisions around model safety as a national security matter that needs executive discretion and secrecy, overshadowing AI’s risks to consumer protection, privacy, and civil rights, said Amos Toh, a senior counsel at the Brennan Center for Justice.
Even as Silicon Valley companies have disclosed their models’ involvement in troubling cyberattacks this year, CAISSI has kept a low profile when it comes to testing for AI safety.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also have been promoting the work of independent evaluation firms to help vet their companies’ safety practices, but the AI giants can limit their access and dispense with their evaluations.
“There’s this unclear mission for government evaluators if the largest AI companies are also being encouraged to set up their own internal evaluation systems and/or hire external evaluators,” said Logan Koepke, a senior project director at the civil rights and technology nonprofit Upturn. “Like, what role does government testing actually play in that scenario?”
Letting the labs police their own models and failing to clarify the role of government in AI safety testing weakens independent checks on AI systems that can cause real-world harms, Toh said.
“At the end of the day, all of these decisions are of immense public consequence and should be explained and rationalized in the public eye,” he said. “And that’s not happening.”

title: On Nature: Observing the Puddle’s Great Blue Heron
text:
A great blue heron’s hunting strategy is ruthless. With piercing yellow eyes slightly angled toward the group, it extends its long neck over the water and stills. Upon spotting prey, the heron moves with seemingly impossible speed, spearing or grasping its intended food before swallowing and stilling again.
Watching a heron, it is easy to see how birds and dinosaurs are really one and the same.
Standing at about four feet tall with wingspans of up to seven feet, great blue herons are North America’s largest predatory wading birds. Their most common prey are aquatic: fish, crayfish, insect larvae. But they can also eat small mammals and other birds.
This year, Bates has been treated to a resident great blue heron. The bird was first reported on campus on Aug. 2 and has made a regular appearance at the Puddle since. Still a juvenile, the heron exhibits muted, gray coloration compared to the bold blues of a typical adult.
It is pretty much the perfect spot for a heron. The Puddle’s main and perhaps only fish species is the goldfish, an invasive and brightly colored fish that is easily seen by predators from above. Ospreys also love to hunt these goldfish. For a young bird who lacks hunting experience, it is a good place to start. But this heron is not just fishing for fish; in one eBird observation on Sept. 6, it was seen eating a young snapping turtle.
Because this bird is a juvenile and was born this year, it lacks a heron’s typical wariness around people. The heron is still learning what it should fear and has spent much of its life close to Puddle pedestrians, so it has not yet figured out that people are meant to be avoided. Older herons, by contrast, tend to be rather skittish, quick to flee humans that get too close.
The Puddle heron can be seen hunting between the cattails, angling its head to get the best view of the goldfish swimming below. It is watchful of those who pass by, but not skittish. Do not worry, though: the bird is uninjured and perfectly capable of flight. It just seems to like it here on campus.
Crouched behind it, I observed last week as the heron patiently waited for prey to swim close enough to grasp. So still and so big it was hard to believe it lived on our small pond, I felt lucky to get such an up-close view of this prehistoric bird.
Make sure you keep an extra eye on the reeds as you walk around the Puddle – you might just catch a glimpse of one of Maine’s coolest birds.

title: Floods bring rare relief to US Southwest reservoirs as Lake Powell rises 20 feet
text:
Floods bring rare relief to US Southwest reservoirs as Lake Powell rises 20 feet
Recent flooding across the U.S. Southwest is providing rare relief to thirsty reservoirs that had fallen to record lows amid a yearslong megadrought.
Storms in late October and early November sent torrents of water through normally small or dry creeks that overflowed their banks and flooded local communities.
Hundreds of people were told to evacuate, and the flooding cut off access to some areas. Yet most of that water will end up feeding depleted lakes and underground aquifers, said Martin Hoerling, a climate scientist and hydrologist at the University of Colorado, Boulder.
“That’s somewhat of an unexpected boost from Mother Nature,” Hoerling said.
Last winter's lackluster snowfall did little to recharge water bodies when it melted in the spring and summer, when they typically get their biggest bump of the year.
Then came the chaotic climate phenomenon, El Niño, which has intensified heavy rain and floods. Experts say its impacts will last several more months, potentially further boosting water supplies across the West where water primarily is stored in lakes, aquifers and snowpack.
Lake Powell, the second-largest reservoir in the U.S., rose more than 20 feet (6.1 meters) from its mid-September low — dwarfing its gains from this year's snowmelt, Hoerling said. Still, the lake remained just over a quarter full, and 15 of its 17 boat launches remained unusable as of Friday.
The floodwaters and additional rain could raise the lake along the Arizona-Utah border further, for a total of over 1.2 million acre-feet — enough to support around 4 million average families for a year, Hoerling estimated.
Rain brings temporary relief to regional and local water supplies
Cities in the region reported some of their wettest weather in decades.
Before storms began dumping about 7 inches (17.78 centimeters) of rain around Pagosa Springs, Colorado, in October, more than 10,000 people in the town and surrounding communities were under water restrictions. Restaurants were encouraged to serve water only on request, town manager David Harris said. Those restrictions are now lifted.
“While the storm was destructive, I think there is a silver lining,” Harris said. “You’re getting a good start to the winter snowpack in the higher elevations.”
Upper Lake Mary, which captures spring snowmelt in Northern Arizona and supplies Flagstaff, Arizona, with up to 40% of its water, received more than 3 billion gallons of water since early October, said Flagstaff water production manager Brian Huntzinger.
Storms last weekend dumped the equivalent of more than two years of water into the town's surface water supply and provided a buffer for an operation that depends heavily on underground aquifers, Huntzinger said.
“It’s just a great, great thing to see,” Huntzinger said. “We might be overflowing at this rate before we see any snow fly.”
In central Arizona, heavy floodwaters that trapped people in their homes gushed into streams that feed the Verde River. That prompted water officials to release water from two nearly full dams into the Verde's normally dry stretch in metro Phoenix, said Bo Svoma, the principal meteorologist at the Salt River Project, which manages reservoirs on the Salt and Verde rivers.
Wet weather is unlikely to change decisions on the Colorado River
The region remains in drought despite the intense rains.
And decisions already have been made to divvy up water in the Colorado River basin. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, which manages reservoirs in the West, is unlikely to change its water releases from Lake Powell or other areas until it knows when snowpack has peaked, typically around April, said Jack Schmidt, a Utah State University professor who studies the Colorado River.
Reclamation spokesperson Mary Carlson acknowledged conditions have improved but added "considerable uncertainty remains."
Under the federal plan for managing the Colorado River's Lower Basin, California, Nevada and Arizona will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet (about 1.54 billion cubic meters) annually in the next two years. That is enough to fill over 600,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools, with the possibility of larger cuts depending on conditions.
Nevada and Arizona are challenging the plan in court.
Some Arizona cities have agreed to fund preliminary work to reduce reliance on the Colorado River by expanding an existing dam on the Verde River to capture runoff from storms, Svoma said.
“We need to figure out how to be resilient in a drier future. And we’re not quite there yet,” Hoerling said.

title: IRS releases 2027 tax brackets. Here’s what you can expect to pay
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - The 2027 tax brackets and standard deductions are now out – and they’re higher to compensate for inflation.
The IRS says brackets for individuals are up a few hundred to a few thousand dollars. Those for married couples are double that for most income levels. The standard deduction for single filers is $500 more at $16,600. For married couples, the increase is $1,000.
The IRS changes tax brackets based on the Consumer Price Index. The 2027 adjustment is a half percentage point more than the previous year’s since inflation is higher.
The IRS is also announcing tweaks, like a $100 Child Tax Credit bump.
“American individuals and businesses will see increased tax benefits next tax year ranging from an increase in the standard deduction and the Child Tax Credit for families,” said IRS CEO Frank J. Bisignano in a news release.
Experts say taxpayers might want to review the changes to consider whether to make withholding adjustments.

title: Obituary: William B. Wise
text:
GORHAM – William B. Wise, New Portland Road, Gorham, Maine, died on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.
“Bill” was born in Skowhegan in 1935, son of William H. and Ruth K. (Ketchum) Wise. He grew up in Norridgewock and attended Skowhegan High School, where he excelled in baseball, football and track. After graduation, he enlisted in the United States Army and was based in Germany. He then attended the University of Maine in Orono and graduated in 1960 with a degree in history.
Bill began his 32-year career in education in 1960 as a teacher, coach, and athletic director at Coburn Classical Institute, in Waterville. In 1964, he returned to UMaine and worked in the admissions office for two years. In 1966, Bill went to work at Gorham State Teachers College (now University of Southern Maine). In his 25 years there, he held a variety of administrative positions, including Dean of Academics, Dean of Education, Vice-President of Academic Affairs, and Executive Assistant to the President.
In 1987, the University of Southern Maine started the William B. Wise scholar-athlete award program, which celebrates students who excel in both athletics and academics. In 2023, the USM athletics department learning center was named the William B. Wise Learning Center. In retirement, Bill was a member of the USM Huskies Sports Hall of Fame committee and served on the board of the USM Retirees Association.
Bill was very involved in community service. He was elected to one term on the Gorham School Committee and two terms on the Gorham Town Council. He was instrumental in the development of Gorham’s first youth basketball and soccer programs in the 1970s. Over the years, he coached many recreation soccer, basketball, and baseball teams, and volunteered as a little league baseball umpire.
A prolific writer of letters, Bill wrote countless personal letters to friends, family, and co-workers to compliment, congratulate, console, or encourage them, whatever the occasion warranted.
Bill was an avid golfer and reader and enjoyed people. He particularly liked traveling with his wife. Bill loved spending time with his family, and his love for family will forever remain in the hearts of his sons, daughters-in-law, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren.
Bill was predeceased by his dear wife, Roberta B. Wise.
Surviving members are son, William D. Wise and his wife Mary Ann, son, Bradford A. Wise and his wife Kathleen; grandchildren William E. Wise and his wife Katie C. Wise, Cameron Wise and his wife Katie W. Wise, Joey Wise and his wife Marissa Wise, Elizabeth Lilly and her husband Ben Lilly, Rebekah Wise; great-grandchildren Charlotte Wise, William J. Wise, Ellie Wise, Noah Wise, Annabelle Lilly, Zoey Lilly, Chloe Wise; and nephew, Craig Lizotte and his wife Linda Lizotte.
A private family service will be held.

title: Susan Collins could confront Trump
text:
I have urged Sen. Susan Collins to confront President Donald Trump.
Pardoning the Jan. 6 insurrectionists; supporting the creation of DOGE; covering up the Epstein files; launching the war against Iran; putting ICE in our streets; pursuing vendettas via lawsuits; rounds of tariffs; bombing fishermen; backing Putin and Netanyahu—Trump has degraded the presidency and the United States.
Collins (or an aide) made a reply that told me she was prevented, procedurally, from doing anything. The reply schooled me about impeachment (yes, I learned). If representatives initiated the process, and representatives and then senators moved it along, up to a Senate vote — then, following deliberation, she would be counted, Nay or Yea.
Collins can do more; confronting Trump would be an on-the-ground, human thing. Being with, listening to, persuading fellow congresspeople — these are the essential steps.
I have suggested that I accompany Susan, even do the speaking.
Susan Collins does, in fact, have agency enough to confront Donald Trump.
Michael Hatem, Ph.D.
Portland

title: Wrong to undo protections for Maine children with disabilities
text:
Alan Cobo-Lewis is the parent of two adult children, one of whom has a disability. He is also on the faculty of the University of Maine, where he is associate professor of psychology and director of the Center for Community Inclusion and Disability Studies. His views are his own.
In June 2022, the U.S. Department of Justice sent Maine a letter finding that the state had violated the rights of children with mental-health or developmental disabilities.
After a long investigation, the DOJ found Maine was violating the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) by failing to provide children sufficient behavioral health support in their communities.
This shortcoming unnecessarily sent Maine children to institutions, including hospitals, residential facilities and juvenile detention — including unnecessary out-of-state placements. And it put more children at risk institutionalization.
The DOJ found this was a violation of both the ADA and the U.S. Supreme Court’s 1999 Olmstead decision, which affirmed the right of people with disabilities not to be institutionalized unnecessarily.
Maine was ripping children away from their families.
In November 2024, the DOJ and Maine entered into a settlement agreement. This agreement was approved by a federal court the following month.
Although Maine didn’t admit to violating children’s rights, the state thankfully agreed to a court-monitored settlement, including having a third party collect and analyze data to assess progress on getting children with disabilities the help they need—help made available to them in their homes and communities, which should always be the first choice.
The DOJ has since moved away from enforcing Olmstead’s integration mandate. This is a big enough deal that Gov. Janet Mills joined 17 other state governors in asking the DOJ not to retreat from protecting the right to community integration.
The governors said they strongly opposed “any federal actions that would weaken protections against unnecessary segregation or diminish the right of people with disabilities to receive services in the most integrated settings appropriate to meet their needs, consistent with established Olmstead precedent.”
Yet, less than a year after entering the settlement agreement to support Maine children with disabilities in their homes and communities, the DOJ and Maine jointly petitioned the federal court to modify the agreement to remove independent review, reduce reporting requirements and weaken other commitments.
Federal Judge Stacey Neumann denied the request, ruling that the DOJ and Maine failed to show changed circumstances and that an amendment would violate rules governing voluntary settlements.
The court having ruled, Maine proceeded on implementation. And yet, now the DOJ and Maine are together appealing Judge Neumann’s decision to the appeals court.
Instead of continuing to move forward on implementation to ensure children with disabilities finally get the support they need in their homes and communities, the DOJ and Maine are again trying to get out from under it.
Why is it that “see you in court” now means “let’s work together in court to remove protections from Maine children with disabilities”?
I am grateful that Governor-elect Hannah Pingree has endorsed the ADA and Olmstead’s integration mandate as a “matter of basic human rights and fairness” and has furthermore recognized that institutionalization is “isolating, harmful, and far more costly to taxpayers than supporting people right where they belong, at home, near their families and connected to their communities.”
Pingree added, “Together, we will need to continue to fight back against federal attempts to undermine the rights of all Americans with disabilities.”
It’s time for us in Maine to live by our values.
Support ADA and Olmstead’s integration mandate. Build out the home- and community-based supports for Maine children with disabilities. Stop putting Maine children at unnecessary risk of institutionalization, away from the families that love them. Recognize that accountability as represented by specific metrics and independent monitoring is important to support Maine’s children. Support Maine children with disabilities. Implement the agreement.
Gov. Mills should immediately withdraw support for this appeal. If she doesn’t, I look forward to Gov. Pingree doing so as quickly as possible after her inauguration.

title: ‘Atlas Shrugged’? No thanks.
text:
A recent letter asks readers to “Please stop vilifying the rich” (Oct. 4). And to read Ayn Rand’s “Atlas Shrugged.” This “Billionaire’s Bible” urges peasants to allow the rich to run the world without rules.
Here’s the Democratic rebuttal. Please read “The Grapes of Wrath” by John Steinbeck. It shows how the rich, given the opportunities of the Great Depression, exploited the working class by paying starvation wages and reaping millions.
Clayton Emery
Windham

title: Wisdom Lady Pioneers Make History With First State Soccer Championship
text:
Wisdom Girls Make History With First State Soccer Title as Five County Teams Finish Championship Saturday
Five Aroostook County soccer teams entered Saturday with state championships on the line, and one made school history.
The Wisdom Lady Pioneers rallied from a halftime deficit to defeat Bangor Christian 3-1 in Presque Isle, capturing the program's first girls soccer state championship and bringing a Gold Ball home to St. Agatha.
It was a fitting finish to a remarkable postseason for the St. John Valley, which had five teams representing three schools in Saturday's state championship games.
Fort Kent's boys and girls, Madawaska's boys and Wisdom's boys all finished as state runners-up, bringing an end to seasons that included Northern Maine regional championships.
Here's how Championship Saturday unfolded for the County.
Girls Soccer
Eight-Player: Wisdom Makes History With First State Championship
Wisdom 3, Bangor Christian 1
For the Wisdom Lady Pioneers, Saturday was about more than winning one final game.
It was about making history.
After previous state championship appearances in 1997, 2021 and 2025, Wisdom finally brought home its first girls soccer Gold Ball, defeating Bangor Christian 3-1 in the Eight-Player state championship at Skyway Elementary School in Presque Isle.
And the Lady Pioneers had to come from behind to do it.
Bangor Christian struck first when Rivers Bradford scored with 16:45 remaining in the opening half, giving the Patriots a 1-0 advantage that held through halftime.
Wisdom needed a response, and Emma Soucy provided it.
With 18:25 remaining in regulation, Soucy sent a long free kick toward the Bangor Christian goal. The ball bounced inside the penalty area and found its way into the net, tying the game at 1-1.
Then Ellie Cyr took over.
With fewer than 11 minutes remaining, Cyr converted a free kick from just outside the penalty area to give Wisdom its first lead of the afternoon.
And with 1:13 left, Cyr scored again, sending the ball into an open net to put the finishing touches on a 3-1 victory.
Wisdom goalkeeper Mikayl Michaud finished with eight saves.
It was a remarkable turnaround against a Bangor Christian team that had defeated Wisdom twice during the regular season and beaten the Lady Pioneers 3-0 in last year's state championship.
The victory also ended a long wait for the program.
Wisdom had previously reached the girls state championship game in 1997 and again in 2021, when the Lady Pioneers fell to North Yarmouth Academy 3-0 in the Class D final.
After another runner-up finish in 2025, the Lady Pioneers returned determined to finish the job.
They earned their opportunity with an impressive Northern Maine tournament run, shutting out previously unbeaten Sumner 5-0 in the semifinals before defeating top-seeded Dexter 3-1 in the regional championship.
Cyr scored all three goals against Dexter, then added two more in Saturday's state final.
For a team whose huddles have ended with the familiar chant of “1, 2, 3, FAMILY,” Saturday provided another word worth celebrating.
Champions.
And for the first time in program history, the Wisdom Lady Pioneers can call themselves state soccer champions.
Class C: Maranacook Defeats Fort Kent for State Championship
Maranacook 2, Fort Kent 0
Fort Kent's girls returned to the Class C state championship after capturing their fourth consecutive Northern Maine regional title.
But Maranacook came away with a 2-0 victory Saturday afternoon at Lewiston High School, winning its second straight Class C championship.
Evelyn Stevenson scored both goals for the Black Bears.
Stevenson opened the scoring just over two minutes into the game, giving Maranacook an early advantage.
Fort Kent continued to battle and increased its offensive pressure in the second half, but Maranacook's defense kept the Lady Warriors off the scoreboard.
Stevenson added the second goal with 9:06 remaining to secure the victory.
Fort Kent finished its season at 14-2-2, another impressive year for a program that has become a consistent presence in Northern Maine championship soccer.
The Lady Warriors earned their fourth consecutive regional title with a 3-0 victory over Orono earlier in the week.
Although Saturday didn't bring the result they wanted, four straight Northern Maine championships are an accomplishment worth celebrating.
Boys Soccer
Class C: Hall-Dale Edges Fort Kent in Defensive Battle
Hall-Dale 1, Fort Kent 0
Fort Kent's boys were involved in one of Saturday's closest state championship games, but a second-half goal proved to be the difference.
Greyson Cary scored with 19:44 remaining in regulation to lift Hall-Dale to a 1-0 victory at Lewiston High School.
Fort Kent goalkeeper Kyle Paradis turned in a strong performance, finishing with seven saves, including several important stops in the opening half.
The Warriors had opportunities of their own, but Hall-Dale goalkeeper Landon Gilbert preserved the shutout with three saves.
The Bulldogs captured their third consecutive Class C state championship, with all three title-game victories coming by 1-0 scores.
Fort Kent had earned its spot in Saturday's final with a dramatic 2-1 overtime victory over Orono in the Northern Maine championship, with Dominic Cyr scoring both goals.
The Warriors finished their season as Class C North champions, joining the Fort Kent girls in representing their school at the state finals.
Class D: Monmouth Takes State Title Over Madawaska
Monmouth 8, Madawaska 0
Madawaska's postseason run ended Saturday at Messalonskee High School, where Monmouth defeated the Owls 8-0 in the Class D boys state championship.
The Owls entered the game following a strong Northern Maine tournament, capped by a 2-0 victory over Fort Fairfield in Wednesday's regional final.
Aiden Gagnon opened the scoring in the 13th minute of that game, Josh Querze added another in the 25th, and Aleck Gendreau recorded the shutout.
Saturday's matchup against Monmouth proved to be a difficult one for Madawaska, but the result doesn't take away from what the Owls accomplished this season.
Madawaska finished as Class D North champion, earning its opportunity to compete for a Gold Ball.
Eight-Player: Telstar Defeats Wisdom in Boys Final
Telstar 4, Wisdom 1
Wisdom's boys were hoping to join the Lady Pioneers as state champions, but Telstar came away with a 4-1 victory in Saturday's Eight-Player championship in Presque Isle.
The Pioneers had battled through a challenging Northern Maine tournament to reach the state final.
Wisdom survived a penalty-kick shootout against Calais in the semifinals before defeating Piscataquis 5-4 for the regional championship.
That victory gave the Pioneers an opportunity to compete for a state title close to home.
Although Telstar took the Gold Ball, Wisdom's boys finished their season as Eight-Player North champions.
A Fall Worth Remembering Across the St. John Valley
Five state championship appearances from three St. John Valley schools is an accomplishment worth recognizing.
Fort Kent sent both its boys and girls teams to the Class C finals, with the Lady Warriors capturing their fourth consecutive Northern Maine championship.
Madawaska brought home the Class D North boys title, while Wisdom swept the Eight-Player North championships.
And on Saturday, Wisdom's girls completed their season with a historic victory.
After coming up short in previous state championship appearances, the Lady Pioneers rallied from a halftime deficit to bring home the program's first girls soccer Gold Ball.
There were plenty of moments worth remembering this fall, from overtime winners and penalty-kick finishes to regional championship celebrations and one final state championship.
Congratulations to all five teams, their coaches, families and communities for representing Aroostook County throughout the postseason.
And a special congratulations to the Wisdom Lady Pioneers, your 2026 Eight-Player girls soccer state champions!
The 2026 MPA Soccer Championships on 101.9 The Rock are proudly presented by Pineland Farms in Mars Hill.

title: Police make arrest in a deadly shooting at Winston-Salem State during homecoming weekend
text:
WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. (AP) — Authorities on Sunday arrested a man in a shooting during homecoming weekend at Winston-Salem State University in North Carolina that left one person dead and at least one other person injured.
Winston-Salem police said officers who were on campus for homecoming events heard gunshots around 9:45 p.m. Saturday. They found a 19-year-old man with a gunshot wound. They rendered aid but the man died at the scene.
A 22-year-old woman who had what appeared to be a gunshot wound was taken to a hospital, where she was treated and later released.
Assistant Chief Jason Swaim said at a news conference the investigation led to Ziyaire Spinks, 20, who was arrested and being held without bond on charges of murder, assault with a deadly weapon and possession of a firearm on educational property.
According to police, the shooting stemmed from an argument between two groups of people. They confirmed Spinks was not a student at the university.
A second shooting on campus happened less than an hour later, with police responding when they heard shots. In that case, Swaim said two people were injured when gunfire erupted following an altercation.
Authorities said they were investigating to determine if there was any connection between the two shootings. No arrests have been made in the second case.
Chief William Penn, Jr. of the Winston-Salem Police Department vowed during a news conference that authorities will find all of those responsible for the violence at the school.
“It’s important that the blame of these tragic events go to the right people and that’s the folks who committed these acts,” he said, asking people not to point fingers while the investigation is ongoing.
University officials canceled the remainder of homecoming activities Sunday, saying instead that a local church planned to lead a call for prayers in support of the community.
On social media, community members were sharing their condolences and asking for prayers.
Chancellor Bonita J. Brown called the shootings “senseless violence.” In a statement, she assured students, faculty and parents that the campus was secure and that additional law enforcement would remain while the investigation continues.
The school offered counseling for anyone in need.
“We also recognize the concern and anxiety these events have created among our students, parents, families and broader community,” Brown said. “We take our responsibility for campus safety seriously.”
Forsyth County Sheriff Bobby Kimbrough, Jr. echoed the sentiments of the chancellor and other law enforcement officials during the news conference.
“Right now, the community is in need of your prayers. The community is in need of us coming together,” Kimbrough said.
___
Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Former Brunswick police officer accused of excessive force, false arrest
text:
A former Brunswick police officer who is facing charges for allegedly assaulting a 17-year-old during a 2025 traffic stop is being sued.
The lawsuit, filed in federal court Friday, names Nathan Day, an additional unnamed officer and the town of Brunswick as defendants.
The filing alleges that Day, 27, used excessive and unprovoked force against the teenage girl, slamming her head into her car and onto the ground and knocking her out, leaving her with severe injuries. It also says Day and the other officer falsely arrested her without cause to believe she had committed a crime.
Day was charged with Class D assault in March. He waived arraignment and has pleaded not guilty to the misdemeanor charge.
Brunswick police Chief Scott Stewart confirmed that Day was no longer with the department Saturday.
The name of the teenager — who is now an adult — is included in the lawsuit. The Portland Press Herald is not identifying her because she was a minor at the time of the alleged assault.
The lawsuit alleges that, on the day of the traffic stop, officers pulled over the teen’s boyfriend in the parking lot of the Cook’s Corner shopping plaza. She had been following him in a separate car while they were driving to a body shop to repair a taillight on his vehicle, and she followed her him into the parking lot when he was pulled over.
The filing says the then-17-year-old was waiting across the parking lot when Day ordered her out of her vehicle and assaulted her, knocking her unconscious.
Officers arrested her for traffic violations that were dismissed in September. She was brought to the hospital in handcuffs. She suffered a head wound that required staples, a concussion and foot fractures, and she experienced seizures, the lawsuit alleges.
In an email Friday, Day’s attorney, Marc Beaudoin, denied the allegations outlined in the complaint and detailed a different narrative of the arrest.
Beaudoin said that, while in the parking lot, Day asked the teenager multiple times to come over to him, intending to give her a ticket for using her cellphone while driving. When she refused, Day approached and began to handcuff her, at which point she attempted to move away from him and kicked him in the knee, Beaudoin said.
Day “did not use any excessive force” during the arrest, Beaudoin said, and the teen’s injuries were “inadvertent and due to her own refusal to comply.”
The teen’s lawsuit also cites multiple instances in which Day was disciplined by the department.
According to department records obtained through a public records request this year, Day was formally disciplined three times before the alleged assault — in September 2023, July 2025 and August 2025.
In the August 2025 incident, Day was disciplined and required to complete remedial training after reportedly tackling a suspect. The other two disciplinary reports involve Day driving a police cruiser and pursuing another vehicle in ways that violated department policy.
The suit accuses the town of failing to properly discipline Day for his “escalating misconduct,” and of demonstrating a broader pattern of deliberate indifference toward reports of officer misconduct.
“While Nathan Day’s actions last December are at the heart of this suit, this case is also about the lack of discipline in the Town of Brunswick’s police department, which allowed Mr. Day to stay on the force despite repeated flouting of the Constitution and departmental regulations,” attorneys representing the plaintiff said in a joint statement Friday.
The plaintiff is seeking compensatory and punitive damages, plus attorney’s fees, and has requested a jury trial.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Katie Langley can be reached at klangley@metln.org
Portland Press Herald Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this report.

title: Notre Dame holds off No. 1 Miami in a classic
text:
Notre Dame holds off No. 1 Miami in a classic
Notre Dame holds off No. 1 Miami in a classic
CJ Carr threw for 319 yards and three touchdowns, and No. 4 Notre Dame avenged its most damaging loss from last season by running out to a 21-point lead and holding on to beat No. 1 Miami 31-24 on Saturday night.
Video above: Notre Dame coaches reflect on meeting Pope Leo while in Rome
Micah Gilbert caught two of those scoring passes, Jordan Faison had the other and Nolan James Jr. had a rushing score for Notre Dame (8-1, No. 11 College Football Playoff), which came into the game knowing another loss to Miami could doom its national championship hopes.
Not to worry. The Hurricanes (8-1, No. 1 CFP) started slowly on offense in their first game without injured wide receiver and Heisman Trophy hopeful Malachi Toney — and Notre Dame, which lost to Miami 27-24 last season in a game that ultimately kept the Irish out of the playoff, never trailed.
“I’m happy for this university,” Notre Dame coach Marcus Freeman said in a televised on-field interview. “I’m happy for our players. There’s a lot of support from Notre Dame Nation and this is special moment for them. ... They’re a dang good football team and they beat a dang good football team.”
Darian Mensah threw three touchdown passes for Miami, twice getting the Hurricanes within a touchdown after they trailed 24-3 early in the third. Cooper Barkate had a pair of those scoring grabs, and Elija Lofton had the other.
Lofton nearly had a touchdown catch that would have made it 31-30 — the score of the Miami-Notre Dame game in 1988 — with 3:36 left, appearing to make a fourth-down grab in the end zone and getting his feet down.
But Notre Dame's Luke Talich — who had an interception in the third quarter — knocked the ball away, with officials ruling that Lofton didn't complete the grab. Notre Dame took over on downs, ran the clock down to about a minute and held on from there.
Miami coach Mario Cristobal said he was “beyond upset” that Lofton's play wasn't ruled a score.
“Obviously, a tough loss to take,” Cristobal said. “Proud of our players for the resilience. ... Don't leave it in the hands of the officials. Play better. Coach better. Find a way to win.”
With Miami falling, only two unbeaten teams remain in the Football Bowl Subdivision — Utah and UCLA, which both moved to 9-0 with wins Saturday. This is the first time since 2003 that only two teams made it through the first nine games unbeaten; TCU and Oklahoma did it that year.
On a night when 43 NFL scouts were part of a jam-packed crowd at Notre Dame Stadium, where it was 40 degrees Fahrenheit at kickoff and fell into the mid-30s as the night went along, the Irish stayed true to their mantra for 2026 — one born from the frustration from not making the CFP field a year ago.
They left no doubt. It got a little shaky at the end, but the Irish's CFP hopes are very much alive.
