title: Maine students become lawmakers for the weekend in Augusta
text:
Maine students become lawmakers for the weekend in Augusta
The Youth and Government program allows students to draft legislation, advocate and take on leadership roles under the State House dome.
Maine students become lawmakers for the weekend in Augusta
The Youth and Government program allows students to draft legislation, advocate and take on leadership roles under the State House dome.
Two hundred students from Presque Isle to York gathered under the State House dome this weekend for the Maine YMCA's Youth and Government program. Over the course of four days, high schoolers drafted and advocated for legislation they would like to see become Maine law.
"This year as a cabinet and as a program, we have stepped up to be more inclusive of everyone's voices," said David Shaw from Presque Isle High School.
The program allows students to form working groups, decide on priorities and write and vote on bills. There is also a governor elected each year.
"I would like to hear everyone's voices, and support all, and be on their side," said Mustafa Muhee, the 2027 youth governor from Deering High School in Portland.
In his inauguration speech, Muhee said the program has given him friendships, leadership lessons and the ability to represent his peers. Muhee said he is inspired by leaders like former President John F. Kennedy Jr.
"It's a lot of great civic engagement. The young people get a chance to see what they are talking about in classrooms and how government works," said Lonnie Steves, who has been the program director for 53 years.
If you would like to learn more about the program or get your high school involved, you can learn more on the Youth & Government Program website.

title: The ads have finished. The problem remains.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The midterm elections are finally over, and so are the nonstop political ads paid for by billionaires and dark money groups.
In Maine alone, $315 million was reportedly spent on political advertising according. Money that could have been spent on better things. I made ample use of my mute button and recycle bin, and I’m sure I wasn’t alone in tuning out the repetitive, inflammatory half-truths these ads foisted upon us.
As disheartening as our current political spending situation is, I’m confident it can be fixed. A solution is gaining momentum: a constitutional amendment that would restore the authority of states to set reasonable rules for money in elections. H.J. Res. 191 has been introduced in Congress and 25 states, including Maine, have already signaled their support for an amendment. This is a unifying issue. More than 70% of Americans, whether Republicans, Democrats or independents, agree we need campaign finance reform.
Yes, it’s over for now. But how long before PACs and out-of-state money flood our airwaves and mailboxes again? Let’s not let our voices be drowned out by elite donors next time. Learn more about this vital issue and urge your members of Congress to co-sponsor H.J. Res 191.
Bonnie Sammons
Belgrade

title: Crews fight wildfire in White Mountain National Forest for seventh day
text:
Crews have been fighting a wildfire just over the Maine border in New Hampshire for a week. Since Wednesday, the fire has shrunk from 1,000 acres to 821 and is 29% contained, according to an update Sunday from the White Mountain National Forest.
“Firefighters have been making significant progress on suppression efforts since the fire started on November 1,” read a Forest Service Facebook post Sunday afternoon. “The recent rain will help firefighters continue with these efforts.”
The fire is on the northwest side of the Wild River in Coos County, New Hampshire, just west of Mount Hastings, which is in Oxford County, Maine.
The Forest Service first responded to the fire in an area of White Mountain National Forest about seven miles southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, on Nov. 1. The fire grew to roughly 300 acres on Monday and more than 375 acres on Tuesday. It was estimated to be 982 acres on Wednesday night.
Sarah Hanken, a Forest Service spokesperson, told the Press Herald on Thursday that much of the fire had spread through inaccessible terrain. Officials attribute the fire’s rapid growth to ongoing drought conditions recently declared a disaster in Maine.
The Forest Service is scheduled to hold a community meeting to provide updates on the Wild River Fire on Tuesday at 7 p.m. at Shelburne Town Hall in Shelburne, N.H.
The wildfire and associated smoke can be tracked online via maps produced by government agencies, such as NASA or the U.S. Department of Environmental Protection, in partnership with the Forest Service.

title: 'Little Rascals' star creates GoFundMe ahead of welcoming sixth child: 'No other choice'
text:
'Little Rascals' star makes GoFundMe ahead of welcoming sixth child: 'I have avoided doing one of these'
A former child actor, known for his role in the movie "The Little Rascals," is asking for help during a desperate time in his life.
Brandon "Bug" Hall, 41, said in a GoFundMe fundraiser that he has reached a point where he can no longer manage everything on his own after years of avoiding public requests for financial assistance.
"I have avoided doing one of these in all that time," Hall said in the fundraiser description, noting he has been "self-cancelled" for six years.
Related video: Couple has golden anniversary beneath McDonald's golden arches
The statement continued, saying, "We've made it onto the new land in record time, but I'm a few materials short of having things working right, and I've fallen a little behind on the few bills we have (phone, propane for the camper, and an unexpected electric hookup service fee). We're all overjoyed to be where we are, and we're even enjoying roughing it, but baby six is less than a month away, and I really need some help getting the last few things buttoned up beforehand."
Hall said he hopes to finish the remaining projects over the next two weeks, ahead of their child's arrival.
According to People Magazine, the fundraiser comes months after Hall made headlines for an arrest in Ohio. In April, the outlet said the actor had been charged with failing to appear in court for a December 2024 hearing related to an October 2024 traffic citation for not having liability insurance.
People Magazine said the actor stepped away from Hollywood in recent years, saying he told other media outlets that he had taken a "vow of poverty" and moved his family to an 80-acre property near Mountain View, Arkansas.
There, he said the soon-to-be family of eight planned to live off the grid and build their own home.
Hall rose to fame as Alfalfa in "The Little Rascals" and went on to appear in films including "The Big Green," "Honey," "We Shrunk Ourselves" and "Hercules." He also had television roles in series including "Charmed," "Cold Case" and "CSI: Miami."

title: After historic rout, Maine Republicans chart course out of the political wilderness
text:
Maine Republicans were largely repudiated up and down the ballot on Tuesday.
The party’s figurehead, Sen. Susan Collins, lost her U.S. Senate seat after 30 years. Their gubernatorial candidate, Bobby Charles, earned only 37% of the vote. And they lost seats in both the state Senate and House of Representatives, after coming tantalizingly close to winning the lower chamber two years ago.
Republicans now have the smallest state Senate caucus (at 11 members) since 1984 and the smallest House caucus (at 61 members) since 2018. That means state Democrats will maintain a governing trifecta it’s held since 2018.
The party’s lone bright spot, former Gov. Paul LePage’s victory in the 2nd District congressional race, came via a razor-thin margin in an overwhelmingly Republican-leaning area.
The electoral disaster has left Maine Republicans trying to decide whether it was a one-off national wave, or a signal that the party needs to fundamentally recalibrate its approach to certain issues.
Some believe that Republicans up and down the ballot were simply the victims of a nationalized election cycle, one that produced a so-called “blue tsunami” in opposition to President Donald Trump.
But others believe the party needs new leadership and a fundamental realignment, one that steers clear of xenophobia and culture wars and focuses more on the economic and pocketbook issues that voters said in poll after poll was their top concern.
“The Republicans are going to be in the wilderness until they drop this culture war stuff and start understanding that they need to acquire power for the right reasons: to make economic change in Maine, to make life less hard for Mainers,” said Lance Dutson, a Republican consultant and former Collins staffer. “I don’t foresee the forces at play in the current Republican Party as having any clue that that’s the case for quite a long time.”
When asked in an interview Friday if Republicans need to change their priorities, Maine GOP Chairman James Deyermond focused on what he viewed as positive results for the party.
Deyermond hailed LePage’s 2nd District win, observing that he was the only Republican in the country to reclaim a Democratic-held seat in Congress without being helped by redistricting. And he noted that the party did not see as big of a backlash at the state level as other states.
“We helped save Maine from the calamity that happened to the rest of the country,” Deyermond said. “We stuck with it, and I think we ran a good program.”
But the election results showed it was likely the moderate Collins who helped her party stave off total annihilation here. While LePage crawled to victory in his district, Collins won the area by double digits. At a time when her party has been defined by Trump, Collins, aided by tens of millions in outside spending, proved once again more popular with voters than the president.
Republican state legislative leaders did not respond to interview requests on Thursday. Incoming Republican lawmakers chose Sen. Trey Stewart, R-Presque Isle, and Rep. Kenneth Fredette, R-Newport, to lead their respective chambers’ minorities on Friday.
But Rep. Amy Arata, a former assistant House Republican leader from New Gloucester who is termed out office, said in a Facebook post that her party needs to be more tolerant of people with differing viewpoints. She went on to criticize Trump’s broad, aggressive — and at at times violent — crackdown on immigrants and his punitive tariffs.
Arata lamented that “at least a dozen” of her colleagues were “swept away in a blue wave caused by a president who has some very unpopular policies, along with some good ones.”
“My colleagues didn’t do anything wrong and they didn’t deserve to lose,” Arata wrote. “We need to be free to disagree with (Trump) when he’s wrong, just as we celebrate when he’s right. Otherwise, we will continue to lose wonderful Republican leaders in our state.”
UNABLE TO SURVIVE THE WAVE?
Former state Rep. Laurel Libby, who runs a conservative nonprofit and super PAC, made a national name for herself by opposing transgender athletes in girls’ sports. She believes that Maine Republicans fell victim to a national backlash from Trump not keeping his campaign promises to fix the economy.
“This was not a Maine-specific issue,” Libby said in an 18-minute Facebook video posted Thursday. “This was a blue wave — a blue tsunami — around the country.”
But Republicans would be making a mistake to attribute the losses to Trump alone, said Nicholas Jacobs, a political science professor at Colby College who has studied rural voters.
“I’d be cautious about assuming their problems disappear when Trump leaves office,” Jacobs said. “The party has increasingly become a Trump party in a state that isn’t a Trump state. And that’s part of a much larger national trend in which state and local politics have become almost indistinguishable from national partisan politics.”
Perhaps no Maine Republican embodied the embrace of Trump as did Charles, who won the primary against more moderate and mainstream opponents by leaning into the anti-immigrant and culture war rhetoric. Early in the race, the Leeds lawyer openly embraced Trump, at one point inviting federal agents to patrol polling locations.
This Trumpification has been fueled by the conservative media ecosystem in the state, led by the Maine Wire website, which has largely trained its fire on nonwhite Mainers alleged of fraud or wrongdoing. The Maine Wire is the media arm of the conservative Maine Policy Institute.
“They amplify a hard-right message,” Kevin Raye, a former chief of staff for former Republican Sen. Olympia Snowe, said of the Maine Wire. “And it resonates with the hardcore base. But the base is shrinking and that amplification doesn’t resonate well with the broader electorate.”
Raye, who was the state Senate president from 2010 to 2012, said he disenrolled from the Republican Party back in 2024 when Trump locked up the presidential nomination for the third straight cycle.
“I think that the co-opting of the party by Donald Trump and the MAGA movement have basically driven the party into virtual extinction in New England,” he said.
LIFE WITHOUT COLLINS
Over the last decade, the rightward shift squeezed Collins into an untenable position. To many in her own party, she was never loyal enough to Trump. And to her opponents, she was never doing enough to stand up to him.
“Everybody ignores the fact that I voted to convict him in the second impeachment trial,” a candid Collins told The New York Times after her defeat this week. “What bigger break could there be? It is never enough. I want results and they want angry rhetoric.”
But Collins’ defeat means more than losing a powerful seat in the U.S. Senate in a Democratic-leaning state. The party is also losing a key cog in its fundraising and organizing machine.
“Many people don’t realize the amount that the Collins team does for the Republican Party here in Maine,” Lauren LePage, a GOP strategist and daughter of Paul LePage, said in a social media post. “They’re quiet, they don’t seek credit for it, but they have given enormous amounts of resources to the party. This loss is devastating for our party, but more importantly, for the people of Maine.”
Maine Republicans also have lost their best statewide candidate. And it’s difficult to imagine who will take up the mantle next. Since 2018, Collins was the only Republican member of Congress from Maine.
With Collins not on the ballot, the party has essentially punted statewide races in recent years. Republicans fielded a former state party chairwoman against Sen. Angus King, the independent who caucuses with the Democrats, in 2024. But she got little financial support and lost in a rout. Charles, the Republican who ran for governor this cycle, also lost in a blowout after getting no help from national Republicans, who saw the writing on the wall.
Even Libby, the rising star who was not on the ballot Tuesday, saw her former legislative district flip blue.
THE PATH FORWARD
Lauren LePage said she hopes — and expects — the national and state parties will take a close look at what went wrong.
Dutson, the Republican consultant, pointed to the 2010 cycle as a model path forward. That year, Dutson contended, Republicans focused on pocketbook issues and largely avoided culture wars. And as a result, Republicans won the Blaine House and majorities in both chambers of the state Legislature.
But Duston said Paul LePage, who won with only 38% of the vote in a three-way race, “squandered” that coalition by focusing on culture war issues once elected — and on fighting with leaders and members of his own party.
LePage made national headlines when he told the NAACP to “kiss my butt” when he refused to attend a Martin Luther King Day event. He also removed a pro-labor mural from a state office and frequently warred with the Legislature and press corps.
The Republican consultant said he doesn’t expect the party to change in the near-term, because lawmakers in more competitive districts are the ones getting swept out of office, while those in safe, deep-red districts are getting reelected.
“The extremists survive, so it’s extra hard for the party to heal itself,” Dutson said.
Deyermond said he plans to seek reelection as the party chairman when Republicans hold elections in early January. He said his party will hold Democrats accountable, especially as they contend with a $1.3 billion structural budget deficit.
“We’re going to hold the Democrats’ feet to the fire,” Deyermond said. “They’re going to be here in two years. President Trump won’t be on the ballot in two years, so they’re going to have to find another bogeyman to scare Maine voters.”

title: Police: Father left 6-year-old sleeping in line for Pokémon card release
text:
Police: Father left sleeping daughter outside Target to hold spot in line for Pokémon card release
A Charleston, South Carolina, man was arrested after police said he left his 6-year-old daughter sleeping outside of Target to hold his spot in line for the release of a new Pokémon trading card set.
The Charleston Police Department responded to the West Ashley Target on Friday around 2:30 a.m. after receiving a report of an unattended child.
Police said when they arrived, they learned the child had been waiting in line with her father, who was later identified as John-Michael Dooley, 35, of Johns Island.
Related video: 9-year-old boy sells rare baseball card for nearly $75,000
Customers had begun lining up outside of the store while awaiting the release of a new Pokémon trading card set.
Witnesses reportedly told police that around 1 a.m., Dooley gave his daughter a pillow and blanket before leaving her sleeping in line. After an hour passed without returning, concerned customers called police.
Officials said Dooley later returned to the store and was identified by witnesses. He was arrested and charged with unlawful conduct toward a child.
In an interview with police, Dooley admitted to returning home and leaving his daughter to hold his place in line in order to avoid missing the opportunity to purchase the cards.
Officials said the child was unharmed and placed into emergency custody by the South Carolina Department of Social Services.
Dooley is being held at the Al Cannon Detention Center.

title: IRS releases 2027 tax brackets. Here’s what you can expect to pay
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - The 2027 tax brackets and standard deductions are now out – and they’re higher to compensate for inflation.
The IRS says brackets for individuals are up a few hundred to a few thousand dollars. Those for married couples are double that for most income levels. The standard deduction for single filers is $500 more at $16,600. For married couples, the increase is $1,000.
The IRS changes tax brackets based on the Consumer Price Index. The 2027 adjustment is a half percentage point more than the previous year’s since inflation is higher.
The IRS is also announcing tweaks, like a $100 Child Tax Credit bump.
“American individuals and businesses will see increased tax benefits next tax year ranging from an increase in the standard deduction and the Child Tax Credit for families,” said IRS CEO Frank J. Bisignano in a news release.
Experts say taxpayers might want to review the changes to consider whether to make withholding adjustments.

title: President Trump and his Justice Department stand defiant as Democrats ready an investigative blitz
text:
President Trump and his Justice Department stand defiant as Democrats ready an investigative blitz
President Donald Trump and his Department of Justice are taking a combative stance toward Democrats after their election victories in the midterms, signaling intense conflict to come as lawmakers prepare aggressive investigations into the executive branch next year.
Trump set the tone, declaring on social media that investigative requests already made by Democrats are “extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable.” Attorney General Todd Blanche echoed the Republican president and said criminal investigations of Democrats are possible.
Related video above: What Democrats will do with control of Congress
“They are not allowed to just go around threatening existing members of the administration, to go around threatening companies, and that’s what President Trump is extremely worried about and he should be,” Blanche said as he and congressional Democrats appeared on the Sunday news shows to discuss the repercussions from last week's elections.
Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, is preparing investigations into what he calls the “Trump crime family.” He said Democrats are not going to be intimidated.
“The days of us not fighting back are over,” said Garcia, D-Calif.
The early rhetoric sets up a showdown ahead that will likely define Trump’s remaining two years in office and test the power of Congress to put a check on the White House. About 7 in 10 voters nationally say Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.
Democrats have made clear that impeachment is an option.
If there are people who have been "shortchanging the American people, screwing over the American people, or stealing from the American people, then they need to be held accountable in a manner consistent with Congress’ role, constitutionally,” said Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York.
Some Democrats are worried about overreach
But the investigative onslaught is also a source of tension for Democrats, with many warning that delivering on their central promise to voters — actions to lower the cost of living — must take precedence.
Some fear their resounding wins Tuesday that have given them healthy majorities in the House and Senate will prove fleeting if conflict with Trump defines the agenda.
Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, the first Democrat elected to the chamber from Kansas in 94 years, expressed skepticism about impeachment, saying his campaign was about trying to bring people together. He said he does not want the next two years to be spent “dividing our country further.”
“I’m not as interested in impeachment as setting up guardrails,” Hamilton said. Still, Hamilton said he understands that some investigations are necessary, and Democrats “have to look at what’s happened in Washington.”
Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, said he wants to hold Trump accountable, but warned there was only so much time.
“We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump," Sanders said. "We’ve got to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives.”
Related video below: How soon could Democrats try to carry out their affordability agenda?
Jeffries casts doubt on working with Stephen Miller
Jeffries, who is on the cusp of becoming the nation's first Black House speaker, was asked on election night about the prospects of working with Trump. He said he would be ready to work with the other side of the aisle “whenever and wherever possible to deliver real results.”
Jeffries on Sunday criticized Trump's choice of longtime adviser Stephen Miller to succeed Susie Wiles as his chief of staff, calling him an “awful choice” and cast doubt on the prospect of working with him.
“There’s not going to be an opportunity, certainly, to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents. And we’re committed to forcefully pushing back against the extremism that they may try to continue to unleash on the American people,” he said.
Related video below: President Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff amid debate over immigration enforcement
Democrats across the ideological spectrum have been critical of the appointment of Miller, an architect of Trump's mass deportation machine that became an issue in the midterm elections. Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the administration’s actions on immigration enforcement had “gone too far,” according to The AP Voter Poll.
Jeffries also said he supports a pending resolution from Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Jeffries said Democrats would be discussing it when they return to the Capitol this week. “Hegseth has got to go,” he said.
“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said.
Hegseth in a video dismissed the impeachment push as “all about the politics of personal destruction.” He said it “won’t work with me."
New senators express skepticism about Schumer
At least two new incoming Democratic senators expressed some reservations Sunday about Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who’s expected to be reelected to his post after leading his party back to the majority.
Hamilton said he’s told Schumer, who is currently running unopposed, that he means no disrespect but that the New Yorker is a polarizing figure in Kansas and Hamilton is aiming for someone less divisive.
“What I’d be looking for is a leader who can lead from the center, somebody who can bring Republicans and Democrats together,” Hamilton said. “It feels like it is a time for fresh and new ideas and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us.”
Hamilton said he wants to get to know the other Democratic senators better before he makes any recommendations.
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, whom Schumer did not back in the Democratic primary, said he had been committed to Sen. Chris Van Hollen, but acknowledged that the Maryland Democrat does not appear to be running for the post.
El-Sayed said he and Schumer, who put $67 million into El-Sayed’s general election campaign, “figured out how to work together” after the primary.
“The question to me is, who wants to be the leader who’s going to make sure that we deliver on the mandate that we just got?” El-Sayed said.
Blanche was interviewed on “Fox News Sunday” and CNN's “State of the Union.” Garcia also was on CNN, Jeffries spoke on ABC's “This Week,” Hamilton and Sanders were on CNN and NBC, and El-Sayed appeared on ABC.
___
Associated Press writers Mary Clare Jalonick and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over foreign intelligence concerns
text:
Nvidia launches investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over foreign intelligence concerns
Nvidia is opening an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company’s board of directors said Sunday.
Video above: House Speaker Mike Johnson discusses voluntary AI safeguards 
The announcement came after Huang acknowledged to the board that he had been intimate with a business executive who U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for Beijing, The New York Times reported.
Huang apologized in a message to the company, according to the Times. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he said. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Nvidia’s board said in a statement it has “no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” the board said.
Huang, 63, will remain CEO during the investigation.
Nvidia has become a central player in the global race to develop artificial intelligence, with its chips powering many of the data centers and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced processors have also been a focus of U.S. export restrictions aimed at limiting China’s access to cutting-edge semiconductor technology.
The Times reported last month that U.S. intelligence agencies had discovered that Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and chip buyer, and determined that she was feeding information directly to Beijing. The two are not related, according to the Times.
Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive of Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times.
President Donald Trump addressed the reports at his Halloween party, calling the situation “very complex” and saying he hoped everything was OK with Jensen Huang, who serves on the president’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. The president has called Huang “smart” and “amazing,” insisting that Huang accompany him on foreign trips.
“I've always found Jensen Huang to be very aboveboard,” Trump told reporters on Oct. 31, adding that the administration would look into the matter “very closely.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday as he was departing the U.S. for a G7 meeting in Paris that he could not address the situation with Huang.
“I just can't comment because of the nature of it,” he told reporters. “And I also can't comment on an internal corporate matter that's going on with Nvidia.”
Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street’s earnings expectations in the three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI’s best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August.

title: Obituary: Jennifer (Andrew) Silberman
text:
STRAFFORD, N.H. – Jennifer Andrew Silberman, 76, left us unexpectedly on Nov. 1, 2026 at her home in Strafford, N.H.
She was born Dec. 31, 1949 in Portland, Maine, the daughter of Laurence Clyde Jr. and Virginia Andrew of Windham, Maine. Jennifer spent her childhood years in Windham before moving to Boston for college to study fine art at Cambridge Junior College, and then ultimately graduating from Boston University School of Fine Art. She spent years learning, practicing, and immersing herself in any and all mediums of art.
Jennifer spent time teaching art in Boston area schools before moving to Strafford, N.H. with Mark Silberman to start a family and bask in the rural life. There, they started Sweet Core Farm apple orchard, which became a cherished meeting spot in town. Jennifer balanced running the family farm stand while raising her two children and helping with after school programs. Her vibrant personality and dedication to Strafford quickly made her a beloved fixture in her community.
In her decade as a paraprofessional at Coe-Brown Northwood Academy, she helped carry her student’s heavy burdens and made life a little lighter, better, and happier for them. She was guided by her empathy and desire to help others, and this true kindness made her a student favorite who had long-lasting impacts on their lives.
She was a gardener, artist, loving mother and grandmother, aunt, friend, neighbor, putterer, tinkerer, and home project fix-it dabbler. Everything she did was done with a profound sense of love and humor, as well as an unmatched ability to laugh at herself.
Jennifer found beauty and usefulness in every object she saw. This, of course, made her a world class collector of trinkets, antiques, clothing, electronics, shoes, papers, home goods, and everything with a yellow sale sticker at the Salvation Army, generally much to everyone’s loving chagrin.
She was lively, zany, kooky in the best way, and filled with laughter. We’ll cherish these aspects as well as her enthusiastic body gestures while telling stories and recounting her latest adventures, most often accompanied with snorting laughter. Her warmth, New Englander grit and spirit, and compassion for everyone she crossed paths with will be impossible to forget.
Jennifer is survived by several cousins; nieces and nephews; daughter, Megan Silberman Jones and granddaughter Elora Jones of New Hampshire; and son, Ben Silberman and his long-time partner Sarah Hebbel-Stone of Brooklyn, N.Y.
A celebration of life will be held in the spring when the warming sun and emerging perennials mirror her bright and sunny disposition and love of the planting season. Official date and location will be announced closer to that time.

title: Poles mourn rare mass killing as authorities say attacker had far-right views
text:
Poles mourn rare mass killing as investigators say attacker had far-right views
Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday after a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him.
The attack, which Poland’s defense minister described as an “act of terror,” happened on Saturday in the Main Square, in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town. The square is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city.
Related video: Russian missile strikes on former Ukraine school
As the authorities continued their investigations, the square reopened Sunday evening with mourners gathering to lay flowers and candles in honor of the victims.
St. Mary’s Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight, the first time the call had been missed since World War II.
On Sunday afternoon, St. Anne’s Church in Krakow filled with mourners attending a memorial service.
Authorities also found the bodies of the assailant’s sister, mother and father at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds.
Woman injured by shrapnel while saving another
Witness Andy Hill told the BBC that he’d felt as though he was in a movie scene.
“It doesn’t feel real,” the British tourist said. “And the trouble is, you have such an instantaneous moment to make a decision: Run. Stand still. There’s an element of shock. But I just thought the easiest thing to do is dive through a doorway and just take refuge behind the windows.”
Warsaw native Magdalena Frączak, meanwhile, was visiting Krakow with her friend when shots rang out Saturday afternoon and the gunman drew closer.
“I threw an elderly woman behind the flower planter because she had become tangled in the blanket she had on her lap. I covered her with my body," Frączak told The Associated Press. "I also saw him out of the corner of my eye — he passed just one meter behind my back. That’s why I have shrapnel wounds in six places on my back. Only after it had passed did I pull the woman up, and we ran into a café."
On Sunday, she forced herself to return to the Main Square to grieve among other mourners.
“I can’t put it into words. Because I knew that I would never come back to Krakow if I didn’t come in here," she said. “When I found out that they had reopened the Main Market Square, I told my friend that I had to come here.”
Maciej Sikorski, a Krakow local, also visited the memorial Sunday.
“I come here so as not to get caught up in a spiral of fear and anxiety," he told the AP. "In a situation like this, it’s all too easy to stop living — to start being afraid instead, and just vegetate. That is something I really want to avoid.”
American tourist Marylin Green mourned the losses in the “beautiful city" during her first trip to Poland that also included the capital.
“I’m Polish, my parents were from here,” she said. "I loved Warsaw. So I was really looking forward to coming here, too.”
Police officers described as heroes
Prosecutors said Sunday they opened an investigation into the murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act “constituting a terrorist offense.”
Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead.
A video posted on social media showed a police officer repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street. The officer later slowly collapsed to the ground.
The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in the hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon.
“If it weren’t for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher,” Klęczar said.
Michał Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak, two local surgeons who were having a bite to eat nearby, also stepped in.
Wierdak "took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help,” Pędziwiatr told Polish news website onet. “Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life.”
Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.
The suspect is also in critical condition after undergoing multiple surgeries. There was confusion on Saturday about his age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed that he is 24.
The suspect’s dead sibling was a young artist studying at the Krakow Academy of Fine Arts. “Nothing will ever be like before. The delicate tissue of our academic community was painfully wounded,” the academy wrote in a statement on Sunday, confirming that Magdalena Oksińska was a third year student and that, additionally, the sister of an academy employee was shot twice.
“Magdalena Oksińska, 21 years old, a queer person, was an absolutely talented painter, photographer, poet and writer,” architect Pavko Krajka wrote in a post on social media, accompanied by images of the artist’s colourful paintings. “Her death is a great loss for Krakow, Polish, European and queer culture.”
The mass killing marks a grim first for Poland
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect holds “very radical” and “ultranationalistic” views.
“Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” Kierwiński said at a news conference Saturday.
Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found on the suspect or in his car in Krakow. Both father and son had gun permits, they said.
Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising.
The Swit shooting club in Starachowice, where the suspect is believed to have trained, issued a statement on Sunday saying it offered only “static shooting,” which involves firing from a fixed position at a stationary target. The club added that the suspect “was never trained in our club in the areas of dynamic, tactical or combat shooting.”
Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The young attackers used knives or other sharp objects. Officials blamed the school attacks on online “glorification of violence,” and said that some of the attackers were active in the far-right environment.
The Krakow shooter’s military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other “extreme right lone actors” committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague.
“We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland,” he said.
___
Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland. Associated Press writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.

title: Here’s what state passed a ban on transgender girls in female sports
text:
(AP) - A ballot measure approved Tuesday by voters in Washington state will prohibit transgender athletes from participating in girls’ school sports.
Proponents said the new law will increase fairness and safety in girls’ sports. Opponents had argued the measure could require invasive exams of many athletes to weed out a small number of transgender ones.
Similar laws are common in Republican-controlled states. But lawmakers in Washington and other Democratic-dominated states have not previously advanced them.
Republicans have emphasized the issue in recent years — and a growing number of Democratic politicians have aligned with them, at least partly.
The measure was placed on the Washington ballot through a citizens’ initiative. The state Legislature could change or repeal the law after two years with a simple majority, or sooner with support of two-thirds of both the House and Senate.

title: This election, Maine wanted one thing: Something different
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUBURN — Kelly LaSalle didn’t vote.
“I’m looking for people that look out for all of us,” the 49-year-old said as she dragged on a cigarette outside Hannaford during the midday drizzle.
The $287 million tidal wave of ads that washed over Maine voters this season left LaSalle unimpressed with both Democrat Troy Jackson and Sen. Susan Collins.
She’d voted for Collins in the past, but has felt lately that the five-term Republican, hailed recently by a former colleague as the “soul of the Senate,” no longer cared for working people. And what seeped out of that advertising wave didn’t leave her any more impressed with Jackson, whom she blamed for the high cost of gasoline.
“He has been elected?” she said Thursday. “Oh shit — sorry. I didn’t know.”
In the trunk of her utility scooter, LaSalle carried a single bag of groceries. For $100, she could once fill several such bags. Now, just the one. She’d like her elected representatives to do something about that, but was convinced by the advertising that Collins was in it to enrich herself and that Jackson was responsible for the high cost of living.
Waking up after Jackson’s poll-predicted but nonetheless astounding victory over Maine’s stalwart senior senator, voters of all persuasions had a single message for their newly elected officials: understand the struggle of the everyday Mainer.
“It’s nice to see someone in the working class position have a seat and a position of power,” said Henry Tardiff, 21, of Old Orchard Beach.
It’s not exactly a novel message. (No need to look further than “Joe the Plumber,” an Ohio man whose dialogue in 2008 with then-candidate Barack Obama sparked widespread conversations about the struggle of working class Americans).
Voters said that things aren’t working for them, and transcended party lines to make that point.
They hope Democratic Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree will improve the state’s public education system. They hope Jackson will work to lower costs.
Their outlook on the future is still, in many cases, shaded by party politics.
“It’s scary economic times,” said Justin Crockett, a Belgrade Republican. “I would not want to be a senior living on a fixed income in the state right now.”
He was among those who told the Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram in a survey this summer that life in Maine was getting worse.
Attendees react to the news that the Maine Senate race was called for Troy Jackson at the Democratic watch party at the Holiday Inn in Portland. (Brianna Soukup/Staff Photographer)
Jackson won, Crockett suspects, “not because he’s such a great articulate candidate,” but because of anger at the national level over gas prices and the Iran war. He has little faith that Maine’s incoming junior senator can do much to prevent oil companies from gouging consumers but remains hopeful that local officials can turn things around.
Compared with Crockett’s tempered pessimism, Brittany Bennett, of South Portland, has a muted sort of optimism.
Loading $230 worth of groceries — about three shopping bags — into the car at Hannaford, she said it was time for Collins to go.
“I think that everybody is concerned about cost of living, I think that everyone is concerned about heat, electricity, all of those things,” Bennett, 49, said. “I’m not sure what we’re actually going to be able to get passed.”
Fern Lake, 61, an Auburn voter who backed Collins, suspects Jackson won’t last in the Senate, citing some of the ethical and moral concerns raised in attack ads against him.
Others are unsure that Democrats will rise to the occasion despite gaining full control of Congress.
“I want to see strategy, I want to see plans. I don’t want to see a lot of arguing back and forth,” said another elated voter, Cathy Moran, 63.
For many voters, the lackluster state of affairs motivated them to try something new.
Auburn represented that perhaps better than anywhere else in the state. Maine’s fifth-largest city swung nearly 13 points, from favoring Collins by 8 points in 2020, to backing Jackson by almost 5 on Tuesday.
Jason Spaulding, 49, lives in Auburn. He was born there and works as a certified residential medication aide. He’s “an everyday guy” who’s really struggled with the price of gas and housing.
Spaulding said he doesn’t really have anything against Collins, and he’s the type of voter Collins successfully relied on in the past to keep her seat. But he hasn’t seen her make his life any better recently, and she’s been in the Senate about as long as he’s been able to vote.
“I just felt that she’s been in there my entire life, so I was like maybe somebody different,” Spaulding said.
So he cast a ballot backing Jackson and Pingree. But his expectations are low.
“Seems like sort of more of the same,” he said. ” I don’t think it’s a big fix.”
Even Nancy Robinson, a Republican from Cornville, a decidedly conservative hamlet of Somerset County, woke up feeling great on Wednesday. The 76-year-old thinks of herself more as an independent, and she voted for Collins for the same reason many centrists, and even some Democrats, have in the past: “she brings a ton of money to the state.”
But she ranked Jackson second, and picked Rick Bennett, an unenrolled former Republican, for governor.
The Iran war needs to end, Robinson said. “I sound just like everybody else,” she acknowledged, but prices need to come down.
“I’m also incredibly happy that the campaign is over with. I don’t ever want to see another ad for anybody again.”
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: AP Top 25 live updates: Notre Dame and Georgia are in line for No. 1
text:
There could be a new No. 1 coming for the AP Top 25.
The question is which team will take over after No. 4 Notre Dame knocked off No. 1 Miami on Saturday night.
The Fighting Irish, whose only loss was to a top-10 BYU, have a strong case. So does No. 2 Georgia, which beat No. 12 Mississippi in an impressive all-around performance.
No. 3 Utah, which remained undefeated with a victory over No. 7 BYU, could also find backers.
Stick around for poll projections, voter Q&A and live updates. The latest rankings drop at 2 p.m. EST.
Who decides the rankings?
By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS
AP Top 25 voters are writers and broadcasters who cover college football.
AP employees do not vote, but they do choose the voters, and they seek wide representation from all over the country. This season, there are 69 voters.
The focus begins with voter representation in states with a Bowl Subdivision school, and the total number of voters from each state increases with the number of FBS teams. There are also spots reserved for national voters.
The AP allows broad latitude for voters to determine their rankings. They are urged to base their votes on performance, not reputation or preseason speculation (except, of course, for the always provocative preseason poll); to avoid regional bias, for or against; to pay attention to head-to-head results; and to make significant changes if desired.
Georgia rolls past Ole Miss
By MAURA CAREY
One of the more highly anticipated Southeastern Conference matchups of the season ended in a blowout, as Georgia cruised to a 42-7 defeat of Ole Miss on Saturday night.
The Bulldogs dominated on both sides of the ball, forcing two turnovers and sacking quarterback Trinidad Chambliss five times while allowing just one score. Quarterback Gunner Stockton accounted for five total touchdowns, four passing and one on foot.
Three of Stockton’s four touchdown passes belonged to receiver Talyn Taylor. The Bulldogs found success in the running game, outrushing a Kewan Lacy-less Ole Miss team 295-66.
It was Georgia’s fifth win by 35 points or more over a top-10 team in the CFP era (since 2014).

title: Crews fight wildfire in White Mountain National Forest for seventh day
text:
Crews have been fighting a wildfire just over the Maine border in New Hampshire for a week. Since Wednesday, the fire has shrunk from 1,000 acres to 821 and is 29% contained, according to an update Sunday from the White Mountain National Forest.
“Firefighters have been making significant progress on suppression efforts since the fire started on November 1,” read a Forest Service Facebook post Sunday afternoon. “The recent rain will help firefighters continue with these efforts.”
The fire is on the northwest side of the Wild River in Coos County, New Hampshire, just west of Mount Hastings, which is in Oxford County, Maine.
The Forest Service first responded to the fire in an area of White Mountain National Forest about seven miles southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, on Nov. 1. The fire grew to roughly 300 acres on Monday and more than 375 acres on Tuesday. It was estimated to be 982 acres on Wednesday night.
Sarah Hanken, a Forest Service spokesperson, told the Press Herald on Thursday that much of the fire had spread through inaccessible terrain. Officials attribute the fire’s rapid growth to ongoing drought conditions recently declared a disaster in Maine.
The Forest Service is scheduled to hold a community meeting to provide updates on the Wild River Fire on Tuesday at 7 p.m. at Shelburne Town Hall in Shelburne, N.H.
The wildfire and associated smoke can be tracked online via maps produced by government agencies, such as NASA or the U.S. Department of Environmental Protection, in partnership with the Forest Service.

title: Greene man faces drug charge after undercover investigation
text:
A 40-year-old Greene man faces an aggravated drug trafficking charge after a months-long undercover investigation by agents with the Maine Drug Enforcement Agency.
The investigation centered on Arthur Hall’s home at 32 Hills Ridge Road in Greene and included surveillance and undercover drug purchases at the residence and in surrounding towns, police said in a statement.
On Saturday, agents learned that Hall, who had been out of state, was on his way back to Maine, allegedly with a supply of drugs for resale in central Maine.
MDEA agents and the Maine State Police tactical team stopped Hall on Route 9 in Sabattus after the car he was in exited Interstate 95.
Hall was arrested and agents searched his vehicle, seizing cocaine base and fentanyl.
Agents — working with the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office and the federal Drug Enforcement Administration — then executed a search warrant at Hall’s home, where they say they found more fentanyl, cocaine base and two handguns, police said.
In total, agents seized 70 grams of cocaine base and 50 grams of fentanyl, with an estimated street value of $12,000.
Hall’s bail was set at $20,000 cash.

title: How to manage your central Maine electric bills in the colder months
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As the weather turns colder and the days get shorter, Mainers will need more of two things: heat and light.
Both cost money, and as heating oil prices rise, many worry how they’ll make ends meet and stay comfortable this winter.
Thanks to a state law, Central Maine Power will not disconnect your electricity service from Nov. 15 to April 15, but staying on top of your bills while winter protections are in place is vital.
If you’re worried about your balance or you just want to be prepared, here are some resources that can help.
DIRECT ASSISTANCE
Rhonda Yorks is Central Maine Power’s customer advocate. She meets with customers to answer account questions and help connect them with assistance and support they might be eligible for.
People often ask Yorks how they can reduce their usage, but she said her biggest challenge is getting people to sign up for assistance programs that could help them.
“What I hear a lot is, ‘Somebody else needs that more than I do,’ or ‘That’s not the generation I was brought up in,'” Yorks said.
Yorks encourages customers not to look at assistance programs as handouts. 
“All of us, as ratepayers, all pay toward these programs,” Yorks said. “Apply. The worst thing that’s going to happen is you find out if you’re over income or not, and you’re not eligible. But if you are, it could be a huge benefit.”
Yorks especially wants people to look into assistance programs because she’s worried about this winter. She said it will be a hard one, thanks to the high cost of heating oil. As people avoid buying oil, Yorks said she thinks they will instead use electric heat or space heaters and spend more on electricity, risking falling behind on their payments.
To avoid having a massive overdue balance come April, Yorks said it’s important customers always pay what they can.
If you budgeted $200 for your electric bill, and it ends up costing $300, pay the $200, she said. The winter months are “the perfect timeframe to pay what you can or as much as you can.”
And fall is the perfect time to make a plan and take advantage of the resources available.
“Use this in-between time … where you’re not necessarily seeing all those impacts yet on your bill,” said Dustin Wlodkowski, senior manager of corporate communications at CMP. “The winter time has all of these pieces that come together at the same time because it is colder, because it is darker.”
LOW-INCOME DISCOUNTS
The Home Energy Assistance Program gives qualified homeowners and renters relief for their heating costs as well as energy-related repairs and utility payments. The program is funded through a federal grant and is limited to those who meet specific income limits.
For a two-person household in Maine, the income limit is $49,784 per year, according to the Maine State Housing Authority. For a four-person household, it’s $73,213. Applications are open through MaineHousing.
The Electricity Lifeline Program, also known as the Low Income Assistance Program is a discount available to year-round, residential customers who qualify based on their annual usage and household income. It gives qualified customers up to $1,200 off their bills, and customers can apply for it as part of their Home Energy Assistance Program applications.
The state’s Arrearage Management Program is another resource available every six years to anyone enrolled in HEAP or the Electricity Lifeline Program, but this one helps with past due balances. The program can help customers reduce their past due balance by as much as $500 every month they pay their current monthly bill on time.
For customers enrolled in the program, a monthly bill paid on time adds a credit worth one 12th of the past due balance to the customer’s overdue account. So if you make your payments on time for 12 months, your past due balance could be forgiven in a year.
To apply, you must have a past due balance of at least $500, part of which is at least 90 days overdue.
PAYMENT PLANS
Low-income assistance isn’t the only resource available, and if you’re in a slightly higher bracket but still struggling, payment plans can help you budget.
For those who call the customer contact center, CMP can offer affordable payment arrangements, Yorks said.
Representatives will work with customers to set up arrangements so they can get caught up on overdue balances, pay current charges and put something toward their past due balance, Yorks said. An arrangement could last anywhere from three to 18 months to help customers stay on top of their bills while they pay off a past due balance.
CMP’s SimplePay Budget Plan also offers a way to customize monthly payments to help with budgeting.
The program takes your last 12 months of usage history and calculates your average monthly payment, so for six months you pay a fixed price. Your price will be reevaluated every six months, but it’s a good way to spread the cost of high-usage months out.
As long as you’re caught up on payments, you can sign up on CMP’s website.
LOWERING YOUR USAGE
While you’re on CMP’s website, you can also sign up for usage alerts — weekly notifications telling you how much power you’ve used and what the costs are so your bill won’t come as a shock — as well as outage alerts.
The Energy Manager helps track energy use and gives tips on how to reduce it, and the Energy Calculator can help you figure out what all your appliances are costing you. Yorks said dehumidifiers, space heaters and medical equipment can be particularly expensive.
Finally, you can use CMP’s rate comparison tool to make sure your delivery rate is right for you.
If you need more help with bills, Yorks recommends 211 Maine, the state’s General Assistance program and The Salvation Army.
CMP’s call center has more than 200 representatives trained to discuss usage and to help with bill problems. Yorks is there for customers who need more direct attention. Reach the call center at 1-800-750-4000.
CMP also hosts community connection events, where customers can stop by to meet team members and ask questions. The next nearby events are set for 1-3 p.m. Thursday at 23 Main St. in Dexter, from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Nov. 18 at 22 Town Farm Road in Hallowell and from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Nov. 19 at 38 Gold St. in Waterville.
The Maine Department of Energy Resources has published a Winter Heating Guide that offers winter heating resources for residents as well as tips to make a home more efficient.

title: UFC’s Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.
Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to “the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior” to become the Republican president’s chief spokesperson.
White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump’s post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.
When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, “Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already.”
He declined to say what conversations he’d had with Trump but said, “I’m sure I’ll have more to talk about after that.”
Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump’s post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words “On to the next chapter.”
The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.
Trump said in his post that he requested that White bring along several UFC fighters as “assistants,” adding, “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”
While White didn’t make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States, he did elsewhere in his news conference describe his ambitions to expand the Zuffa Boxing organization he also runs with Saudi Arabian backers and hold more of its events around the world.
Trump’s post came as his White House is in a period of major transition and struggling with his party’s deep losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections. The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.
Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president’s impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump’s inner circle.
The shake-up at the heart of his administration follows the brief but tumultuous week when Trump tried out a new press secretary in Katie Zacharia, who seemed uncomfortable in her sole appearance before reporters before leaving the job after five days.
The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August. Trump remains without a chief spokesperson.
Trump is close friends with White and has attended several UFC events with him since returning to the White House in January 2025.
He brought White and the sport to the White House’s South Lawn in June for the celebration of America’s 250th year of its independence and the president’s own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed near the executive mansion under " The Claw,” a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.
“It was an amazing experience, this was a one-of-one,” said White afterward.
White also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
___
Associated Press writers Daniel Gelston in Philadelphia and Jesse Bedayn in Austin, Texas, contributed to this report.

Russia targets emergency crews at the site of a deadly strike in southern Ukraine
text:
Russia targets emergency crews at the site of a deadly strike in southern Ukraine
A Russian drone struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine on Sunday, hitting a former school and nearby shelter that had been earlier blasted by multiple Russian guided bombs as residents waited for humanitarian aid, authorities said.
Ukraine said Monday's attack killed at least 55 people in the village of Komyshuvakha, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.
No one was injured in Sunday's strike on the same location, but specialized rescue equipment was damaged, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service.
Related video:
Around 50 people were still listed as missing, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, said. Many of the bodies recovered have not been identified and DNA analysis is ongoing.
Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, told The Associated Press on Saturday that he was still looking for his wife, but had heard no word from rescuers.
“She went to get humanitarian aid, and a 3-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?” he said. “She didn’t come home, and they didn’t find her body there. She isn’t in the morgue, and she isn’t here alive.”
HUR said Saturday that it had identified some of the Russian service members involved in the “double tap" strike with aerial bombs, which destroyed the former school and underground facility used by residents as shelter.
Ukraine has routinely accused Russia of conducting multiple strikes at the same site in quick succession to target emergency crews responding to the initial attack.
The community bids farewell to police officers and neighbors
On Saturday, police officers and relatives gathered in Zaporizhzhia for a farewell ceremony for six officers killed in Russian strikes on Komyshuvakha, including four who died near the former school.
Rain fell as families wept beside the coffins, and officers held portraits of their fallen colleagues.
“They used every skill at their disposal to protect themselves. But when the enemy deliberately gathered civilians in one place and then launched strikes against them, no skills could have helped,” said Andrii Khomenko, a police lieutenant colonel who had worked alongside the victims.
Yuliia Nykonenko, a senior police lieutenant, said the officers had risked their lives to save others, including children. She said they had once escaped a Russian FPV drone together.
The community also said goodbye to three residents among the dead. They were buried near one another, in a part of the Zaporizhzhia cemetery where authorities plan to create a memorial.
Among those mourning was Yurii Karapetian, a community leader whose wife, Natalia Karapetian, was killed. He said she was distributing bread to those in the shelter when the Russian bombs struck.
“This pain, I would say, is unbearable,” he said.
He said his wife chose to stay in Komyshuvakha to help other residents, many of them elderly and living alone. He also urged the international community to act.
“The whole world must understand that if (the Russians) are not stopped, they will not stop. They will not stop at Ukraine. They will not stop anywhere,” he said.
Zelenskyy calls for sanctions on suppliers of Russian missiles
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday called the attack on emergency crews in Komyshuvakha “absolute cynicism and brutality.”
In a post on X, Zelenskyy also said that overnight Russian strikes on energy infrastructure in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region had left more than 600,000 people without power. Other regions also faced outages.
Russia launched 115 missiles, 1,900 guided aerial bombs and more than 3,000 drones against Ukraine in the past week, he said. Many of the missiles had been produced this year, he added, calling on Kyiv's partners to sanction entities involved in their production.
“If the world does not have enough anti-ballistic capabilities to protect Ukrainian skies, then the missiles must be stopped on the production lines," he said, urging the European Union to impose a strong 22nd package of sanctions against Russia.
Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant loses external power supply
The Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, the largest in Europe, has lost its external power supply after a damaged power line was disconnected for safety, the plant’s management reported Sunday.
It said the plant was powered by backup diesel generators since an automatic protection system shut down the damaged Ferosplavna line.
The plant went offline soon after being captured by Russia early in the war, but needs power to keep essential cooling systems running. Its external power supply has been periodically severed, raising fears of a nuclear accident in case of protracted outages, as Moscow and Kyiv blamed each other for strikes that damaged nearby power lines.
___
This story corrects the number of police officers killed in the strike on the former school.
