title: Maine is holding nearly $400 million in unclaimed property. Who’s owed what?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mark Lewyn is the founder of UnclaimedMoneyGuy.com and a former staff writer for BusinessWeek and USA Today. He can be reached at [email protected].
Somewhere in Maine, there are people who have forgotten bank accounts, uncashed checks, missing insurance payments or investments they don’t know exist.
The state knows about that money. In fact, it’s holding nearly $400 million of it.
But when I recently asked Maine’s state treasurer for detailed records showing who is owed the money, how much they are owed and where those people live, the answer was “no.”
On Oct. 13, the Office of the Maine State Treasurer denied my request, citing new confidentiality protections under Maine’s unclaimed property law.
That’s a troubling response from a government agency whose principal responsibility is to reunite people with their own money.
According to Maine’s latest unclaimed property figures, the state was holding $383.1 million as of June 30, 2026, spread across more than 6 million unclaimed accounts.
During the past fiscal year, Maine collected another $63.9 million in unclaimed property while returning $43.2 million to rightful owners.
To its credit, Maine paid 77,286 claims, averaging $560 each. One claimant received $1.5 million.
But consider the larger picture. Between fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2026, Maine’s reported unclaimed property liability climbed from $299 million to $383.1 million. That’s an increase of more than $84 million in just three years.
At what point should a growing mountain of unclaimed money become a public policy concern?
Unclaimed property programs were established to protect consumers. When a bank, insurance company, employer or other institution loses contact with someone who is owed money, it eventually must turn that property over to the state for safekeeping. The state is supposed to hold it until the owner or an heir comes forward.
But there’s an inherent tension in this arrangement.
Under Maine law, unclaimed property is held in custody for its owners. Yet the law also directs the treasurer to transfer money exceeding a specified reserve in the Unclaimed Property Fund to the state’s General Fund.
The money remains claimable, but while it goes unclaimed, the state can use those funds. That creates an obvious question: Does the state have sufficient incentive to find every person it owes money to?
I’m not suggesting Maine is deliberately preventing residents from collecting their property. But when government benefits financially from money remaining unclaimed, transparency and independent scrutiny become especially important.
My Oct. 12 request under Maine’s Freedom of Access Act sought an electronic listing of unclaimed property owners, their last-known addresses, individual property values and other available information. I also requested existing records showing how much unclaimed money is associated with different counties, ZIP codes and legislative districts.
My objective was straightforward: use modern data analysis to help identify people with missing money and better understand which communities are owed the most. I specifically excluded Social Security numbers, bank account numbers and other sensitive information.
The Oct. 13 response stated that the requested information was considered confidential under newly enacted administrative protections. Rather than explaining why each category of requested records was protected, the response summarized legislative changes involving virtual currency, retirement accounts and other provisions.
I asked the office to reconsider its denial and identify the specific legal grounds for withholding the requested information. Again, the response was “no.”
Privacy is important. Nobody needs access to Social Security numbers or confidential financial documents. But Maine already operates a public website where people can search for unclaimed property by name. If identifying owners and reuniting them with their money is the goal, why shouldn’t the state make more of its already public information available in a useful, downloadable format?
And why not disclose approximate dollar-value ranges, allowing people to distinguish between a forgotten $20 check and a potentially life-changing inheritance? Maine law permits the treasurer to publish additional information when doing so would help identify owners and return property, subject to privacy protections.
The issue isn’t simply what information Maine must release. It’s also what information the state could make available to help people recover their property.
There are other important questions worth asking:
- How many accounts have remained unclaimed for 10, 20 or even 30 years?
- How much of Maine’s unclaimed property belongs to deceased residents whose heirs may have no idea the money exists?
- What percentage of the dollars received each year eventually makes it back to rightful owners?
- How much money has been transferred to the General Fund, and how much investment income has the state earned from unclaimed property?
And perhaps most importantly, what proactive steps does Maine take to locate owners beyond maintaining a searchable website and conducting periodic outreach?
These are not unreasonable questions. They are fundamental measures of whether the program is accomplishing its purpose.
Today, sophisticated data-matching technology can connect public records with updated addresses, identify possible heirs and help locate people who might otherwise remain unaware of their money.
Maine deserves credit for returning tens of millions of dollars annually. But collecting $63.9 million while returning $43.2 million in the same fiscal year should prompt a broader examination of whether enough is being done to reduce the growing backlog.
Those figures are not a formal recovery rate, since money collected and returned in a given year can involve different accounts. Still, the long-term accumulation warrants attention.
Maine’s nearly $400 million in unclaimed property isn’t a state windfall. It’s money belonging to individuals, families and businesses. The measure of success shouldn’t be how much money Maine holds. It should be how much money Maine gives back.

title: Exploring our Maine maritime history
text:
Last week science at the Boothbay Sea and Science Center (BSSC) was chalk full of field trips and guest speakers. On Monday, after introductions were done, the campers learned about Wabanaki Birch Bark canoes, cartography with map making, and about maritime use of lighthouses.
The fun didn’t slow down. On Tuesday Craig Condon from the Darling Marine Center spoke with us about Maine’s oyster farming and shellfish industry – bringing us to a better understanding of the impact of climate change on this sector. The Stay’s’ls (ages 9–17) also went to Bristol Marine-Sample’s Shipyard in Boothbay Harbor, where they assembled models of a Sample’s Shipyard wooden dory and took a tour of the maritime museum, learning the history of the shipyard. Many thanks to project managers, Eric Graves and Ross Branch, who led the charge on these activities.
Wednesday was dedicated to learning about the history of Maritime music and songs of the sea with Muriel Curtis - founder and director of Station Maine Leadership located in Rockland, Maine.
To close out the week, the campers learned about celestial navigation and compass bearings with an orienteering challenge. The heat was rough at weeks end ... so lots of water was had by all with cool downs in the ocean.
Last week’s sailing was wet and windy! The start of the week brought showers, keeping us on land knot tying, practicing rigging and derigging on the simulator, and sailing jeopardy. On sunny days, we were able to get both Mizzens and Stay’s’ls out on our big sailboats and Turnabouts. As summer here at BSSC comes to a close, some of our summer long campers who have advanced so much in their sailing skills got the opportunity to solo sail around Linekin Bay. This is our last week of this summer program. We’re looking forward to our annual “Summer Olympics” on Thursday, Aug. 13!

title: Maine needs Hannah Pingree to take the lead on the environment
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kate Sinding Daly is senior vice president for law and policy at the Conservation Law Foundation in Portland.
As we congratulate Governor-elect Hannah Pingree as Maine’s next governor, we need to recognize that this is a moment of opportunity for our state.
Mainers are grappling with rising costs; growing threats to public health; and the impacts of severe storms, droughts and heat waves.
Meanwhile, our federal government is rolling back vital environmental protections. These challenges are deeply connected. Protecting our environment goes hand in hand with making life more affordable, improving public health and building a stronger future for Maine families. The governor-elect has the chance to address some of the most pressing challenges facing our communities.
Here are three key priorities that should be at the forefront of her administration.
First, making polluters pay.
Polluters — not Maine families — should pay for the mess large fossil fuel companies create from peddling oil and gas. Next year, Maine will conduct an assessment of the costs that cities, towns, homeowners, and businesses are now paying to respond to and repair damage after extreme weather events caused by climate change and to adapt to minimize future damage.
The next step is for Pingree to set up a climate superfund program, similar to the hazardous waste superfund programs that already exist, to ensure Maine has the revenue to take the necessary steps to protect its communities, residents and businesses.
We continue to see increased flooding, stronger storms, and more frequent heat waves — which the fossil fuel industry knew for decades would result from ongoing use of its products. A strong climate superfund program would put the responsibility of paying for protecting our state from these impacts on the companies that caused it, rather than where it rests now: on the shoulders of hardworking Maine families.
When polluters pay their fair share of the costs they create, Mainers can better protect public health and invest in safer, more resilient communities.
Second, our next governor must ensure affordability — and accountability.
Maine families and businesses are facing higher energy bills when household budgets are already stretched thin. The cost of propane, oil, diesel fuel, and gasoline is breaking low- and middle-class family budgets, and driving up costs for practically everything, including electricity. Governor-elect Pingree must ensure that our state brings affordable, clean power online and reduces our reliance on fossil fuels with unpredictable prices.
We’ve already seen how clean sources like wind and solar — both of which are free and are not subject to price shocks caused by wars — saved our region millions of dollars during recent cold snaps and heat waves. Bringing more clean energy sources online is critical to lower costs, clean the air we breathe, and reduce the climate-damaging emissions that are raising the levels and temperature of our waters.
Bringing clean energy online is only part of the solution. Maine’s families and businesses also deserve transparency and accountability from the companies delivering our electricity. The state’s Public Utilities Commission is an important body that regulates our utilities, like our electricity and water, and determines what type of energy we use and how much we pay. The Pingree administration has a number of steps it can take to support the PUC and increase transparency around its ongoing work.
As governor, Pingree should also adequately fund the Office of the Public Advocate, an effective but under-resourced voice for Maine families, who should not have to choose between paying their energy bills and meeting other basic needs.
Strong oversight and timely, transparent decisions from those agencies can help protect Maine families and ensure the public interest comes first.
Third, Pingree must work on modernizing permitting while protecting communities.
Maine needs to build clean energy faster, and this must be done with regard for important environmental safeguards and community perspectives.
Governor-elect Pingree should advance sensible permitting reforms to expedite the deployment of clean energy infrastructure and other priority projects. We need to rethink, revise and speed up how state agencies plan and decide on such projects. We must reduce the unnecessary barriers that hinder responsible renewable energy development while maintaining strong environmental protections.
Permitting reform does not mean cutting corners or silencing communities. Transparent decisions and meaningful public participation can identify problems early and help ensure projects serve the public interest.
Environmental justice must remain central to each of these efforts.
Maine needs a clear definition of “environmental justice” and policies that address the disproportionate pollution burdens some communities face. The ongoing battle over the Juniper Ridge Landfill highlights these concerns, particularly for the Penobscot Nation. Working together, we can make sure Maine accelerates clean energy development while protecting natural resources, upholding environmental safeguards and ensuring affected communities have a meaningful voice.
As Governor-elect Pingree prepares for office, she should be focused on tackling significant challenges facing the health of our communities, our environment and our state economy. Pingree can show that environmental protection and economic security go hand in hand. The challenges are real, but with leadership, and by embracing these priorities with urgency and determination, they can and must be addressed.
Together, we can create a brighter, more sustainable future for Maine.

title: Obituary: John E. Thron
text:
PORTLAND – John E. Thron, 93, passed away in Portland on Nov. 6, 2026. He was born in New York City, N.Y. on April 24, 1933 and attended schools in Montclair, N.J. He graduated magma cum laude in philosophy from Princeton University and attained a master’s degree in applied physics from Harvard.
John joined the computer industry in its infancy, working first for Honeywell on their earliest computers. He left the corporate world in the late 1960s to form his own computer consulting firm in Cambridge, Mass. Between consulting assignments, he and his partners developed a computer system that measured the performance of applications running on IBM mainframe computers. That soon became the entire focus of the company and his wife, Anna Marie joined the company. Their program product was sold throughout the United States, Canada, Europe, and Japan and the company grew to 250 employees. He sold the company at the turn of the century and joined Anna Marie in retirement in Maine, spending summers in their Boothbay home and winters in the Portland area.
John served on the boards of the University of New England, Maine Audubon, and Maine Conservation Voters and volunteered with SCORE.
He was predeceased by his brothers, doctors Dennis and Thomas Thron and is survived by his wife, Anna Marie; and his brothers’ extended families.
The family thanks The Cedars Portland for his years of care.
There will be no service. Arrangements are under the direction of the Conroy-Tully Walker, Cremation, Funeral, and Gathering Center, 300 Allen Ave., Portland. To view John’s memorial page or to leave an online condolence, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com.

title: An 11-month-old girl weighed just 4 pounds when she died. Now, her mom is facing charges
text:
NORTH CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) - A South Carolina mother is facing charges after her 11-month-old daughter was found dead and emaciated in an insect-infested apartment.
Janette Clayton, 27, has been charged with homicide by child abuse after her 11-month-old daughter, Nomai Weathers, was found dead in June at an insect-infested apartment in North Charleston.
The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division, which is leading the case, made the announcement about the new charge Friday. Clayton was initially charged with three counts of unlawful conduct toward a child.
Documents show Nomai was born prematurely and diagnosed with sickle cell disease, which required medically necessary appointments. Clayton allegedly failed to take her daughter to these appointments.
Nomai was found dead June 17 near the front doorway of her family’s apartment, partially wrapped in a blanket. She was emaciated, weighing only 4 pounds, 13 ounces.
The apartment was reportedly in “deplorable” conditions, infested with cockroaches and flies. Officials say no food or child care supplies were found.
An autopsy revealed Nomai’s cause of death to be starvation with acute bronchopneumonia due to neglect. The manner of her death was ruled a homicide.
The case also led to two North Charleston Police Department officers, who had previously responded to the apartment, being placed on leave. One was later fired and charged, while the other was reinstated.

title: Patriots take a step back offensively in loss to Packers
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Members of New England’s 2016 Super Bowl-winning team reunited at Gillette Stadium on Sunday for Rob Gronkowski’s induction into the Patriots Hall of Fame.
The current Patriots could have used Gronkowski’s playmaking abilities against Green Bay. The defending AFC champions would also have benefited from having a quarterback who placed a premium on ball security. Alas, Tom Brady was calling the game from the Fox television booth.
From Drake Maye throwing three interceptions in a game for the second time this season, to Rhamondre Stevenson fumbling the ball on a four-turnover day for the Patriots, the signs of regression were everywhere in a 45-27 loss to the Packers.
“I wasn’t good today,” Maye said.
It’s been an up-and-down season for Maye, who was named the AFC Offensive Player of the Month for October after a rough opening month. The 2025 MVP runner-up kicked off the season with a three-interception game against defending Super Bowl champion Seattle.
Maye now has 11 picks, tied with Justin Herbert of the winless Chargers for the most in the NFL.
Maye’s first interception came two plays into the first series of the game. The bad throw gave the Packers a short field, and they needed just two plays to cover 14 yards for a touchdown.
“You can’t put the team in the hole straight off the bat, first possession,” Maye said.
Green Bay made New England pay for the turnovers, scoring 21 points after takeaways. Coach Mike Vrabel said his team became predictable after the Packers took a 17-0 lead.
“It’s tough to spot good teams any sort of lead, and we’ve done that,” Vrabel said.
Once again, the Patriots were without their top two offseason acquisitions at wide receiver, A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs. Running back TreVeyon Henderson remains sidelined indefinitely after revealing last week that he had spent several days in a hospital undergoing tests to determine the cause of unexplained neurological symptoms that have affected his strength and coordination.
Having a healthy complement of offensive options might solve some of the problems currently plaguing the Patriots. Taking care of the ball is another important area to shore up after Stevenson committed his second fumble of the season and the 19th of his career, 11 of which he lost. Stevenson left the game in the fourth quarter after suffering a knee injury.
“We’ve been through a lot, and we’ve got a lot of bumps and bruises. Got some big wins, got some bad losses. We’ve got to find a way to be consistent. Coach (Vrabel) preaches being consistent,” Maye said. “We won the AFC, played in the Super Bowl. Everybody’s coming after us, and we’ve got to respond.”

title: Obituary: Rita (Digilio) Scott Oellers
text:
HALLOWELL – Rita Digilio Scott Oellers, 95, died peacefully at home on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. She was born on June 9, 1931, in New London, N.H., to parents Gaetano and Assunta (Covelli) Digilio. She grew up in Sunapee, N.H., on The Digilio Family Farm, which sold fruits and vegetables. She graduated from Sunapee High School and attended the University of New Hampshire as part of the Class of 1953.
Rita had a lifelong love for learning and was always a “joiner.” She once said there wasn’t one club in high school that she didn’t join. This spirit followed her all the way to the last years of her life, where she proudly served on many committees at Granite Hill Estates retirement community.
Her favorite job was being a mom to her five children. Her home in Winthrop on Maranacook Lake overflowed with the smells of freshly baked goods. Every visit to Rita’s house included a tour of the flower and vegetable garden and a taste of a fresh cherry tomato.
Rita was never idle, always finding ways to enjoy life. In 1984, Rita married Richard “Dick” Oellers and gained four bonus children. They met through mutual friends and in their early years enjoyed going out dancing together and motor homing with friends. Following her retirement, Rita and Dick traveled extensively throughout the country in their motorhome, spending many winters at their second home in Venice, Fla. When she couldn’t travel anymore, she loved to hear the stories of adventures from her children and grandchildren.
For the past 11 years Rita made her home at Granite Hill Estates. Never one to let a new adventure go to waste, she participated in everything they had to offer. She worked out daily, shared the fruits of her garden with the kitchen, and took classes at the senior college. At 93, she took her first writing class and proudly shared her new skill.
She loved the residents and staff at Granite Hill, and could always be counted on for a smile and kind conversation, and they loved her back in turn. Some friends there were new, others she enjoyed 60-plus years of friendship with over her adult life in the Winthrop area. She could not be more grateful for the tender, love, and care she received at Granite Hills from the staff and residents alike.
She is survived by her children, Brad Scott, Greg (Chantal) Scott, Cindy (J.) Brown, Bill (Victoria) Scott, and John (Khristine) Scott, her grandchildren Brian Scott, Amanda Vickery, Jacqueline (Jordan) Kennedy, Weston (Erin) Scott, Leika (Ian) Pinette, Gibson Scott, Jeremy Brown, Julia (Abben) Brown, Kimberly (Liam) Brown, Vincent, Vita, and Rocco Scott, Nicole (Ryan) Conant, Jessica, and Nathan Scott; and great-grandchildren, Colette and Evelynn Vickery, Brayden, Dylan, and Skye Scott , Rowan Conant, and Sawyer Pinette.
Her bonus children, Wendy (Ron) Fulmer, Suzanne (Russell) Naughton, Rick (Teri) Oellers Jr., Elizabeth (George) Oellers; her bonus grandchildren, Katie (Rocco) Criscone, Heather (Zachary) West, Christopher (Kim) Roche, Tori (Garner) Blume, Eric Oellers, James DeTullio, Alexander and Julia Latham; bonus great-grandchildren, Maya and Zoe Criscone, and Emilia and Watson Blume.
Rita was preceded in death by her husband, Richard Oellers; as well as her parents, Gaetano and Assunta Digilio; her siblings, Joe Digilio, Mary Weinstein Hingston and John Digilio; daughter-in-law Margaret Scott.
A celebration of life will be held at a later date.

title: Maine is holding nearly $400 million in unclaimed property. Who’s owed what?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mark Lewyn is the founder of UnclaimedMoneyGuy.com and a former staff writer for BusinessWeek and USA Today. He can be reached at [email protected].
Somewhere in Maine, there are people who have forgotten bank accounts, uncashed checks, missing insurance payments or investments they don’t know exist.
The state knows about that money. In fact, it’s holding nearly $400 million of it.
But when I recently asked Maine’s state treasurer for detailed records showing who is owed the money, how much they are owed and where those people live, the answer was “no.”
On Oct. 13, the Office of the Maine State Treasurer denied my request, citing new confidentiality protections under Maine’s unclaimed property law.
That’s a troubling response from a government agency whose principal responsibility is to reunite people with their own money.
According to Maine’s latest unclaimed property figures, the state was holding $383.1 million as of June 30, 2026, spread across more than 6 million unclaimed accounts.
During the past fiscal year, Maine collected another $63.9 million in unclaimed property while returning $43.2 million to rightful owners.
To its credit, Maine paid 77,286 claims, averaging $560 each. One claimant received $1.5 million.
But consider the larger picture. Between fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2026, Maine’s reported unclaimed property liability climbed from $299 million to $383.1 million. That’s an increase of more than $84 million in just three years.
At what point should a growing mountain of unclaimed money become a public policy concern?
Unclaimed property programs were established to protect consumers. When a bank, insurance company, employer or other institution loses contact with someone who is owed money, it eventually must turn that property over to the state for safekeeping. The state is supposed to hold it until the owner or an heir comes forward.
But there’s an inherent tension in this arrangement.
Under Maine law, unclaimed property is held in custody for its owners. Yet the law also directs the treasurer to transfer money exceeding a specified reserve in the Unclaimed Property Fund to the state’s General Fund.
The money remains claimable, but while it goes unclaimed, the state can use those funds. That creates an obvious question: Does the state have sufficient incentive to find every person it owes money to?
I’m not suggesting Maine is deliberately preventing residents from collecting their property. But when government benefits financially from money remaining unclaimed, transparency and independent scrutiny become especially important.
My Oct. 12 request under Maine’s Freedom of Access Act sought an electronic listing of unclaimed property owners, their last-known addresses, individual property values and other available information. I also requested existing records showing how much unclaimed money is associated with different counties, ZIP codes and legislative districts.
My objective was straightforward: use modern data analysis to help identify people with missing money and better understand which communities are owed the most. I specifically excluded Social Security numbers, bank account numbers and other sensitive information.
The Oct. 13 response stated that the requested information was considered confidential under newly enacted administrative protections. Rather than explaining why each category of requested records was protected, the response summarized legislative changes involving virtual currency, retirement accounts and other provisions.
I asked the office to reconsider its denial and identify the specific legal grounds for withholding the requested information. Again, the response was “no.”
Privacy is important. Nobody needs access to Social Security numbers or confidential financial documents. But Maine already operates a public website where people can search for unclaimed property by name. If identifying owners and reuniting them with their money is the goal, why shouldn’t the state make more of its already public information available in a useful, downloadable format?
And why not disclose approximate dollar-value ranges, allowing people to distinguish between a forgotten $20 check and a potentially life-changing inheritance? Maine law permits the treasurer to publish additional information when doing so would help identify owners and return property, subject to privacy protections.
The issue isn’t simply what information Maine must release. It’s also what information the state could make available to help people recover their property.
There are other important questions worth asking:
- How many accounts have remained unclaimed for 10, 20 or even 30 years?
- How much of Maine’s unclaimed property belongs to deceased residents whose heirs may have no idea the money exists?
- What percentage of the dollars received each year eventually makes it back to rightful owners?
- How much money has been transferred to the General Fund, and how much investment income has the state earned from unclaimed property?
And perhaps most importantly, what proactive steps does Maine take to locate owners beyond maintaining a searchable website and conducting periodic outreach?
These are not unreasonable questions. They are fundamental measures of whether the program is accomplishing its purpose.
Today, sophisticated data-matching technology can connect public records with updated addresses, identify possible heirs and help locate people who might otherwise remain unaware of their money.
Maine deserves credit for returning tens of millions of dollars annually. But collecting $63.9 million while returning $43.2 million in the same fiscal year should prompt a broader examination of whether enough is being done to reduce the growing backlog.
Those figures are not a formal recovery rate, since money collected and returned in a given year can involve different accounts. Still, the long-term accumulation warrants attention.
Maine’s nearly $400 million in unclaimed property isn’t a state windfall. It’s money belonging to individuals, families and businesses. The measure of success shouldn’t be how much money Maine holds. It should be how much money Maine gives back.

title: Want to fly to the moon? NASA is looking for new astronauts to help grow its Artemis program
text:
Want to fly to the moon? NASA is looking for new astronauts to help grow its Artemis program
Want to fly to the moon and help build a permanent lunar base? NASA is accepting applications for a new astronaut class that will help grow the Artemis program.
Officials announced the news Saturday during a Kennedy Space Center air show promoting lunar exploration as well as advances in aviation and technology.
NASA’s last call for new astronauts was two years ago. More than 8,000 applied, with 10 making the final cut in September 2025.
Related video above | America’s space journey from Apollo to Artemis | America 250
With only 32 active astronauts, the space agency needs more recruits as it looks to expand humanity’s presence beyond low-Earth orbit as quickly as possible. April's lunar flyaround by the Artemis II crew kicked off the lunar campaign.
“We have far more work than we have astronauts,” Artemis III commander Randy Bresnik told The Associated Press on Saturday.
Aspiring astronauts have between now and Dec. 3 to submit their applications. NASA expects to make its final selection by late 2027, with the new candidates beginning their training by early 2028 — the same year that NASA intends to return astronauts to the lunar surface after an absence of more than half a century.
By then “we're going to have people on the moon — so don't delay," Bresnik urged potential candidates.
Bresnik and his three crewmates will blast into orbit next summer to practice docking their capsule with a pair of lunar landers, one built by Elon Musk's SpaceX and the other by Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Their mission will stick close to Earth — no lunar flyby — and serve as a dress rehearsal for the following year's Artemis IV mission that will attempt to land two astronauts near the lunar south pole.
The moon base will materialize as more rovers, robots, structures and power grids are launched.
Patience is essential for becoming an astronaut, noted Artemis III's Frank Rubio, whose 371 consecutive days in space is a U.S. endurance record. Candidates must also be U.S. citizens with college degrees and professional work experience.
The two years of mandatory training can be grueling, and it could take another several years on top of that before finally rocketing into space.
“It's important for them to realize most of that work is not going to the moon, right?" Rubio told the AP. “That will be about 1% of your experience. What you're doing is contributing to the mission of going to the moon.”
This will be NASA's 25th astronaut class since the original Mercury Seven in 1959.

title: Marveling at Maine from afar
text:
In his Nov. 5 column (“Susan Collins will be remembered for her service – and her shortcomings”), Steve Collins makes an important point: Sen. Susan Collins has a lot to explain. I think what Maine voters said by their votes is that they didn’t buy the explanations Sen. Collins has offered to date — and were tired of waiting for her to step away from President Trump.
As one who has marveled from afar at how Collins seemed, for years, to convince folks that she was carrying on the legacy of a truly great senator, Margaret Chase Smith, I kept hoping Collins would show the courage Sen. Smith displayed in her “Declaration of Conscience “speech. But all Mainers ever got were declarations of concern.
This election, voters sent a clear message to Sen. Collins: Enough. Our democracy is all the better because of that message. My thanks to Mainers.
Stephen Gladstone
Cleveland, Ohio

title: Rain winds down, then a calmer week
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Rain will clear out this evening leaving lingering cloudiness that will stick around overnight into Monday with the chance for a shower especially to the north and along the coast. Lows will drop into the 30s for most. This week will be much calmer than last week for the most part with seasonable temps and mainly sunny skies. We are keeping an eye on next weekend for our next system potentially.
Sunday night: Rain finally fully departs
After a soggy few days things settle down and a seasonably cool night arrives with some lingering cloudiness. Temps will be in the upper 30s for most.
Monday: A drier day
Things dry out and Monday looks to be a somewhat cloudy day but otherwise typical November weather with highs in the upper 40s and low 50s. There may be a few isolated showers in the morning but otherwise a more placid day.
Tuesday and beyond: A more settled week then watching the weekend
After last week was more active this week looks quieter with few chances of active weather besides the weekend. Highs will mostly be in the upper 40s and low 50s. With lows mainly staying in the upper 20s and 30s. However, we are watching a system for late in the week towards next weekend that could provide some early season snow especially for inland and northern regions. It’s a long way off and there are lots of details to work out but it is something we are watching.
Sunday: Showers early, clearing late. Highs in the upper 40s and low 50s. Winds NE at 10-15 mph.
Sunday night: Rain ends clouds stick around. Lows in the upper 30s and low 40s. Winds NE 5-10 mph then going calm.
Monday: Mostly cloudy but dry. Highs in the upper 40s and low 50s. Winds W 5-10 mph.
Monday night: Still mainly cloudy. Lows in the 30s. Light wind.

title: Obituary: Margaret Pratt
text:
RANDOLPH – Margaret Pratt, 97, passed away peacefully on Oct. 31, 2026, at the Andwell Hospice House in Auburn, Maine.
Born in Farmingdale, Maine, on July 30, 1929, she was the daughter of Alfred and Violet (Leveque) Firlotte. One of nine children, Margaret, was proud of her family and her upbringing on the Marston Road in Gardiner. She attended Gardiner schools and graduated from Gardiner Area High School.
On Aug. 16, 1949, Margaret married James “Bud” Pratt. Together, they built a life on North Street in Farmingdale, where they raised their five children. Following Bud’s passing in 1989, Margaret shared many happy years with her dear companion, Richard “Dick” Howe. In 1963, Margaret opened Margaret’s Beauty Shop in their family home, establishing a successful business while raising her children. She was also active in her profession, serving as both secretary and president of the Maine Hairdressers Association.
Margaret was a woman of remarkable energy, creativity, and determination. A talented seamstress, she took great pride in making clothing for her children and beautifully tailored garments for herself. Her many interests included knitting, crocheting, quilting, embroidery, decorating, gardening, playing cards, bingo, bowling, and dancing. She especially treasured memories of dancing at Island Park Dance Hall in Winthrop and Whippoorwill Dance Hall in Litchfield during her late teenage years.
Never one to sit idle, Margaret maintained a beautiful vegetable garden, prepared countless homemade meals and desserts, and always found time for her love of animals. Her household was rarely without a dog and a cat, and at one time she even raised Angora rabbits.
Margaret generously shared her talents with others. In retirement, she knit matching sweaters for her six Florida grandchildren and made rag dolls, hats, and mittens. She later crafted hundreds of knitted and fleece hats, donating them annually to local elementary school children. One Christmas, she presented each of her five children with a handmade quilt, a special gift created with love and care.
In retirement, Margaret enjoyed spending summers at the home she and Bud built in Randolph, and winters in Largo, Fla., where she developed a love for golf and enjoyed playing cards and spending time with friends. Fiercely independent and mindful of her health, she remained active well into her 90s, driving herself to the Kennebec Valley YMCA several times a week for Silver Sneakers fitness classes.
Margaret was predeceased by her husband, Bud Pratt; her parents, Alfred and Violet Firlotte; her in-laws, Charles and Margaret Pratt; her grandson, Douglas Dill; her brothers, Theophilus, Ivan, and Vincent Firlotte, her sisters, Yvonne Firlotte, Dorothy Astle, and Lorraine Richardson, her sisters-in-law, Margaret “Peggy” Firlotte, Ruth Desrosby, Mary Bowman, and Joan Pratt, her brothers-in-law, Ormand Astle, John Desrosby, and Eugene Bowman; her sons-in-law, Richard Reitchel and Gary Quintal; her beloved companion, Dick Howe; and Dick’s daughter, Karen Howe.
She is survived by her children, Janine Chinn (Jim), Debra Reitchel, Maria Quintal, Bruce Pratt (Kay), and Teresa Despres (Mike); her grandchildren, Ann Marie Creel, Crystal Hadley, Cristy Ingram, Corey Allen, Eliot Dill, Dicky Reitchel, Stacey Sutter, Katherine Reitchel, Vin Pratt, Haley Pratt, Aaron Quintal, Cassandra Quintal, Jessica Despres, and Blair Despres; her brother, John Gary Firlotte (Marilyn), her sister, Sheila Lemar (Norman); as well as several great-grandchildren; great-great-grandchildren; nieces, and nephews. She is also survived by Dick Howe’s children, Robert Howe (Debbie), Ralph Howe (Katrina), Richard Howe, and Kathy Nason (John).
The family would like to thank the staff at Woodlands Memory Care of Lewiston for the kindness and support they provided Margaret, affectionately known to them as “Maggy,” over the past four months, as well as Angie, Donna, and Jacki, her home healthcare providers.
Services will be announced and held in the Summer of 2027.

title: This election, Maine wanted one thing: Something different
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUBURN — Kelly LaSalle didn’t vote.
“I’m looking for people that look out for all of us,” the 49-year-old said as she dragged on a cigarette outside Hannaford during the midday drizzle.
The $287 million tidal wave of ads that washed over Maine voters this season left LaSalle unimpressed with both Democrat Troy Jackson and Sen. Susan Collins.
She’d voted for Collins in the past, but has felt lately that the five-term Republican, hailed recently by a former colleague as the “soul of the Senate,” no longer cared for working people. And what seeped out of that advertising wave didn’t leave her any more impressed with Jackson, whom she blamed for the high cost of gasoline.
“He has been elected?” she said Thursday. “Oh shit — sorry. I didn’t know.”
In the trunk of her utility scooter, LaSalle carried a single bag of groceries. For $100, she could once fill several such bags. Now, just the one. She’d like her elected representatives to do something about that, but was convinced by the advertising that Collins was in it to enrich herself and that Jackson was responsible for the high cost of living.
Waking up after Jackson’s poll-predicted but nonetheless astounding victory over Maine’s stalwart senior senator, voters of all persuasions had a single message for their newly elected officials: understand the struggle of the everyday Mainer.
“It’s nice to see someone in the working class position have a seat and a position of power,” said Henry Tardiff, 21, of Old Orchard Beach.
It’s not exactly a novel message. (No need to look further than “Joe the Plumber,” an Ohio man whose dialogue in 2008 with then-candidate Barack Obama sparked widespread conversations about the struggle of working class Americans).
Voters said that things aren’t working for them, and transcended party lines to make that point.
They hope Democratic Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree will improve the state’s public education system. They hope Jackson will work to lower costs.
Their outlook on the future is still, in many cases, shaded by party politics.
“It’s scary economic times,” said Justin Crockett, a Belgrade Republican. “I would not want to be a senior living on a fixed income in the state right now.”
He was among those who told the Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram in a survey this summer that life in Maine was getting worse.
Attendees react to the news that the Maine Senate race was called for Troy Jackson at the Democratic watch party at the Holiday Inn in Portland. (Brianna Soukup/Staff Photographer)
Jackson won, Crockett suspects, “not because he’s such a great articulate candidate,” but because of anger at the national level over gas prices and the Iran war. He has little faith that Maine’s incoming junior senator can do much to prevent oil companies from gouging consumers but remains hopeful that local officials can turn things around.
Compared with Crockett’s tempered pessimism, Brittany Bennett, of South Portland, has a muted sort of optimism.
Loading $230 worth of groceries — about three shopping bags — into the car at Hannaford, she said it was time for Collins to go.
“I think that everybody is concerned about cost of living, I think that everyone is concerned about heat, electricity, all of those things,” Bennett, 49, said. “I’m not sure what we’re actually going to be able to get passed.”
Fern Lake, 61, an Auburn voter who backed Collins, suspects Jackson won’t last in the Senate, citing some of the ethical and moral concerns raised in attack ads against him.
Others are unsure that Democrats will rise to the occasion despite gaining full control of Congress.
“I want to see strategy, I want to see plans. I don’t want to see a lot of arguing back and forth,” said another elated voter, Cathy Moran, 63.
For many voters, the lackluster state of affairs motivated them to try something new.
Auburn represented that perhaps better than anywhere else in the state. Maine’s fifth-largest city swung nearly 13 points, from favoring Collins by 8 points in 2020, to backing Jackson by almost 5 on Tuesday.
Jason Spaulding, 49, lives in Auburn. He was born there and works as a certified residential medication aide. He’s “an everyday guy” who’s really struggled with the price of gas and housing.
Spaulding said he doesn’t really have anything against Collins, and he’s the type of voter Collins successfully relied on in the past to keep her seat. But he hasn’t seen her make his life any better recently, and she’s been in the Senate about as long as he’s been able to vote.
“I just felt that she’s been in there my entire life, so I was like maybe somebody different,” Spaulding said.
So he cast a ballot backing Jackson and Pingree. But his expectations are low.
“Seems like sort of more of the same,” he said. ” I don’t think it’s a big fix.”
Even Nancy Robinson, a Republican from Cornville, a decidedly conservative hamlet of Somerset County, woke up feeling great on Wednesday. The 76-year-old thinks of herself more as an independent, and she voted for Collins for the same reason many centrists, and even some Democrats, have in the past: “she brings a ton of money to the state.”
But she ranked Jackson second, and picked Rick Bennett, an unenrolled former Republican, for governor.
The Iran war needs to end, Robinson said. “I sound just like everybody else,” she acknowledged, but prices need to come down.
“I’m also incredibly happy that the campaign is over with. I don’t ever want to see another ad for anybody again.”
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: Rockefeller Christmas tree arrives in New York City
text:
NEW YORK (WCBS) - New York’s Rockefeller Center is getting ready for the holidays with the delivery of the traditional Christmas tree on Saturday.
The 2026 tree is a 76-foot-tall Norway spruce from West Edmeston, New York. It’s about 75 years old, measures about 50 feet in diameter and weighs about 11 tons.
The tradition of the Rockefeller Center Christmas Tree dates back to 1931, when construction workers building Rockefeller Center erected a small tree decorated with handmade garlands.
The first formal tree lighting ceremony followed in 1933, beginning a tradition that has become synonymous with the holidays in New York City.

title: A tree stand fall left a Massachusetts hunter paralyzed. It was a wake-up call for me, too.
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Tree stands are so routine for deer hunters that it’s easy to forget how dangerous they can be. I had a humbling reminder of this recently.
A seasoned Massachusetts hunter slipped while stepping from a climbing ladder onto his tree stand platform and fell backward to the ground. The fall left him paralyzed from the “breastbone down,” according to Massachusetts outdoor writer Joe Judd, who writes a monthly column for the Northwoods Sporting Journal.
Two other similar tree stand accidents occurred during this hunting season, all involving serious injuries, Judd reported.
The statistics are sobering. Without question, tree stands, which are a highly effective way to hunt deer and get your scent off the ground, pose a serious risk to hunters.
Between 2005 and 2007, tree stand accidents resulted in 41 deaths and approximately 19,000 serious injuries nationwide, according to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.
More recent data show that the problem hasn’t gone away. An estimated 1,704 hunters required emergency room treatment for tree stand injuries in 2021, based on an analysis of federal injury data by the Tree Stand Safety Awareness Foundation.
The risk isn’t just theoretical. A 2016 Wisconsin study found that deer hunters who hunt during both archery and firearms seasons face a 1-in-20 lifetime chance of suffering a tree stand fall injury.
The danger is especially concerning for older hunters. A 2022 study of Pennsylvania hunting accidents from 1990 through 2017 found that tree stand falls had become the leading cause of deer hunting accidents in the state, with hunters ages 50 to 59 experiencing the highest fall rates. No doubt the same can be said for falling down stairs or when walking the dog.
This is not meant to be a screed against hunters who use tree stands. I have used them for years and still do, even at my advanced age. But I do so oh so carefully.
If you hunt, you know full well that there are, like everything else, many choices of tree stands and mechanical devices to get the hunter elevated and away from the deer’s scent channel.
I have tried them all. The trendy climbing saddle with all the ropes and pulleys and the ugly climber stand with the shark’s teeth and the platform that you haul up behind you with your feet just were not my cup of tea.
I found the harness lashups with the adjustable crotch straps and assorted carabiners were more trouble than they were worth. Not only are they dangerously cumbersome when trying to get up the tree, but what do you do if you wind up falling and hanging from your straps?
I know. I know. There is a device to handle that eventuality. Not for me. Too much gear and folderol. Hunting is supposed to be an escape into solitude and simplicity, not a gear fest.
As a younger hunter, I found that a simple climbing “stick” and a small platform, which was ratchet-strapped to the tree, were ample.
I tried that the other day. Made it to the top, but not without overextending myself and spooking any nearby deer with some choice curses. Not a good setup for an aged hunter. I won’t do that again, Diane, I promise.
I have found that the two-person ladder stand with a shooting rail is the cat’s meow for a senior deer hunter. There is room for my pack and me, and enough space to wiggle around without slipping off the edge.
The rage in tree stands seems to be to go higher and higher. My hunting buddy Mark Cain has one near our northern Maine deer camp that is so high that, I swear, it is unusable when a low-pressure front ushers in the low-hanging clouds.
You do not make any missteps that far up.
For the hunter who uses any kind of tree elevation system, regardless of age, the takeaway is clear: Situational awareness is the key to safe tree stand use.
Putting it another way: “Never lose your edge of awareness.”
There is an alternative to getting up in a tree. Ground blinds have been perfected. They are much easier to put up and take down than they used to be.
And they are a lot more comfortable during extended deer vigils.
Hunt safely.

title: Death Notice: John E. Baker
UFC CEO Dana White to visit White House after Trump offers him press secretary role
text:
UFC CEO Dana White to visit White House after Trump offers him press secretary role
President Trump has offered UFC CEO Dana White the position of White House press secretary as part of a series of changes in his administration following Republican losses in Congress.
UFC CEO Dana White to visit White House after Trump offers him press secretary role
President Trump has offered UFC CEO Dana White the position of White House press secretary as part of a series of changes in his administration following Republican losses in Congress.
President Donald Trump is shaking up his administration after Republicans lost control of Congress, including publicly offering UFC CEO Dana White the job of White House press secretary.
White, a longtime friend and political ally of the president, says he plans to meet with Trump Monday but has not publicly accepted the position. CNN reports White has declined the offer, while a White House aide described it as a joke.
Trump even suggested White could bring six UFC fighters to serve as his assistants, saying they would defend his administration against his political opponents.
The unusual offer comes as the White House searches for a new spokesperson. The position has been vacant following the departure of Karoline Leavitt in August and the dismissal of her successor after just five days on the job.
But the changes extend well beyond the White House briefing room.
Trump announced he is replacing his longtime chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller, a key architect of his hardline immigration policies. Wiles, who helped manage both of Trump's successful presidential campaigns, is moving to his political operation.
"I wanted to make a change," Trump said Friday. "Sometimes in life you have to make moves."
Miller, who officially takes over Monday, has been one of the most influential voices behind the president's immigration crackdown. His promotion comes as some Republicans question whether the administration's aggressive approach contributed to their losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.
The decision also raises questions about whether Trump intends to moderate his agenda or double down on the policies that have defined his presidency.
In an interview with "60 Minutes," Trump said he is considering replacing "a few" Cabinet members as he prepares for a new political reality.
Starting in January, Democrats will control both chambers of Congress, giving them the power to block presidential nominees, issue subpoenas and launch investigations into his administration.
But Trump may not have to wait until January to face challenges from Congress.
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie plans to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth when lawmakers return to Washington this week.
The effort comes amid growing frustration among some Republicans over the administration's war with Iran, which has contributed to rising energy costs and become a political liability for the party.
CNN reports that multiple Republican sources expect the impeachment effort to pass, potentially putting Hegseth at risk even before Democrats assume control of the House.
"Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me. You can rest assured of that," Hegseth said in response to the impeachment effort.
Trump, however, has publicly defended his defense secretary, telling "60 Minutes" that he continues to have confidence in Hegseth.
The potential confrontation underscores a growing challenge for the president: maintaining Republican unity while preparing for two years of divided government.
For now, Republicans still control Congress, leaving them with just weeks to advance the president's legislative priorities before Democrats take power in January.
Their most immediate challenge is avoiding another government shutdown. Federal funding expires December 11, and lawmakers must reach an agreement to keep the government operating.
Congress also faces unfinished work on defense and farm legislation, along with other priorities Republicans had hoped to accomplish while controlling both chambers.
But with slim majorities and growing divisions within the Republican Party, it remains unclear how much lawmakers can accomplish before the new Congress is sworn in.
And even after Democrats take control, Trump will retain the power to veto legislation, potentially forcing both parties to negotiate over government funding and other must-pass bills.

title: Wrong to undo protections for Maine children with disabilities
text:
Alan Cobo-Lewis is the parent of two adult children, one of whom has a disability. He is also on the faculty of the University of Maine, where he is associate professor of psychology and director of the Center for Community Inclusion and Disability Studies. His views are his own.
In June 2022, the U.S. Department of Justice sent Maine a letter finding that the state had violated the rights of children with mental-health or developmental disabilities.
After a long investigation, the DOJ found Maine was violating the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) by failing to provide children sufficient behavioral health support in their communities.
This shortcoming unnecessarily sent Maine children to institutions, including hospitals, residential facilities and juvenile detention — including unnecessary out-of-state placements. And it put more children at risk institutionalization.
The DOJ found this was a violation of both the ADA and the U.S. Supreme Court’s 1999 Olmstead decision, which affirmed the right of people with disabilities not to be institutionalized unnecessarily.
Maine was ripping children away from their families.
In November 2024, the DOJ and Maine entered into a settlement agreement. This agreement was approved by a federal court the following month.
Although Maine didn’t admit to violating children’s rights, the state thankfully agreed to a court-monitored settlement, including having a third party collect and analyze data to assess progress on getting children with disabilities the help they need—help made available to them in their homes and communities, which should always be the first choice.
The DOJ has since moved away from enforcing Olmstead’s integration mandate. This is a big enough deal that Gov. Janet Mills joined 17 other state governors in asking the DOJ not to retreat from protecting the right to community integration.
The governors said they strongly opposed “any federal actions that would weaken protections against unnecessary segregation or diminish the right of people with disabilities to receive services in the most integrated settings appropriate to meet their needs, consistent with established Olmstead precedent.”
Yet, less than a year after entering the settlement agreement to support Maine children with disabilities in their homes and communities, the DOJ and Maine jointly petitioned the federal court to modify the agreement to remove independent review, reduce reporting requirements and weaken other commitments.
Federal Judge Stacey Neumann denied the request, ruling that the DOJ and Maine failed to show changed circumstances and that an amendment would violate rules governing voluntary settlements.
The court having ruled, Maine proceeded on implementation. And yet, now the DOJ and Maine are together appealing Judge Neumann’s decision to the appeals court.
Instead of continuing to move forward on implementation to ensure children with disabilities finally get the support they need in their homes and communities, the DOJ and Maine are again trying to get out from under it.
Why is it that “see you in court” now means “let’s work together in court to remove protections from Maine children with disabilities”?
I am grateful that Governor-elect Hannah Pingree has endorsed the ADA and Olmstead’s integration mandate as a “matter of basic human rights and fairness” and has furthermore recognized that institutionalization is “isolating, harmful, and far more costly to taxpayers than supporting people right where they belong, at home, near their families and connected to their communities.”
Pingree added, “Together, we will need to continue to fight back against federal attempts to undermine the rights of all Americans with disabilities.”
It’s time for us in Maine to live by our values.
Support ADA and Olmstead’s integration mandate. Build out the home- and community-based supports for Maine children with disabilities. Stop putting Maine children at unnecessary risk of institutionalization, away from the families that love them. Recognize that accountability as represented by specific metrics and independent monitoring is important to support Maine’s children. Support Maine children with disabilities. Implement the agreement.
Gov. Mills should immediately withdraw support for this appeal. If she doesn’t, I look forward to Gov. Pingree doing so as quickly as possible after her inauguration.

title: Maine needs Hannah Pingree to take the lead on the environment
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kate Sinding Daly is senior vice president for law and policy at the Conservation Law Foundation in Portland.
As we congratulate Governor-elect Hannah Pingree as Maine’s next governor, we need to recognize that this is a moment of opportunity for our state.
Mainers are grappling with rising costs; growing threats to public health; and the impacts of severe storms, droughts and heat waves.
Meanwhile, our federal government is rolling back vital environmental protections. These challenges are deeply connected. Protecting our environment goes hand in hand with making life more affordable, improving public health and building a stronger future for Maine families. The governor-elect has the chance to address some of the most pressing challenges facing our communities.
Here are three key priorities that should be at the forefront of her administration.
First, making polluters pay.
Polluters — not Maine families — should pay for the mess large fossil fuel companies create from peddling oil and gas. Next year, Maine will conduct an assessment of the costs that cities, towns, homeowners, and businesses are now paying to respond to and repair damage after extreme weather events caused by climate change and to adapt to minimize future damage.
The next step is for Pingree to set up a climate superfund program, similar to the hazardous waste superfund programs that already exist, to ensure Maine has the revenue to take the necessary steps to protect its communities, residents and businesses.
We continue to see increased flooding, stronger storms, and more frequent heat waves — which the fossil fuel industry knew for decades would result from ongoing use of its products. A strong climate superfund program would put the responsibility of paying for protecting our state from these impacts on the companies that caused it, rather than where it rests now: on the shoulders of hardworking Maine families.
When polluters pay their fair share of the costs they create, Mainers can better protect public health and invest in safer, more resilient communities.
Second, our next governor must ensure affordability — and accountability.
Maine families and businesses are facing higher energy bills when household budgets are already stretched thin. The cost of propane, oil, diesel fuel, and gasoline is breaking low- and middle-class family budgets, and driving up costs for practically everything, including electricity. Governor-elect Pingree must ensure that our state brings affordable, clean power online and reduces our reliance on fossil fuels with unpredictable prices.
We’ve already seen how clean sources like wind and solar — both of which are free and are not subject to price shocks caused by wars — saved our region millions of dollars during recent cold snaps and heat waves. Bringing more clean energy sources online is critical to lower costs, clean the air we breathe, and reduce the climate-damaging emissions that are raising the levels and temperature of our waters.
Bringing clean energy online is only part of the solution. Maine’s families and businesses also deserve transparency and accountability from the companies delivering our electricity. The state’s Public Utilities Commission is an important body that regulates our utilities, like our electricity and water, and determines what type of energy we use and how much we pay. The Pingree administration has a number of steps it can take to support the PUC and increase transparency around its ongoing work.
As governor, Pingree should also adequately fund the Office of the Public Advocate, an effective but under-resourced voice for Maine families, who should not have to choose between paying their energy bills and meeting other basic needs.
Strong oversight and timely, transparent decisions from those agencies can help protect Maine families and ensure the public interest comes first.
Third, Pingree must work on modernizing permitting while protecting communities.
Maine needs to build clean energy faster, and this must be done with regard for important environmental safeguards and community perspectives.
Governor-elect Pingree should advance sensible permitting reforms to expedite the deployment of clean energy infrastructure and other priority projects. We need to rethink, revise and speed up how state agencies plan and decide on such projects. We must reduce the unnecessary barriers that hinder responsible renewable energy development while maintaining strong environmental protections.
Permitting reform does not mean cutting corners or silencing communities. Transparent decisions and meaningful public participation can identify problems early and help ensure projects serve the public interest.
Environmental justice must remain central to each of these efforts.
Maine needs a clear definition of “environmental justice” and policies that address the disproportionate pollution burdens some communities face. The ongoing battle over the Juniper Ridge Landfill highlights these concerns, particularly for the Penobscot Nation. Working together, we can make sure Maine accelerates clean energy development while protecting natural resources, upholding environmental safeguards and ensuring affected communities have a meaningful voice.
As Governor-elect Pingree prepares for office, she should be focused on tackling significant challenges facing the health of our communities, our environment and our state economy. Pingree can show that environmental protection and economic security go hand in hand. The challenges are real, but with leadership, and by embracing these priorities with urgency and determination, they can and must be addressed.
Together, we can create a brighter, more sustainable future for Maine.

title: Paul George scores 27 in Celtics’ rout of Bucks
text:
MILWAUKEE — Paul George scored 27 points, Jayson Tatum added 21 and the Boston Celtics rolled to a 117-97 victory over the slumping Milwaukee Bucks on Sunday night.
This marked the second matchup between these teams in five nights. The Celtics had beaten the Bucks 109-102 on Wednesday in Boston while resting Tatum.
Boston (8-2) built a big enough lead Sunday to sit Tatum for the entire fourth quarter as the Celtics continued a four-game trip that started with a 119-80 win at Charlotte on Friday. The Celtics next head to Philadelphia and Toronto.
Kyle Kuzma led Milwaukee with 27 points.
Myles Turner scored just three points for the Bucks, though he did have five rebounds and a career-high seven assists. Turner, who has shot 1 of 15 over his last two games, was coming off a scoreless performance in a 121-107 NBA Cup loss to the Toronto Raptors on Frieday.
The Bucks (1-9) are off to their worst start since 1993-94, when they lost 10 of their first 11 games and went on to finish 20-62.
Kuzma scored 14 points in the first five minutes of the game to help Milwaukee grab an early 20-6 lead. Tatum and George sparked an 18-0 run that enabled the Celtics to take control later in the first half.
Tatum scored the final 10 points of the first quarter to cut Milwaukee’s lead to 27-25. George delivered the first eight points of the second period.
George’s 3-pointer in the opening minute of the second quarter gave Boston its first lead at 28-27. George then hit a layup and another 3-pointer to cap the 18-0 spurt.
Boston owned a 58-45 halftime advantage. The Celtics scored the first nine points of the third period to extend their lead to 22, and they stayed in front by at least 15 the rest of the way.
Up next
Celtics: At Philadelphia on Tuesday night.
Bucks: At New York on Tuesday night.

title: Obituary: Edward James Valente
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Edward James Valente, 94, passed away peacefully on Nov. 4, 2026, at his home in Scarborough, surrounded by his loving wife.
Ed was born on Jan. 26, 1932, in Portland, Maine, the son of Anthony T. Valente and Mary F. Canning. He graduated from Deering High School, where he played varsity football. On Aug. 30, 1951, Ed enlisted in the United States Air Force, beginning a 20-year career in military service. He retired on Dec. 1, 1971. He later worked as a civilian employee for the United States Coast Guard at the South Portland base from 1973 until 1999.
Ed had a way of lighting up any room he walked into with his infectious smile, quirky sense of humor, and the twinkle in his eye. He loved sharing his gifted vocals and was always ready to sing a beloved song whenever someone asked. He spread joy to so many people and made many friends along the way. Ed was incredibly kind, endearing, and truly one of a kind. He enjoyed music, playing guitar, ham radio, gardening, and, of course, singing.
Above all, Ed treasured his family. As a husband and father, he always did his best to protect and provide for those he loved. To his wife, Sandi, he was not only a wonderful husband but also her best friend. He made her laugh often, even when she didn’t quite understand the story he was telling. He was passionate about food and always told Sandi she was the best cook. Ed especially loved sweets, and together they shared many happy years enjoying one of his favorite pastimes, dancing. He even taught Sandi how to dance, and it became something they cherished doing together.
Ed will be dearly missed by his wife, Sandi; his daughter, Cindy, and her husband, Eric Jurgenson, his sons Chuck Valente and James Valente; and his grandsons, John and Michael Valente. He is also survived by his sisters Roseanne and Gloria, and his brothers Robert and Anthony.
He was predeceased by his parents; and his first wife, Mitsuko Valente.
Ed leaves behind a lifetime of memories, laughter, music, and friendships. He will be remembered for his wonderful sense of humor, his kindness, his love of singing, and the happiness he brought to those fortunate enough to know him. He will be deeply missed by his family and many friends.
A funeral service will be held on Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 10 a.m. at Hobbs Funeral Home in Scarborough, followed by a burial at Black Point Cemetery at 11 a.m. and a reception at Hobbs Funeral Home, Scarborough at 12 p.m.
In lieu of flowers,
the family requests that
donations be made to
Andwell Health Partners
