title: A language of belonging: Advice for learning the mother tongue of your ancestors
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Losing a tangible connection to your family’s ancestral homeland can bring unexpected sorrow, whether through the death of an older relative, the sale of a property passed down for generations gets sold or the destruction a handful of surviving heirlooms.
Learning a language spoken by their parents, grandparents or great-grandparents is a way some English-speaking children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren of immigrants choose to reinforce ties to the old country and nurture their cultural identity.
Knowing the mother tongue of one’s ancestors could unlock a stack of letters that clarify hazy chapters of family history. Basic speaking skills may lead to meeting cousins in another country. Listening to stories and songs in the original language conveys nuances and meaning that often are lost in translation, experts say.
Imparting an ancestral language to their children also is important to some parents. Adults who grew up speaking a language other than English, perhaps because they had immigrant parents or they were born abroad themselves, may see the language as a way to foster intergenerational bonds, preserve family traditions and expand future career options.
Whether you’re a parent who wants a child to know their roots or someone eager to acquire an ancestral language yourself, here are tips for claiming a legacy through language.
Don’t let a fear of making mistakes derail you
Linguists and educators generally categorize foreign language students into two broad groups, each with different starting points and perhaps motivations. Most children and adults are second-language learners, who begin formal instruction with little or no prior knowledge.
Most heritage language learners, by contrast, organically acquired some familiarity with a language other than English as young children, said Tanya Ivanova-Sullivan, associate director of the National Heritage Language Resource Center at the University of California, Los Angeles. They typically heard the language spoken at home and understand or speak it themselves to varying degrees.
“Heritage language speakers are home chefs,” Ivanova-Sullivan said. “They learned the language in the family kitchen from parents and grandparents rather than in the classroom.”
Repeated early exposure tends to give heritage language students an advantage over second-language learners, but they may be reluctant to speak up in class if they aren’t confident in their grammar or relatives teased them for not being fluent, experts say.
Many people are embarassed about making mistakes when conversing in a language they don’t know very well, said Arturo Diaz, executive director of the UCLA Center for World Languages. He encouraged students to use what they already know, saying perfection doesn’t have to be the goal.
“So just remove any apprehension you may have in learning language and then just have fun with the experience,” Diaz said.
Look for opportunities to learn and practice
Some scholars and educators say that someone with a cultural or familial relationship to a language also could be considered a heritage language student even if they are starting pretty much from scratch, according to the Center for Applied Linguistics, a nonprofit research and teacher education organization that promotes language learning and linguistic diversity.
Listening to relatives whose first language isn’t English is an effective way to learn a heritage language, Yang Xiao-Desai, a professor of Chinese at San Francisco State University, said.
“Ask your grandparents for stories,” she said. “Ask them to share a story of a dish, a story of a recipe, a piece of furniture. Whatever you can.”
Podcasts, music and subtitled movies and videos in a target language also may help learners pick up words and phrases.
Ivanova-Sullivan recommends expanding the circle of people with whom you practice. Some communities have programs that pair an English speaker learning a foreign language with a native speaker who wants to learn English.
“When you’re expanding your network, you’re expanding the opportunities to use the language in different ways, and that’s how your vocabulary (grows),” she said.
Book a trip to the place your people are from
Visiting your family’s country of origin can be a valuable experience for people who can afford the trip, Ivanova-Sullivan said. She takes her 12-year-old to her native Bulgaria for two months every summer.
Organized tours overseas for people who want to visit their ancestral homelands have multiplied in the last decade, in part due to at-home DNA test kits.
If you’re interested in learning a language while traveling but have limited time off from work, check out intensive programs like EF Language Abroad, which has campuses in Spain, France, Korea, Italy, Germany, Japan and the United Arab Emirates.
Before or after traveling, connect with members of your extended family on social media platforms like Facebook and Instagram. Even beginner students can pick up phrases and customs from their relatives.
Consider a local heritage language school
Parents who want their children to learn a family language and embrace their heritage can consider community language schools, which integrate language lessons with cultural traditions. Volunteers and parents from local immigrant communities often operate such schools as nonprofit organizations.
Classes typically are held after school or on weekends. Most are designed for children learning or maintaining a language spoken at home, but some serve adult learners as well, said Joy Peyton, president of the Coalition of Community-Based Heritage Language Schools.
“They use their languages with their parents, with their friends,” Peyton said. “They recognize that their language has value.”
The coalition, a nationwide initiative that connects and advocates for these schools, has documented nearly 1,000 programs teaching 62 languages in 44 states, she said. Korean is the most-taught language, according to Peyton.
Ana Lúcia Lico, a co-founder and board member of the organization, came to the U.S. from São Paulo, Brazil, at age 35. She made sure her two sons, now 20 and 23, learned Portuguese and were immersed in Brazilian culture while growing up in Northern Virginia.
Her older son, Gabriel Lico Bickham, attended a local heritage language school for two hours every Saturday for about a decade, starting at age 4. He remembers learning grammar but also being immersed in games like “Corre cotia,” similar to the American duck, duck, goose.
Classes aren’t the only way for children to learn a family language
Lico, whose husband was born in the U.S., said she also exposed her boys to Brazilian Portuguese through music, dance and playing sports.
“Soccer is huge in Brazil,” she said. “Through soccer, my kids developed a whole amazing set of vocabulary, words that I never had to teach them.”
Hiring childcare providers who are native speakers or shopping in neighborhoods where a heritage language is spoken are additional ways for children to learn the ancestral tongue, said Richard Brecht, co-director of the American Councils Research Center, a nonprofit group devoted to the improvement of language learning worldwide.
Comic books about a group of children living in a fictitious neighborhood in Brazil helped Bickham learn Portuguese, a skill he says is helping shape his future. Also fluent in Spanish, he recently graduated from the University of Virginia. In January, he leaves for Mozambique, where Portuguese is the official language, for an English teaching assistant position through the Fulbright program.
“Growing up today, I feel very close to my Brazilian identity,” Bickham said. “And the language is probably the most important aspect out of that because the language is what unlocks all these cultural aspects.”

title: Cheverus, Foxcroft Academy defend state field hockey titles; Nokomis wins first since 2013
text:
The Cheverus High School field hockey team from Portland made it four state titles in a row, Foxcroft Academy of Dover-Foxcroft made it two straight and Nokomis High of Newport won its first since 2013 on Saturday at Edward Little High in Auburn.
The Stags received first-half goals from Avery Tinker and Sydney Brunelle and survived a second-half goal by Krystah Coen to edge first-time finalist Mt. Ararat High of Topsham, 2-1, in the Class A championship game.
Cheverus concluded an 18-0 campaign while Mt. Ararat finished up at 17-1.
Nokomis captured the B title with a 1-0 win over Freeport.
MaKenzie Watson scored the game’s only goal as the Warriors won for the 17th time in 18 games.
Freeport wound up 14-4.
In Class C, sophomore and Penobscot Valley Conference Player of the Year Addie Rayfield, scored both goals in the second half with Jenna Hartford assisting on both as the Ponies from Foxcroft Academy completed an 18-0 season with a 2-0 win over Winthrop.
Foxcroft Academy outscored its four post-season opponents, 18-0.

title: Lost class ring returned 47 years later
text:
PAWTUCKET, R.I. (WJAR) - A class ring lost nearly 50 years ago on a beach near Seattle has been returned to its owner after turning up in Washington state.
“The ring means a lot to me because it brings back great memories of my mother,” Paul Benson said.
Ring lost at beach near Seattle
Benson graduated from St. Raphael Academy in Pawtucket nearly 50 years ago. One summer, his brother, Eric Benson, borrowed the ring and took it out West, eventually to a beach near Seattle, where he was wrestling with friends.
“I just took the ring off, put it down on the rock,” Eric Benson said.
As the tide rolled in, the ring was gone. Eric Benson said he thought, “My brother is going to kill me.”
Asked by reporter Jake Baum what his reaction was when he learned his brother had borrowed and lost the ring, Paul Benson said Eric never told him.
Found with a metal detector
The ring stayed on the beach off Puget Sound for nearly 50 years. In November 2025, Seattle native Lucas Thrun found it with a metal detector.
Thrun said parts of the beach were exposed that normally are not. He said there is a video of him finding the ring.
Thrun has hunted for items on Seattle beaches for years.
“This is the stuff that people in my hobby dream about,” Thrun said.
Returned in person
Thrun contacted the school, but the school had no way to reach Benson. Through friends, Thrun and others found Benson’s address and went to his door.
“I was napping,” Benson said.
Benson said he was stunned. After initial disbelief, he was eager to meet the man who would return his ring.
“If it wasn’t for him, it would just be a lost memory,” Benson said.
Thrun flew to Rhode Island, nearly 3,000 miles from where he found the ring, to hand it back in person. Eric Benson, who now lives in Israel, made it a priority to be there.
“Little did I know it would be a 47-year history. He forgave me. But trust me, he never forgot,” Eric Benson said.
Eric Benson also said, “Next time I take the ring, I’m gonna ask him.”
Baum asked Paul Benson whether the experience showed that there are still good people in the world. Benson answered, “Yes.”
“It’s about life in general and how pieces fall into place, and Lucas kind of brought that all together for me,” Benson said.

title: Poles mourn rare mass killing as authorities say attacker had far-right views
text:
KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — Mourners on Sunday laid candles and flowers alongside bullet holes in Krakow, Poland, after the city’s central square turned into a site of bloodshed and grief. A 24-year-old man with far-right views opened fire a day earlier, killing six people and wounding 15 before police shot and wounded him.
Poland on Sunday began two days of national mourning following the attack the day before, which Poland’s defense minister described as an “act of terror.”
The violence began Saturday at around 3 p.m. when the assailant drove through the Main Square, in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town. The square is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city.
St. Mary’s Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight, the first time the call had been missed since World War II.
On Sunday afternoon, St. Anne’s Church in Krakow filled with mourners attending a memorial service. The square reopened soon after and locals and visitors alike showed up to reclaim it after the tragedy.
“I come here so as not to get caught up in a spiral of fear and anxiety,” Krakow local Maciej Sikorski told The Associated Press from the square. “In a situation like this, it’s all too easy to stop living — to start being afraid instead, and just vegetate. That is something I really want to avoid.”
Authorities also found the bodies of the assailant’s sister, mother and father at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds.
Woman injured by shrapnel while saving another
Witness Andy Hill told the BBC that he’d felt as though he was in a movie scene.
“It doesn’t feel real,” the British tourist said. “And the trouble is, you have such an instantaneous moment to make a decision: Run. Stand still. There’s an element of shock. But I just thought the easiest thing to do is dive through a doorway and just take refuge behind the windows.”
Warsaw native Magdalena Frączek, meanwhile, was visiting Krakow with her friend when shots rang out and the gunman drew closer.
“I threw an elderly woman behind the flower planter because she had become tangled in the blanket she had on her lap. I covered her with my body,” Frączek told the AP. “I also saw him out of the corner of my eye — he passed just one meter behind my back. That’s why I have shrapnel wounds in six places on my back. Only after he had passed did I pull the woman up, and we ran into a café.”
On Sunday, she forced herself to return to the Main Square to grieve among other mourners.
“I can’t put it into words. Because I knew that I would never come back to Krakow if I didn’t come in here,” she said. “When I found out that they had reopened the Main Market Square, I told my friend that I had to come here.”
American tourist Marylin Green mourned the losses in the “beautiful city” during her first trip to Poland that also included the capital.
“I’m Polish, my parents were from here,” she said. “I loved Warsaw. So I was really looking forward to coming here, too.”
Police officers described as heroes
Prosecutors said Sunday they opened an investigation into the murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act “constituting a terrorist offense.”
Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead.
A video posted on social media showed a police officer repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street. The officer later slowly collapsed to the ground.
The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in the hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon.
“If it weren’t for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher,” Klęczar said.
Michał Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak, two local surgeons who were having a bite to eat nearby, also stepped in.
Wierdak “took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help,” Pędziwiatr told the Polish news website onet. “Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life.”
Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.
The suspect is also in critical condition after undergoing multiple surgeries. There was confusion on Saturday about his age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed that he is 24.
The suspect’s dead sibling was a young artist studying at the Krakow Academy of Fine Arts. “Nothing will ever be like before. The delicate tissue of our academic community was painfully wounded,” the academy wrote in a statement on Sunday, confirming that Magdalena Oksińska was a third year student and that, additionally, the sister of an academy employee was shot twice.
“Magdalena Oksińska, 21 years old, a queer person, was an absolutely talented painter, photographer, poet and writer,” architect Pavko Krajka wrote in a post on social media, accompanied by images of the artist’s colourful paintings. “Her death is a great loss for Krakow, Polish, European and queer culture.”
The mass killing marks a grim first for Poland
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect holds “very radical” and “ultranationalistic” views.
“Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” Kierwiński said at a news conference Saturday.
Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found on the suspect or in his car in Krakow. Both father and son had gun permits, they said.
Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising.
The Swit shooting club in Starachowice, where the suspect is believed to have trained, issued a statement on Sunday saying it offered only “static shooting,” which involves firing from a fixed position at a stationary target. The club added that the suspect “was never trained in our club in the areas of dynamic, tactical or combat shooting.”
Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The young attackers used knives or other sharp objects. Officials blamed the school attacks on online “glorification of violence,” and said that some of the attackers were active in the far-right environment.
The Krakow shooter’s military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other “extreme right lone actors” committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague.
“We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland,” he said.
___
Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland. Associated Press writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.
___
This story corrects the spelling of Frączek.

title: Cooper Flagg’s 3rd straight double-double leads Mavericks past Nets
text:
DALLAS — Newport native Cooper Flagg had 25 points and a career-high 12 assists for his third consecutive double-double and fourth of the season as the Dallas Mavericks beat the Brooklyn Nets 130-93 on Sunday night.
Kyrie Irving scored 21 points and Daniel Gafford added 18 as the Mavericks played the first of a home back-to-back.
Michael Porter Jr. had 19 points and nine rebounds for the Nets, who were swept in a back-to-back to begin a four-game road trip. Nolan Traore added 14 points.
The Nets didn’t trail until the final two minutes of Saturday’s 124-121 loss at Atlanta but never led against the Mavericks.
Flagg, last season’s Rookie of the Year, had his 16th career 20-point half and first this season after opening hot by hitting 5 of 6 shots in the first period. He had missed 6 of 8 shots and scored four points in the first half on Friday against Utah but finished with 21 points in Dallas’ 112-100 win.
The Mavericks shot a season best 57.1% and scored a season high in points on Sunday. They led 66-46 at halftime, and the 37-point final margin was the largest of the game.
Brooklyn’s Julius Randle grew up in the Dallas area and went into play averaging 23.5 points in his homecoming games but finished with 13 points.
Nets rookie Mikel Brown Jr., who tied his career-high with 18 points on Saturday, sat out, not yet cleared for back-to-backs as he recovers from a back injury that limited him to 21 games last season for Louisville.
Up next
Nets: Visit New Orleans on Wednesday night.
Mavericks: Host Indiana on Monday night.

title: Why this Aroostook veteran wishes more could experience Honor Flight
text:
With decades of public service behind him, Percy Thibeault thought he’d experienced just about every milestone there was.
Then the Frenchville veteran went on an Honor Flight. Weeks later, he still teared up when he recalled how it felt.
Every state participates in the nonprofit program that has sent nearly 340,000 veterans to view memorials in Washington, D.C., and Arlington, Virginia, over the past 20 years. Designed to recognize the service and sacrifices of veterans nationwide, the experience offers the welcome home some never had.
Thibeault served in the Marine Corps during the Vietnam War. He had a positive homecoming, but knows many others did not, he said. Still, when his Honor Flight group made its first stop, the reception blew him away.
“The thing that really hit me is we arrived at the Baltimore airport [and] they had kids, 7, 8 years old, and adults welcoming us and saying, ‘Thank you for serving.’ And to me — tears,” he said. “To see that, it was something.”
Thibeault made the trip through Honor Flight Maine, which has sent more than 1,600 veterans to view the memorials since its 2014 launch. The statewide group conducts four flights a year. Veterans choose a companion to accompany them.
Free to veterans, the tours stop at sites such as the Marine Corps Memorial (the statue of Iwo Jima), Air Force Memorial, U.S. Navy Memorial, Military Women’s Memorial, World War II Memorial, Vietnam Wall and Korean War Memorial. They also observe the solemn changing of the guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Arlington National Cemetery, according to a state itinerary.
Thibeault’s group departed from Bangor on Oct. 15, he said. They may have been strangers when they started, but became family through the journey.
“When you’re in the service, there are a lot of things that happen, but you don’t talk about it,” he said, adding that for some in his group, the trip allowed them to talk for the first time about their war experiences with people who understood.
He had “a couple of close calls” in Vietnam, he said, including in January 1968, when he landed in the aftermath of the Chu Lai bombing during the Tet Offensive.
The Viet Cong had attacked the Marines’ Chu Lai Air Base and blew up the bomb storage site, resulting in a mushroom cloud explosion from the ordnance and napalm, according to an account by James Ronan on the social media page Vietnam Air War.
Many jets were damaged, Thibeault recalled. His unit spent seven days in a bunker for protection.
Following Vietnam, he eventually returned to the St. John Valley and began a more than 40-year law enforcement career with the Madawaska Police Department. He was the first officer from the department to graduate from the Maine Criminal Justice Academy, he said.
In combination with his Madawaska job, he also worked stints as a sheriff’s deputy, school DARE officer and court security.
Then things took a different turn.
“I was at the Zayre’s in Madawaska and there was a kid there with his mother who choked on a piece of candy,” he said. “I was in uniform, waiting in line, and the mother said, ‘You’re a police officer. Can you help him?’ And I didn’t know what to do.”
He immediately started emergency medical services training, he said. That became his new full-time venture, and eventually he became director of Madawaska’s ambulance services while he continued part-time policing.
Now retired, he participates in the American Legion and other veterans groups, along with church and community efforts. He’s written a book about his life: “Percy Thibeault: A Life of Service,” published last month.
He had heard about Honor Flight for years. To share it with fellow servicemembers was one thing. But Thibeault went with this son, Bruce, a current Marine. That made the trip all the more meaningful, he said.
Bruce had a surprise for his father during the journey. He read a letter to Thibeault from the whole family, which includes Thibeault’s wife, Claudette, daughter Kelly, Bruce and his wife, Renee, and grandchildren Peighton, Sterling and Greyson.
The family may not know what Thibeault experienced in the military, but they do know what he brought home and the values he instilled, Bruce Thibeault’s letter stated.
“You brought home the leadership, strength, discipline, courage and core values that you learned in the service,” he wrote. “I am especially grateful that you asked me to be your guardian on Honor Flight Maine. It is an honor I will carry with me for the rest of my life.
“We love you, we are proud of you, and we are forever grateful that you chose to serve our country,” the letter concluded.
Though every memorial Thibeault’s group visited made an impact, he was most struck by the changing of the guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, where the elite U.S. Army Old Guard unit patrols meticulously and incessantly.
It is precise and there is absolute silence, Thibeault said. Four from the group joined in placing a wreath there.
A favorite part of the trip was the final mail call, which occurred when they returned to Bangor. In a celebration reminiscent of soldiers receiving mail from home, each veteran received a packet with Honor Flight memorabilia and letters from people across the country thanking them for their service.
Honor Flight Maine’s next trip is slated to leave from Portland on April 16.
Thibeault wishes more veterans could experience Honor Flight. He urged anyone undecided to apply.
“They treated us like royalty,” he said. “I mean, this is all of us. It doesn’t matter what branch of service or what state. It’s America.”

title: Here’s what state passed a ban on transgender girls in female sports
text:
(AP) - A ballot measure approved Tuesday by voters in Washington state will prohibit transgender athletes from participating in girls’ school sports.
Proponents said the new law will increase fairness and safety in girls’ sports. Opponents had argued the measure could require invasive exams of many athletes to weed out a small number of transgender ones.
Similar laws are common in Republican-controlled states. But lawmakers in Washington and other Democratic-dominated states have not previously advanced them.
Republicans have emphasized the issue in recent years — and a growing number of Democratic politicians have aligned with them, at least partly.
The measure was placed on the Washington ballot through a citizens’ initiative. The state Legislature could change or repeal the law after two years with a simple majority, or sooner with support of two-thirds of both the House and Senate.

title: Week Ahead in Washington: Nov. 8
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Lawmakers return to Capitol Hill this week for the lame-duck session after the midterm elections, with a potential impeachment vote on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and government funding on the agenda.
Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, (R-Ky.) has promised to bring a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth. The House must vote on a privileged resolution.
Massie said the only way to avoid a vote is if Hegseth resigns or President Donald Trump fires him.
In response, Hegseth posted a video to X vowing to fight.
“Their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents,” Hegseth said. “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. It didn’t work with President Trump and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”
Lawmakers also will start work this week on keeping the government open.
Government funding is set to run out Dec. 11, when the continuing resolution passed earlier this year expires.
The newest members of Congress come to Washington this week for freshman orientation.
House Republicans plan to hold their leadership vote after losses in last week’s election.
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he will not be in the running for the next Minority Leader. Two candidates vying to replace him as GOP leader are current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio).

title: Strong earthquake shakes central Japan: At least 22 people injured
text:
Strong earthquake shakes central Japan: At least 22 people injured
A strong earthquake shook central Japan early Sunday, shattering store windows, causing people to flee buildings and leaving at least 22 people injured, according to local media.
Japan’s Meteorological Agency put the quake’s magnitude at 5.7, while the U.S. Geological Survey reported it at magnitude 5.5. Smaller aftershocks were reported.
A wide area near Aichi Prefecture was affected, including the city of Hamamatsu, the ancient capitals of Kyoto and Nara and nearby prefectures of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located, as well as Gifu.
Related video: Bell tower of St. John the Baptist Cathedral in Panama’s central province of Coclé collapses, Oct. 2026
Japanese TV footage showed shattered store windows and scattered shards of glass on the streets. A bookstore was left with mounds of books that had flown off the shelves. The injuries included people who fell from stairs while they were trying to flee.
The quake, which struck at 1:04 a.m., was located about 40 kilometers (25 miles) below the earth's surface in Shizuoka Prefecture. Aichi and Shizuoka are neighboring regions. They are far enough from Tokyo that the quake was not felt there. The most violent shaking was felt in Aichi, according to official seismic assessments.
The meteorological agency warned people to brace for possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially the next two to three days.
“Please be on the lookout for mudslides, falling rocks and the possible effects from rainfall,” Ayataka Ebita, an agency official, told reporters.
He said no apparent change was detected so far to the Nankai Trough plate, where scientists say a megaquake can possibly hit.
The Shinkansen bullet trains were running at slower speeds in the affected areas as a precautionary measure. Sometimes quakes can damage the railways the trains run on.
Japan is located in an area that is prone to earthquakes. Authorities frequently instruct people to stock up on bottled water, food and batteries, have plans ready to hide under tables and keep comfortable walking shoes at hand.

title: It’s the economy, stupid
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Democrats don’t need to highlight Trump’s lies, corruption (by himself and his cronies) and bumbling mistakes; he takes care of that himself. But, to get elected or reelected in 2028, Democrats need to address the U.S. economy by making sure every person in it has enough and no one has too much.
There are many ways to do that. Here are a few: (1) Raise the minimum wage and make sure every worker is paid a living wage; (2) Tax wealthy (the top 5%) people at a much higher rate, especially for capital gains; (3) Stop building data centers and using AI to eliminate jobs that real people need; (4) Start treating the environment and climate as an ally, not an opponent; (5) Most importantly, gear the economy to the needs of the worker, not to the investor or the corporation. Make the economy human-centered, not just about GDP, stock prices and corporate profits.
Good luck, Democrats, and any elected official who cares about affordability. The economy should be functioning for the well-being of everyone.
Larry Dansinger
Bangor

title: Maine Republicans must reconstruct anew
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sam Patten worked for Maine’s last three Republican senators, including Susan Collins’ first electoral campaigns, is a former managing editor of the Maine Wire and is the author of “Dangerous Company: The Misadventures of a Foreign Agent.”
From her first run for elected office 32 years ago to last Tuesday’s “blue wave,” Sen. Susan Collins was often confronted with — and usually prevailed over — circumstances that could be called unfair.
When Collins ran for Maine governor in 1994, a right-wing activist challenged her eligibility, arguing she wasn’t really from Maine (having defeated that spurious claim in court, later that year Collins lost the general election to Angus King, a man born and raised in Virginia).
The principal complaint against Collins this year was that she was a stooge of President Donald Trump, which her record will show was not actually the case.
Even though I made a case for her opponent in my last column for this paper, watching Collins lose this week I couldn’t help but be struck by the magnitude of effort it took for her to persist in politics this whole time. Could Collins, the national press asked in the weeks running up to Tuesday, “defy gravity” yet again?
Born into a cold climate with a sense of scarcity hard-wired in at the earliest of ages, most Mainers well understand that life isn’t fair. When all the confetti is swept from the floor and the righteous gloating wears itself out, some may eventually come to miss Collins. Only time will truly tell.
Without the last standing Republican senator in the Northeast, another truth will become more quickly apparent in Maine: The state’s GOP can no longer expect to run on life support.
After eight years without a Republican governor, or majority in either chamber of the Legislature, the rationale for backers of the party coffers to keep giving has been waning for some time. Without Collins to support, it is now gone altogether.
Beyond the seismic loss of her Senate seat, the Republican ranks in Augusta also shriveled — especially in the House, where the minority lost a dozen seats. Democrats, who have been largely unopposed in state government for some time, can now change the Constitution at will. For those who believe in limited government, that is a terrifying thought.
For too long, Maine’s Republican Party has sustained itself with external aid (analogous, in a way, to the U.S. Agency for International Development which Elon Musk’s boys triumphantly shuttered last year).
There was once the Bush family foothold in Kennebunkport and, more recently, there was the Trump administration, to which Republicans in the State House repeatedly turned for help on a host of issues over the past two years.
Former governor and now congressman-elect Paul LePage left behind his own set of strap-hangers as the party apparatus. It is likely that the most junior member of a minority faction in he U.S. House will have no ability to keep them fed any longer.
What is left of the Republican Party in Maine will have to stand on its own feet. But how?
Shouting into the void like madmen aggrieved by the world’s decline is probably not a winning strategy. Successive, discrete wins, on the other hand, dot the only viable path out of the wilderness.
When the Gov. Hannah Pingree administration takes office early next year, it will be staring down the barrels of a grim financial reality. Maine state government is perilously over-leveraged. Its appetites swelled by COVID-19 money after 2020, it must now adapt to austerity. It must learn to live as most Mainers do.
Wild-eyed visions of a green energy paradise, for instance, are simply unsustainable. So too is the state-supported ecosystem of nonprofits that has become accustomed to cranking out diktats disguised as policy papers.
During the debates, Sen. Collins countered attacks by Troy Jackson, now senator-elect, by pointing out how the high cost of living in Maine is the result of Augusta’s policies on everything from energy to taxes and regulations on the drowning businesses that have yet to flee the state.
But as Collins’ loss has shown us, that was not the argument for a U.S. senator to make.
Now even further diminished, Maine Republicans must pick their battles wisely and find what fissures may exist in the post-midterms mega-party of power. Single-issue campaigns offer some promise, but they must be winning issues with broad popular support. Conservatives can’t afford another failed referendum drive.
Just as importantly, Maine Republicans must find new financial backers. The right ones will follow the right issues: improving our beleaguered business environment, fixing the depleted quality of education in the classroom as opposed to getting hung up on who goes to what bathroom and taking aim at bloated — and in some already identified instances, fraudulent — state spending.
Rome wasn’t built in a day. A political party that effectively champions the rights and needs of those who aren’t celebrating right now won’t be either. But a focused effort to construct one from the ground up is long past due.
Is this possible? Only time will truly tell.

title: A father who taught his daughter to love flying is mourning after her Learjet crashed in Florida
text:
A father who taught his daughter to love flying is mourning after her Learjet crashed in Florida
Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras was 12 when she started going up in planes while her father was at the controls, watching the ground fall away beneath them. By the time she was 17, she had her own pilot’s license, having fallen in love with flying just as her father had. 
Allan Filgueiras fought back tears Friday as he remembered the daughter who followed him into the sky.
“She’s my soulmate,” Filgueiras told CNN. “Having her to talk about aviation. Now, I feel like my life is missing.”
Related video above | 911 calls reveal shock, confusion in aftermath of deadly Learjet crash
Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, was the copilot of the Learjet 60 that plunged 35,000 feet nose-first into a South Florida roadway Sunday. All nine people on board were killed. The cause of the crash isn’t yet known, and the weather and the aircraft will be among many factors examined during the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation.
Nathalia’s voice is heard on a chilling audio recording of the flight’s final minutes – first calmly telling an air traffic controller they were experiencing turbulence and manageable icing; then declaring an emergency as the plane dove hundreds of feet per second; and eventually ending with her last transmission: “We’re out of time.”
On Friday, Allan Filgueiras held a news conference to talk about the daughter he treasured. He was flanked by his lawyer, who said Allan wanted to “preserve not just her memory but her reputation.”
“We’re not making allegations against anybody at this time,” attorney Stuart Grossman said. “We’re going to do the right thing. We’re going to listen to what the government uncovers. Then we’ll have our experts look at it and say they agree or not. But I think everyone should stay out of the government’s way.”
For the father, what he wants remembered about his daughter is how enamored she was with flight, and how good she was at it.
When she was just starting out, she said: “Dad, there’s nothing else that I want to do in my life other than flying,” he recalled to CNN after the news conference.
“I told her that there’s nothing in this planet that you want that bad that you can’t achieve,” Allan Filgueiras said. “So you are going to be the pilot you wish to be.”
The young pilot graduated from American Flyers, one of the most prestigious aviation schools in the United States, her family told CNN Brasil.
By the time of the crash, Nathalia had commercial pilot and flight instructor licenses and was rated to fly larger, more complicated planes and serve as a first officer in the Learjet 60, according to Federal Aviation Administration records.
It was her dream come true, her father said.
“She said, ‘Dad, can you believe (it)? … I would pay for this, but they’re actually paying me,’” he said at the news conference. “It was her happiest moment, to fly.”
Remembered for her love of being in the air
The Learjet 60 was heading from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas. Killed were seven passengers – tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp; their two children, Emma and Charlie; caregiver Anita Maria Cetina; and another couple, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr – and Nathalia Filgueiras and pilot Jeff Gregory.
Footage from a vehicle’s dashboard camera shows the crash, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said the plane came down so fast, it “looked like a missile going down.” Investigators are still searching the crater in the pavement for clues to how the flight ended in catastrophe. On Thursday, they recovered part of the plane’s engine.
Four days before the crash, Nathalia and her father spent the afternoon together at a boat show and had lunch.
“I spent the day with her, and I was saying (to her), ‘This is the best day of my life to spend this afternoon with you,’” he told CNN.
Allan Filgueiras describes himself as someone who has always been happy. But after they said goodbye that day, he felt a sudden pang of sadness he couldn’t explain.
“I don’t know why. For a second, because I wouldn’t let (it) last more than that, I felt so sad, and it’s a feeling that I never had before in my life,” he said. “I can’t believe that was the last day that I spent with her.”
Flying was at the heart of their relationship. “Put her and I together,” he said, and aviation was “the only thing that we want to talk about.”
Allan Filgueiras started learning to fly when Nathalia was 12, and he would take her on flights with an instructor aboard, he said. He would receive his private pilot certificate from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2021, FAA records show.
He’s rated to fly single-engine planes and holds an instrument rating, which lets him fly through clouds and low visibility using only the plane’s instruments.
His daughter went further.
“She became an extraordinary pilot,” he told CNN. Eventually, the roles reversed. Nathalia ran him through drills, simulating instrument panel failures so he could learn to conduct night flights without them.
“She would put the plane in upset situations for me to recover. The other day, she said, ‘You know what? I think you can do better. Let’s do it again,’” he said. “So I became a student, and she became an instructor to keep me sharp and safe.”
He plans to keep flying.
“I will continue her legacy,” he said. “Each time that I’m gonna be flying, I’m gonna be connecting with her. I want to make her proud.”
Nathalia Filgueiras’ family is Brazilian but lives in Florida, where she was born, Camila Gadelha Corteleti, her mother, told CNN Brasil this week.
“She was a very good girl – responsible, hardworking,” Corteleti said.
She received her pilot’s license before she even got her driver’s license, her stepfather Thiago Corteleti told CNN Brasil.
“I like being different than everyone, so to me, I think it’s, like, cool,” Nathalia Filgueiras told CNN affiliate WPEC in 2023, adding that her goal was to become a commercial airplane pilot or fly private jets. “Some people think that it’s, like, weird because I can fly planes, but I can’t drive a car … but a lot of people think it’s funny.”
The school district paid for Filgueiras to get her private pilot’s license, according to WPEC.
The investigation
On Sunday, the two pilots in the Learjet had been working around bad weather for much of the Bahamas-bound flight from Texas. While the plane was near Florida’s Gulf Coast, less than 20 minutes before the crash, an air traffic controller warned that the turn they’d requested toward the Bahamas could take them into a thunderstorm.
“The turn to Freeport looks pretty bad,” the controller said in audio captured by LiveATC.net. “There is moderate to extreme precipitation 11 o’clock, and 25 miles. 100 miles in diameter.”
The jet flew south around the storm before it was cleared to turn east. The controller said the pilots could change course as needed to avoid the worst of it.
When Nathalia Filgueiras later checked in with a controller covering the West Palm Beach area, she reported that turbulence was bouncing the plane up to 700 feet and that light ice was building on the aircraft.
“If you have any better rides, let us know,” she said.
“The rides do improve in my airspace,” the controller replied. “You can expect better rides ahead.”
Moments later, Filgueiras reported precipitation and asked to climb to 37,000 feet, and the controller approved. Less than 30 seconds later, something went terribly wrong and the plane plummeted toward the ground.
“We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday – we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” she said. It wasn’t long before she cried out, in her final transmission, “We’re out of time.”
The plane passed through a strong storm cell just before the sudden descent. Though it is unclear if the weather contributed to the crash, it is “certainly a key focus of the investigation,” NTSB member Tom Chapman said this week.
Another big clue landed miles from the crash site. Most of the jet’s left elevator, the part of the tail that controls whether the nose tilts up or down, was found in three pieces between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the crater, Chapman said. That distance shows the part broke away before impact. But investigators don’t yet know whether its loss caused the dive or whether the forces of the dive tore it off.
Investigators are also searching the crater for the rest of the wreckage, and for a cockpit voice recorder. Maintenance records show the jet had one installed, but it’s unclear whether it was still on board.
“Our mission is to understand not just what happened, but why it happened, and to recommend changes to prevent it from happening again,” Chapman said.

title: At least 21 dead after boat carrying migrants sinks off Senegal coast, interior ministry says
text:
At least 21 dead after boat carrying migrants sinks off Senegal coast, interior ministry says
At least 21 people died after a boat carrying migrants sank off Senegal's coast, the country's interior ministry said on Sunday.
The ministry said in a post on X that as of Saturday evening one person had been found alive, and that teams had been mobilized to continue searching for any more possible survivors. It did not specify how many people were believed to have been on board.
The ministry said the boat sank off the coast of the town of Kébémer, north of Dakar. It added that Senegal’s interior minister will visit the site on Monday.
Related video: Teen rescued after days on capsized boat off Alaska coast; brother and cousin die
The Atlantic migration route from West Africa to Spain's Canary Islands is one of the deadliest in the world. At least 635 people died in the first five months of 2026, according to the Spanish rights group Walking Borders.
The group said for every 100 migrants that made it to the Canary Islands in that period, around 21 died.
In July, the United Nations refugee agency said nearly 150 people died or went missing within the space of one week from boats that sank off Mauritania as they were trying to make their way to Europe. It added that almost 400 people were rescued.
On New Year's Eve 2025, a boat carrying more than 200 migrants sank off the coast of Gambia. Red Cross officials reported that 44 bodies were recovered.

title: Susan Collins’ loss carries a particular sadness
text:
Rev. Steve Edington is minister emeritus of the Unitarian Universalist Church of Nashua, New Hampshire, and a former minister of the First Universalist Church of Rockland.
I began my career in the Unitarian Universalist parish ministry in 1979 when I was called to serve the congregation at the First Universalist Church of Rockland, Maine.
The chair of the search committee was State Sen. Samuel W. Collins, a prominent member of that church. He was also the Republican majority leader of the Maine State Senate. Collins went on to become an associate justice on the Maine State Supreme Court.
Sam Collins, who passed away in 2012, was one of the most decent and honorable politicians —and human beings — I have known. Despite being a longtime Democrat, I was pleased to vote for him when he ran for, and won, reelection in 1982. Although he and I did not always see eye to eye on various issues, his bedrock integrity gained him my vote.
I had concluded my ministry in Rockland and moved on to another ministerial assignment when Sam’s niece, the now departing U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, began her political career.
The last time I saw Sam was when I returned to Rockland to take part in a memorial service at the Universalist Church. Susan had just been elected to her first term in the United States Senate. In the brief conversation we had, Sam spoke of how proud he was of his niece, Sen. Susan Collins.
I thought on these things as I watched Maine’s U.S. Senator-elect, Troy Jackson, celebrate his victory over Collins this past election night. I was pleased with Troy Jackson’s win. Had I been a resident of Maine (for now, I live in New Hampshire), Jackson would have had my vote.
At the same time, I could not help but feel sadness for Susan Collins.
She comes from a well-established Yankee Republican family of good and honorable people. She did much good for the people of Maine in her 30-year Senate career, often working across the aisle for legislation she felt served the greater common good and going beyond partisan politics. I believe she entered the Senate with the idea of being Maine’s next Sen. Margaret Chase Smith.
Many years in, Collins found herself engulfed in the age of Donald Trump.
When Trump became the Republican presidential nominee in the summer of 2016, Sen. Collins — by then in her fourth term in the Senate — announced that she would not support him, saying she felt he lacked the character and integrity to hold the office of president.
During Trump’s first, and now second, terms as president, Collins did vote to oppose several of his major initiatives, including Trump’s effort to overturn the Affordable Care Act and his so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
Following Trump’s second impeachment in the wake of the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection, an insurrection he instigated, Collins voted to convict and remove the president from office.
But when it came to her dealings with Trump, Sen. Collins also often found herself playing two ends against the middle. Analysis tells us that she reliably voted in line with his initiatives and appointments.
Perhaps Collins’ most telling move in this regard was her casting her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court. Kavanaugh, in turn, cast the deciding vote to overturn the 1973 Roe v. Wade decision that had established a constitutional right to abortion.
It was Collins’ approach/avoid dance with the Trump presidency that finally caught up to her in last week’s midterm election.
Collins had arguably managed to bring herself around to accommodating Trump more often than she did standing up to him. Most of the senator’s moves to oppose him were taken when she knew Trump would still get the outcome he wanted, allowing her to demonstrate a kind of independence while remaining in Trump’s good graces.
I daresay this was the kind of game Sen. Margaret Chase Smith never would have played, whatever the political consequences. At this point, though, it no longer matters.
Ms. Collins has had her Senate career. She did good in numerous ways, while making decisions that finally cost her the office she held for three decades.
A few months from now, my wife and I will once again become residents of Maine when we move to Kennebunk to be near our son, daughter-in-law and two granddaughters. I look forward to having Troy Jackson and Angus King as my United States senators.
And I wish Susan Collins the best, wherever her life may take her from here.

title: Light snow falls in Rangeley
text:
The first signs of winter appeared early Sunday morning with light snow flurries in Rangeley.
A spokesperson for the National Weather Service couldn’t say how much it snowed, but said western Maine could continue to see bouts of winter weather throughout the week.
There’s also potential for a more widespread system headed into the weekend, most likely Friday or Saturday, that would bring light snow and heavier rain to coastal areas.

title: Gender identity has no place in election headlines
text:
Do we really need the news highlighting a person’s gender identity, seemingly validating their worthiness of their job or success? Why do we care what someone’s gender identity is? Can they do the job or not?
Now, according to this paper, Maine has its “first openly nonbinary” state lawmaker (Nov. 4).
I don’t care.
If you feel it “news” to share that, how about sharing every legislator’s gender identity? Just make it a blanket practice in every news article.
Or, wait. Are you consciously discriminating against cisgender people because they are not hip, cool or woke? Now I worry that nonbinary lawmakers will focus only on nonbinary issues and not be “for the people” but only for their people.
Once we in Maine voted in legal gay marriage, didn’t it reflect that “we” accept everyone? Just stop already. It’s not news, it’s irritating and discriminatory.
Elza Allen
Arundel

title: Hero dog who was shot twice saving his owner from her ex now needs surgery
text:
SEATTLE (KIRO) - Two years after a Seattle woman says her dog was shot twice while saving her from her ex, she is asking for help to save him from complications caused by his injuries.
A split second proved just how deep the bond between Lauren Wiggins and her dog, Judah, ran.
“My best friend, my wingman,” Wiggins said of Judah. “He did save my life, and he did get shot twice doing so.”
Wiggins says she was living with an ex in 2024, and things weren’t good. Her parents helped her develop a plan to leave, but as she was packing to go, she says her ex pulled out a gun and began shooting.
“My ex walked into our bedroom, went in the underwear drawer, grabbed his gun and started shooting,” Wiggins said.
She was shot twice in her right leg, leaving her paralyzed on that side from the knee down.
“I think I just kind of went numb. It was kind of like a movie scene. Everything went quiet,” Wiggins said.
Then, Judah rushed in.
“He came right in, attacked him, but he got shot in the head and in the shoulder in the process of doing that,” Wiggins said.
Wiggins thought Judah was dying as he lay on the ground after the incident. She says adrenaline kicked in, and she ran to get help, not knowing whether her dog would survive.
It wasn’t until she was at the hospital that she learned Judah was still alive.
“Oh, it was really emotional. My heart dropped in my stomach thinking about what he did for me,” Wiggins said.
At the time, Judah’s veterinarian thought it would be safer to leave the bullet fragments inside the dog’s body rather than attempt to remove them. For roughly two years, Wiggins says Judah seemed to handle it OK – but things changed this summer.
“I noticed that the middle of his head started to swell, and he developed this really hard lump,” Wiggins said.
A veterinary visit confirmed the fragments were moving, with the possibility they could eventually migrate to Judah’s eyes. On the low end, surgery would cost around $10,000.
“I felt so much guilt that he stepped in to save me. I wish in a lot of ways that he didn’t, so that he wouldn’t have to be dealing with what he is now,” Wiggins said.
Faced with Judah’s mounting veterinary costs, she decided to ask others for help. She started a GoFundMe, never expecting the response she would get. So far, the fundraiser has raised more than $41,000.
“It was really overwhelming,” Wiggins said. “The process of going through the courts trying to get restitution for what happened to Judah and I was terrible. We got nothing but a restraining order and kind of just was like, ‘Well, sorry, that happened to you.’ It was really nice and overwhelming to see that people actually cared.”
Judah is more than Wiggins’ dog. After everything that happened, she says he is one of the few pieces of her old life she still has.
“He’s like the only thing that I was able to take with me after everything happened,” she said. “I mean, there will never be another dog like him.”

title: Obituary: Elwood Gerry Johnson
text:
PORTLAND – Elwood Gerry Johnson, 92, a lifelong Portland resident, died Oct. 27, 2026, at Mercy Hospital.
“Gerry” was born in Portland on Jan. 19, 1934, to Elinor and Maurice Johnson. He attended Deering High School, where he ran track. He later earned an associate’s degree from Gorham State Teachers College. He served four years in the Army and nine years in the National Guard. While in the Army, he met and married Betty in Pennsylvania.
For many years, Gerry was president of E.G. Johnson & Co., the family construction company established in 1869. He also served as a director of Deering Savings and Loan.
Gerry was a lifelong member of Stroudwater Baptist Church, a member of Gideons International, and a former member of the Portland Kiwanis Club. He especially loved spending summers on Sebago Lake with his family. He also enjoyed reading, boating, and tending his strawberry and vegetable gardens.
He is survived by his wife of 68 years, Betty Johnson; and their six children, Mark Johnson and his partner, Lori Van Dusen, Randy Johnson and his wife, Susan Carr, David and Julie Johnson, Glenn Johnson, Nancy and Kevin Tuttle, and Karen and Walter Jacobsen. He is also survived by 10 grandchildren; nine great-grandchildren; and his sister, Carolyn Rumery.
He was predeceased by his parents.
A visiting hour will be held at 10 a.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at Port City Baptist Church, 1729 Congress St., Portland, followed by a celebration of his life at 11 a.m.
In lieu of flowers, memorial
donations may be made to

title: Obituary: Rita G. Drew
text:
WELLS – Rita G. Drew, 96, died on Nov. 2, 2026.
Rita was born Rita Adeline Grant on Feb. 7, 1930, to Franklin and Aurore (Ricard) Grant. She grew up on the family farm at the end of the Fort Ridge Road in North Alfred. The middle of three girls, she always said she had no brothers so it was she who worked in the gardens, the orchards, and the woods with her father, planting vegetables, picking apples and cutting firewood. Rita attended Alfred schools, played basketball upstairs over the town hall, and graduated from the old Alfred High School on Kennebunk Road in 1947. She worked a couple summers as a chambermaid at the Seaside at Kennebunk Beach and attended two years of Gorham Normal School before getting married.
Rita married Donald L. Drew of Arundel and together they raised four children, Bob, Cindy, Pam and Tina. Rita worked as a chambermaid and waitress and also as a substitute teacher. In the late ’60s, she returned to school and completed her teaching degree. She taught for two years at Dayton Elementary School and first grade at Cousens School in Kennebunk for over 20 years, retiring in 1990.
After 46 years of marriage, Don died in 1995. Following Don’s death, Rita participated in senior college at Nasson, bus trips with the Retired Teachers Association, and the Alfred High School reunions.
Rita loved animals, and had many pets over the years, especially cats. At one time, she had eleven cats. She also had a pet skunk back in the ’60s. Rita especially enjoyed family gatherings, birthday parties, Christmas get-togethers and summer BBQs. She participated in community activities in Arundel, serving as officer in the local Mothers’ Club.
In 2018, Rita stopped living alone and moved into the other side of the house of her daughter, Cindy and son-in-law, Dana. In her later years, she enjoyed word search, playing solitaire, watching “Wheel of Fortune” on TV and doing puzzles with her family.
Rita was predeceased by her parents; her sisters; her husband, Don; her son-in-law, Dana and her son, Bob.
She is survived by her three daughters, Cindy Johnson of Wells, Pamela Drew of Arundel and her partner John Jellison of Kennebunkport, her daughter, Tina Hoag and her husband Michael of Alfred; grandchildren, Mike Drew of Arundel, Steve Drew of Wells, Amy Sharpe of Ohio, Jeff Johnson and wife Penny of Wells, Hank (Dana Jr.) and wife Roxanne of Wells, Becky Hamelin and husband Shawn of Scarborough, Sarah Hoag of Saco, and Joe Hoag and wife Carol of Alfred; along with great-grandchildren; great-great-grandchildren; and many nieces and nephews.
Visiting hours will be held at Bibber Memorial Chapel, 67 Summer St., Kennebunk, on Friday, Nov. 13, from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. A funeral service will be held on Saturday, Nov. 14, at 10 a.m., with interment in Hope Cemetery to follow. A luncheon will then be provided, with details to be determined.
To share a memory or leave a message of condolence, please visit Rita’s Book of Memories Page at http://www.bibberfuneral.com.
Arrangements are in care of Bibber Memorial Chapel, 67 Summer St., Kennebunk, ME 04043

Boston Children’s Hospital Trust,

Boston, MA 02215;
or to the
American Heart Association,

Dallas, TX 75284-0692

title: UFC’s Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.
Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to “the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior” to become the Republican president’s chief spokesperson.
White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump’s post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.
When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, “Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already.”
He declined to say what conversations he’d had with Trump but said, “I’m sure I’ll have more to talk about after that.”
Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump’s post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words “On to the next chapter.”
The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.
Trump said in his post that he requested that White bring along several UFC fighters as “assistants,” adding, “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”
While White didn’t make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States, he did elsewhere in his news conference describe his ambitions to expand the Zuffa Boxing organization he also runs with Saudi Arabian backers and hold more of its events around the world.
Trump’s post came as his White House is in a period of major transition and struggling with his party’s deep losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections. The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.
Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president’s impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump’s inner circle.
The shake-up at the heart of his administration follows the brief but tumultuous week when Trump tried out a new press secretary in Katie Zacharia, who seemed uncomfortable in her sole appearance before reporters before leaving the job after five days.
The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August. Trump remains without a chief spokesperson.
Trump is close friends with White and has attended several UFC events with him since returning to the White House in January 2025.
He brought White and the sport to the White House’s South Lawn in June for the celebration of America’s 250th year of its independence and the president’s own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed near the executive mansion under " The Claw,” a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.
“It was an amazing experience, this was a one-of-one,” said White afterward.
White also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
___
Associated Press writers Daniel Gelston in Philadelphia and Jesse Bedayn in Austin, Texas, contributed to this report.

title: Woman allegedly killed by husband texted sister she was ‘not good’ days before her body was found
text:
QUITMAN, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A Texas man charged in his wife’s murder allegedly shot her in the head and left her in the bathroom for several days, according to newly released arrest documents.
Deputies with the Wood County Sheriff’s Office arrested Weldon Powell on Wednesday for the murder of his wife, Brittany Powell.
According to the probable cause affidavit, Brittany Powell’s brother-in-law called Wood County dispatch on Wednesday with a welfare concern. He and his wife, Brittany Powell’s sister, had not heard from her in three days, which he said was unusual.
A deputy met with the brother-in-law at the Powells’ home in Quitman. The brother-in-law said the last contact he and his wife had with Brittany Powell was three days prior when she told them about a physical altercation between herself and her husband. Her sister asked her if she was safe, and she texted back that she “was not good.” She told them she would call them as soon as she could.
Now, days later, the couple were concerned Brittany Powell was in danger. Her brother-in-law told the deputy that neither she nor her husband had shown up for work in three days, which was unusual for both of them.
According to the affidavit, he also told the deputy that he had Brittany Powell on his Life360 app on his phone, and the last time he saw her location was three days ago. The location at that time was Lake Quitman, so he went there Wednesday around noon to try to find her but was unsuccessful.
The brother-in-law told the deputy he tried again at 2:30 p.m. to contact the Powells. He said Weldon Powell answered his phone that time and told him he was out running errands while his wife was at home, according to the affidavit. The brother-in-law drove by the store but did not see Weldon Powell or his truck, so he went to the couple’s home.
When the brother-in-law got to the home, he says Weldon Powell was not there. He knocked on the door and called out to Brittany Powell but got no response. He then called Weldon Powell again and was told again that his wife was at the house.
The brother-in-law told Weldon Powell that he was about to call the police out of concern for Brittany Powell, and he said that Weldon Powell acted as if he did not care either way. However, he never answered any further calls from the brother-in-law after that.
Wood County dispatchers pinged the Powells’ phones around 6 p.m., and Brittany Powell’s phone pinged at Lake Quitman.
About 45 minutes later, the couple’s landlord called dispatch and said he had stopped by the house. He became concerned about the pets being left alone and went inside to check on them. It was then that he found Brittany Powell’s body in the bathroom, the affidavit said.
The landlord called 911 then said Weldon Powell pulled up to the home but sped off at high speed when he saw the landlord was there. He told deputies when they arrived that he saw Weldon Powell head toward the front gate of Holiday Villages, and they found him there and took him into custody.
The affidavit said that Brittany Powell had been shot in the temple. Deputies said they observed marks of blood on the floor leading into the bathroom where she was found that indicated she had been dragged there from an outside back door, as if she had been shot elsewhere and then brought into the house.
The affidavit alleges Weldon Powell then placed his wife in the bathroom, surrounded with ice, and left her there for several days.
The suspect is being held in the Wood County Jail on $1,000,000 bond.

title: Maine men’s basketball falls to Manhattan in home opener
text:
ORONO — Ben Tweedy’s 3-point play with 3:05 left Manhattan a four-point lead and the Maine men’s basketball team couldn’t recover in a 68-62 loss in its home opener on Sunday at The Pit.
“Tough loss,” said Maine coach Chris Markwood. “I thought the game was within our control, but we didn’t do the things necessary to win those type of close games. Had opportunities at the free-throw line, didn’t take advantage of that, was a big part of it. (Manhattan) doubled us at the free-throw line.”
Manhattan finished 23 of 33 from the foul line, while Maine made just eight of 16.
The Black Bears fall to 1-2, while Manhattan improves to 1-2.
In the first half, the Black Bears and Jaspers both shot 35.7% from the field. Both teams were weighed down by fouls and turnovers as Maine carried a 29-27 lead into the break.
Manhattan, however, outscored Maine 41-33 in the second half.
Villiam Garcia Adsten finished with a 16 points and 10 rebounds for the Black Bears, while Ben Pearce led the Jaspers with 19 points.
Ace Flagg of Newport, who entered the game averaging 10.5 points per game, was held scoreless on Sunday. He had three rebounds and two assists
“Early (in the season), these games, you’re still learning,” Flagg said. “We’re going to take this, we’re going to watch it, we’re going to go over it, talk about it and get better from it.”
The Black Bears return to action Tuesday at Rhode Island.

text:
The midterm elections are finally over, and so are the nonstop political ads paid for by billionaires and dark money groups.
In Maine alone, $315 million was reportedly spent on political advertising according. Money that could have been spent on better things. I made ample use of my mute button and recycle bin, and I’m sure I wasn’t alone in tuning out the repetitive, inflammatory half-truths these ads foisted upon us.
As disheartening as our current political spending situation is, I’m confident it can be fixed. A solution is gaining momentum: a constitutional amendment that would restore the authority of states to set reasonable rules for money in elections. H.J. Res. 191 has been introduced in Congress and 25 states, including Maine, have already signaled their support for an amendment. This is a unifying issue. More than 70% of Americans, whether Republicans, Democrats or independents, agree we need campaign finance reform.
Yes, it’s over for now. But how long before PACs and out-of-state money flood our airwaves and mailboxes again? Let’s not let our voices be drowned out by elite donors next time. Learn more about this vital issue and urge your members of Congress to co-sponsor H.J. Res 191.
Bonnie Sammons
Belgrade

Former Governor Paul LePage says he is headed to Washington, D.C., for new member orientation in the U.S. Congress.
"In the coming weeks and months, I will be laser focused on policies that lower your cost-of-living, bring prosperity back to rural Maine, and crack down on welfare fraud and corruption," LePage said in a Facebook post Sunday morning.
This comes after Lepage declared victory Wednesday afternoon, and his opponent, Democrat Matt Dunlap, conceded on Thursday.
The Secretary of State's Office says ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled to start at 10 a.m. Monday, Nov. 9.
In ranked-choice voting races, a candidate must receive more than 50% of first-choice votes as counted on Election Day in order to win the race outright. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the total ballots cast, the Secretary of State's Office makes the determination to proceed with a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
The Secretary of State's Office telling Maine's Total Coverage that even though Dunlap has conceded, the ranked-choice tabulation is required under state law.
More info about CD2
Maine's 2nd Congressional District is the largest congressional district by area east of the Mississippi River. CD2 includes all of Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties, as well as the Kennebec County communities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne and Winthrop.

title: Rockefeller Christmas tree arrives in New York City
text:
NEW YORK (WCBS) - New York’s Rockefeller Center is getting ready for the holidays with the delivery of the traditional Christmas tree on Saturday.
The 2026 tree is a 76-foot-tall Norway spruce from West Edmeston, New York. It’s about 75 years old, measures about 50 feet in diameter and weighs about 11 tons.
The tradition of the Rockefeller Center Christmas Tree dates back to 1931, when construction workers building Rockefeller Center erected a small tree decorated with handmade garlands.
The first formal tree lighting ceremony followed in 1933, beginning a tradition that has become synonymous with the holidays in New York City.

title: A shooting in the Polish city of Krakow killed 6 people. Here's what to know
text:
A shooting in the Polish city of Krakow killed 6 people. Here's what to know
Poland was in shock Sunday, a day after a gunman opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 in the city of Krakow before police shot and wounded him.
Authorities say the attacker held far-right views, though they have not disclosed whether he was affiliated with any organized extremist group. Prosecutors say they are investigating the shooting as a terrorist offense.
Related video above: Italian tourist recalls fleeing gunfire in Krakow
Police have also found the bodies of the suspect's parents and sister at the family's home.
Here is what we know about the mass killing that marked a grim first in modern-day Poland:
The attacker drove into a crowd of people
Police say the 24-year-old attacker, wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, drove into the city's Main Square and opened fire. The square, in Krakow’s Old Town, is a major tourist destination in Poland’s second-largest city.
What unfolded Saturday was a scene of chaos and terror.
Warsaw native Magdalena Frączak was visiting Krakow with her friend when shots rang out Saturday afternoon and the gunman drew closer.
“I threw an elderly woman behind the flower planter because she had become tangled in the blanket she had on her lap. I covered her with my body,” Frączak told The Associated Press on Sunday. “I also saw him out of the corner of my eye — he passed just one meter behind my back. That’s why I have shrapnel wounds in six places on my back. Only after it had passed did I pull the woman up, and we ran into a café.”
Videos posted on social media show people running away from the square into narrow streets nearby, as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims.
Even after he was wounded by police officers, the attacker continued firing, Krakow police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said.
The victims were of different nationalities
Four women and two men were killed in the square.
Three of the women and one man were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead. The wounded included people from Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.
The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities described as heroic, remained in the hospital. They were both conscious, with one emerging from a coma on Sunday afternoon.
After the shooting, authorities overnight paused St. Mary’s Trumpet Call — a traditional five-note melody that is played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on Main Square — in tribute to the victims.
It was the first time the call had been missed since World War II.
On Sunday afternoon, St. Anne’s Church in Krakow filled with mourners attending a service for the victims.
The square reopened Sunday evening with mourners gathering to lay flowers and candles in honor of the victims.
Few details have been released about the attacker
The attacker, a 24-year-old Polish national, remained in critical condition on Sunday after undergoing several surgeries. Police have not released his name.
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński described his views as radical and ultranationalist, and said evidence indicated he had a fascination with far-right ideologies.
Prosecutors said they had opened an investigation into murder and attempted murder, including attacks on police officers, describing the shooting as a terrorist offense.
At the suspect's home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow, authorities said they discovered three bodies.
Police identified them as the suspect's parents and sister. They said the three likely died from gunshot wounds.
The suspect’s dead sibling was a young artist studying at the Krakow Academy of Fine Arts. “Nothing will ever be like before. The delicate tissue of our academic community was painfully wounded,” the academy wrote in a statement Sunday, confirming that Magdalena Oksińska was a third-year student.
“Magdalena Oksińska, 21 years old, a queer person, was an absolutely talented painter, photographer, poet and writer,” architect Pavko Krajka wrote on social media, in a post accompanied by images of the artist’s paintings. “Her death is a great loss for Krakow, Polish, European and queer culture.”
What is known about the weapons used in the attack
Police found four firearms at the scene of the attack. They were recovered from the attacker or from his car.
Klęczar said the attacker’s father legally owned more than 10 guns and that the attacker also owned firearms. Local officials said seven weapons were also seized from the family home, bringing the total number of firearms recovered to 11.
The Swit shooting club in Starachowice, where the attacker is believed to have trained, issued a statement Sunday saying it offered only “static shooting,” which involves firing from a fixed position at a stationary target.
The suspect, it said, “was never trained in our club in the areas of dynamic, tactical or combat shooting.”
Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland, a country of 37 million people where about 411,000 people hold gun permits. Interest in gun ownership has been rising.
Kacper Rekawek, a researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague, Netherlands, said the attack resembled incidents of far-right “lone wolf” attacks in Europe over the past years.
