title: Colin Kaepernick named Muhammad Ali Humanitarian of the Year
text:
Colin Kaepernick receives Muhammad Ali Humanitarian of the Year award
Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick was in Louisville Saturday night to receive the Muhammad Ali Center's Humanitarian of the Year award.
Kaepernick, who played six seasons in the NFL, primarily with the San Francisco 49ers, is being recognized during the center's 13th annual awards ceremony.
Video above: From Colin Kaepernick to NFL Moment of Unity, how America reacts when athletes protest
He became a national figure in 2016 after kneeling during the national anthem before games to protest racial injustice and police brutality.
The protests sparked widespread debate and drew both support and criticism.
Kaepernick has not played in the NFL since the 2016 season.
In announcing the award, the Muhammad Ali Center cited Kaepernick's work addressing racial injustice and underserved communities.
Kaepernick said Muhammad Ali's leadership and example helped prepare him for his own journey as an activist.
Video below: Colin Kaepernick works out in New Orleans
"I think of the influence of Ali. In many ways, he was training me before the world ever saw. He was preparing me for what was to come," Kaepernick said.
The ceremony honored Louisville philanthropists Steve and Amy Trager with the Kentucky Humanitarian Award and recognized six changemakers age 30 or younger for their work in accessibility, technology, environmental sustainability and refugee support.
"We know what we want. And we are so eager to go and get it. And this is just the tip of the iceberg of what young people have and the potential we actually have to carry in changes across the world," said Joseph Nguthiru, Dedication Award recipient.
Among them was Confidence Award recipient Mateo Salvato, whose mobile app is helping more than half a million people with disabilities in 75 countries communicate.
"We believe that dignity should not have a price tag to it," Salvato said.
Other honorees included environmental activists Franziska Trautmann and Gab Mejia.
"The fighting spirit to use your passion, your purpose and your dreams and your imagination as a way forward. What can we do on this planet? What are the simple ways that we could do to make this bearable for each one of us?" Gab Mejia, Spirituality Award recipient.
Giving Award Recipient Franziska Trautmann work focuses on recycling, coastal restoration and environmental sustainability.
"We recycle glass in the Gulf South, expanding accessibility to recycling and then using that product to help fight coastal erosion. And so we hope to continue to expand our work and, you know, one day continue to live up to the Muhammad Ali name," she said.
The annual awards celebrate the values Ali championed throughout his life, including equality, human dignity and social justice.
The event also serves as the Muhammad Ali Center's largest annual fundraiser. Money raised supports the center's mission and its work throughout the community.

title: Maine men’s basketball falls to Manhattan
text:
ORONO — Ben Tweedy’s 3-point play with 3:05 left Manhattan a four-point lead and the Maine men’s basketball team couldn’t recover in a 68-62 loss in its home opener on Sunday at The Pit.
“Tough loss,” said Maine coach Chris Markwood. “I thought the game was within our control, but we didn’t do the things necessary to win those type of close games. Had opportunities at the free-throw line, didn’t take advantage of that, was a big part of it. (Manhattan) doubled us at the free-throw line.”
Manhattan finished 23 of 33 from the foul line, while Maine made just eight of 16.
The Black Bears fall to 1-2, while Manhattan improves to 1-2.
In the first half, the Black Bears and Jaspers both shot 35.7% from the field. Both teams were weighed down by fouls and turnovers as Maine carried a 29-27 lead into the break.
Manhattan, however, outscored Maine 41-33 in the second half.
Villiam Garcia Adsten finished with a 16 points and 10 rebounds for the Black Bears, while Ben Pearce led the Jaspers with 19 points.
Ace Flagg of Newport, who entered the game averaging 10.5 points per game, was held scoreless on Sunday. He had three rebounds and two assists
“Early (in the season), these games, you’re still learning,” Flagg said. “We’re going to take this, we’re going to watch it, we’re going to go over it, talk about it and get better from it.”
The Black Bears return to action Tuesday at Rhode Island.

title: Hero dog who was shot twice saving his owner from her ex now needs surgery
text:
SEATTLE (KIRO) - Two years after a Seattle woman says her dog was shot twice while saving her from her ex, she is asking for help to save him from complications caused by his injuries.
A split second proved just how deep the bond between Lauren Wiggins and her dog, Judah, ran.
“My best friend, my wingman,” Wiggins said of Judah. “He did save my life, and he did get shot twice doing so.”
Wiggins says she was living with an ex in 2024, and things weren’t good. Her parents helped her develop a plan to leave, but as she was packing to go, she says her ex pulled out a gun and began shooting.
“My ex walked into our bedroom, went in the underwear drawer, grabbed his gun and started shooting,” Wiggins said.
She was shot twice in her right leg, leaving her paralyzed on that side from the knee down.
“I think I just kind of went numb. It was kind of like a movie scene. Everything went quiet,” Wiggins said.
Then, Judah rushed in.
“He came right in, attacked him, but he got shot in the head and in the shoulder in the process of doing that,” Wiggins said.
Wiggins thought Judah was dying as he lay on the ground after the incident. She says adrenaline kicked in, and she ran to get help, not knowing whether her dog would survive.
It wasn’t until she was at the hospital that she learned Judah was still alive.
“Oh, it was really emotional. My heart dropped in my stomach thinking about what he did for me,” Wiggins said.
At the time, Judah’s veterinarian thought it would be safer to leave the bullet fragments inside the dog’s body rather than attempt to remove them. For roughly two years, Wiggins says Judah seemed to handle it OK – but things changed this summer.
“I noticed that the middle of his head started to swell, and he developed this really hard lump,” Wiggins said.
A veterinary visit confirmed the fragments were moving, with the possibility they could eventually migrate to Judah’s eyes. On the low end, surgery would cost around $10,000.
“I felt so much guilt that he stepped in to save me. I wish in a lot of ways that he didn’t, so that he wouldn’t have to be dealing with what he is now,” Wiggins said.
Faced with Judah’s mounting veterinary costs, she decided to ask others for help. She started a GoFundMe, never expecting the response she would get. So far, the fundraiser has raised more than $41,000.
“It was really overwhelming,” Wiggins said. “The process of going through the courts trying to get restitution for what happened to Judah and I was terrible. We got nothing but a restraining order and kind of just was like, ‘Well, sorry, that happened to you.’ It was really nice and overwhelming to see that people actually cared.”
Judah is more than Wiggins’ dog. After everything that happened, she says he is one of the few pieces of her old life she still has.
“He’s like the only thing that I was able to take with me after everything happened,” she said. “I mean, there will never be another dog like him.”

title: Poles mourn rare mass killing as authorities say attacker had far-right views
text:
KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — Mourners on Sunday laid candles and flowers alongside bullet holes in Krakow, Poland, after the city’s central square turned into a site of bloodshed and grief. A 24-year-old man with far-right views opened fire a day earlier, killing six people and wounding 15 before police shot and wounded him.
Poland on Sunday began two days of national mourning following the attack the day before, which Poland’s defense minister described as an “act of terror.”
The violence began Saturday at around 3 p.m. when the assailant drove through the Main Square, in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town. The square is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city.
St. Mary’s Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight, the first time the call had been missed since World War II.
On Sunday afternoon, St. Anne’s Church in Krakow filled with mourners attending a memorial service. The square reopened soon after and locals and visitors alike showed up to reclaim it after the tragedy.
“I come here so as not to get caught up in a spiral of fear and anxiety,” Krakow local Maciej Sikorski told The Associated Press from the square. “In a situation like this, it’s all too easy to stop living — to start being afraid instead, and just vegetate. That is something I really want to avoid.”
Authorities also found the bodies of the assailant’s sister, mother and father at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds.
Woman injured by shrapnel while saving another
Witness Andy Hill told the BBC that he’d felt as though he was in a movie scene.
“It doesn’t feel real,” the British tourist said. “And the trouble is, you have such an instantaneous moment to make a decision: Run. Stand still. There’s an element of shock. But I just thought the easiest thing to do is dive through a doorway and just take refuge behind the windows.”
Warsaw native Magdalena Frączek, meanwhile, was visiting Krakow with her friend when shots rang out and the gunman drew closer.
“I threw an elderly woman behind the flower planter because she had become tangled in the blanket she had on her lap. I covered her with my body,” Frączek told the AP. “I also saw him out of the corner of my eye — he passed just one meter behind my back. That’s why I have shrapnel wounds in six places on my back. Only after he had passed did I pull the woman up, and we ran into a café.”
On Sunday, she forced herself to return to the Main Square to grieve among other mourners.
“I can’t put it into words. Because I knew that I would never come back to Krakow if I didn’t come in here,” she said. “When I found out that they had reopened the Main Market Square, I told my friend that I had to come here.”
American tourist Marylin Green mourned the losses in the “beautiful city” during her first trip to Poland that also included the capital.
“I’m Polish, my parents were from here,” she said. “I loved Warsaw. So I was really looking forward to coming here, too.”
Police officers described as heroes
Prosecutors said Sunday they opened an investigation into the murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act “constituting a terrorist offense.”
Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead.
A video posted on social media showed a police officer repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street. The officer later slowly collapsed to the ground.
The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in the hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon.
“If it weren’t for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher,” Klęczar said.
Michał Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak, two local surgeons who were having a bite to eat nearby, also stepped in.
Wierdak “took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help,” Pędziwiatr told the Polish news website onet. “Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life.”
Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.
The suspect is also in critical condition after undergoing multiple surgeries. There was confusion on Saturday about his age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed that he is 24.
The suspect’s dead sibling was a young artist studying at the Krakow Academy of Fine Arts. “Nothing will ever be like before. The delicate tissue of our academic community was painfully wounded,” the academy wrote in a statement on Sunday, confirming that Magdalena Oksińska was a third year student and that, additionally, the sister of an academy employee was shot twice.
“Magdalena Oksińska, 21 years old, a queer person, was an absolutely talented painter, photographer, poet and writer,” architect Pavko Krajka wrote in a post on social media, accompanied by images of the artist’s colourful paintings. “Her death is a great loss for Krakow, Polish, European and queer culture.”
The mass killing marks a grim first for Poland
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect holds “very radical” and “ultranationalistic” views.
“Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” Kierwiński said at a news conference Saturday.
Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found on the suspect or in his car in Krakow. Both father and son had gun permits, they said.
Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising.
The Swit shooting club in Starachowice, where the suspect is believed to have trained, issued a statement on Sunday saying it offered only “static shooting,” which involves firing from a fixed position at a stationary target. The club added that the suspect “was never trained in our club in the areas of dynamic, tactical or combat shooting.”
Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The young attackers used knives or other sharp objects. Officials blamed the school attacks on online “glorification of violence,” and said that some of the attackers were active in the far-right environment.
The Krakow shooter’s military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other “extreme right lone actors” committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague.
“We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland,” he said.
___
Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland. Associated Press writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.
___
This story corrects the spelling of Frączek.

title: Week Ahead in Washington: Nov. 8
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Lawmakers return to Capitol Hill this week for the lame-duck session after the midterm elections, with a potential impeachment vote on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and government funding on the agenda.
Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, (R-Ky.) has promised to bring a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth. The House must vote on a privileged resolution.
Massie said the only way to avoid a vote is if Hegseth resigns or President Donald Trump fires him.
In response, Hegseth posted a video to X vowing to fight.
“Their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents,” Hegseth said. “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. It didn’t work with President Trump and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”
Lawmakers also will start work this week on keeping the government open.
Government funding is set to run out Dec. 11, when the continuing resolution passed earlier this year expires.
The newest members of Congress come to Washington this week for freshman orientation.
House Republicans plan to hold their leadership vote after losses in last week’s election.
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he will not be in the running for the next Minority Leader. Two candidates vying to replace him as GOP leader are current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio).

title: Bruins start fast in win over Panthers
text:
BOSTON — Elias Lindholm, Mikey Eyssimont and Morgan Geekie each scored a goal in an opening period that started out testy, carrying the Boston Bruins past the Florida Panthers 4-1 on Sunday.
Jeremy Swayman made 40 saves, 17 coming in the first period, for the Bruins, who improved to 7-0-0 at home by winning their fourth straight game a day after placing young star James Hagens on injured reserve.
JJ Peterka added a goal for Boston, which owns a plus-21 goal differential at TD Garden. David Pastrnak and Pavel Zacha each added two assists.
Carter Verhaeghe scored a power-play goal for the Panthers, and Jacob Markstrom stopped 32 shots. Florida has lost three of four games.
Boston’s 6-foot-7 defenseman Nikita Zadorov dropped the gloves against 6-foot-1 forward Brady Tkachuk at the opening faceoff, setting the stage for 126 total penalty minutes.
Just over six minutes later, Florida’s Garnet Hathaway squared off against forward Mark Kastelic.
The Panthers swept the three games against Boston last season, winning each by one goal.
Following a lengthy review, Lindholm was credited with a goal that made it 1-0 just 4:50 into the game after his wrister broke off Markstrom and trickled behind him, nearing the goal line as he attempted to pull it back with his glove.
Eyssimont poked a loose puck into the net following his wraparound shot, making it 2-0 less than two minutes later.
Geekie then scored for the fourth straight game, one-timing a shot for a power-play goal at 15:59 with the Bruins on a two-man advantage.
Verhaeghe’s one-timer cut it to 3-1.
The Bruins, who entered with the NHL’s second-best goal differential behind Carolina, were off since rolling to a 6-2 victory at Pittsburgh on Thursday.
Up next
Panthers: Close their three-game road trip Tuesday at Columbus.
Bruins: Play the second of four straight at home Thursday, facing longtime rival Montreal.

title: Support the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
There’s a new bill being considered in Congress, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, that deserves support. As we see the climate changing around us — storms strengthening and pollution increasing due to the burning of fossil fuels — we could speed the change to renewables by asking Sens. King and Collins and Reps. Pingree and Golden to support this bill.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) has a reasonable chance of passage if we support it. This bill would expand and improve electrical transmission lines, engage the community early in the environmental approval process and speed up the building of needed electrical infrastructure.
Being a bipartisan bill, no one is entirely happy with it. Thankfully, experts agree it could significantly reduce carbon emissions. There are many energy generation projects on hold because the developers cannot get permission to connect them to the grid. This is the case for both renewable projects and fossil fuel projects, but a majority of such projects are renewable.
Moving to renewables, as well as decreasing the pollution in the air and slowing the warming of our planet, will gradually decrease the cost of electricity in America. The blanket of CO2 surrounding and heating our planet is getting worse daily. We have no time to waste.
Email your legislators and ask them to support BAAJA. Our electricity will be more dependable — and eventually cheaper — if this passes.
Nancy Hasenfus
Brunswick

title: There’s no need to feel bad for Susan Collins
text:
On election night last week, I went to bed at 10 p.m. (I have a baby). Even by that time, the sky was looking blue, if you know what I mean.
I woke up again at around 3 a.m. and was up for an hour rocking the baby back to sleep — he’s teething — and I didn’t even mind that much because I just kept scrolling through Democratic win after Democratic win.
The biggest congrats of the night must go to Troy Jackson, who not only beat a 30 year incumbent, but who did it with a campaign lasting less than four months, a fraction of his opponent’s funding and, as he himself has pointed out, a funny accent.
(Hey, if a successful campaign can happen in under four months, maybe it’s time to legally set time limits on when campaigns can start advertising. Imagine the peace in our mailboxes.)
I have been waiting years for Sen. Susan Collins to lose. Years.
Specifically, I have been waiting eight years. Eight years since 2018 and her vote for Brett Kavanaugh which, along with her vote for Neil Gorsuch, led directly to the end of a nationwide right to abortion (as well as a ton of other terrible Supreme Court decisions, such as “anything the president does while President isn’t a crime ever.”)
I honestly thought Collins would die in office or retire on her own terms, and while I would have been satisfied to not have her in the Senate anymore under almost any circumstances, it’s so much nicer to have her definitively lose a race, to be rejected by Maine voters.
After the Jan. 6 Capitol insurrection, I wrote of Sen. Collins that I would “use my meager talents to make sure her legacy is remembered the way she deserves it to be remembered – as a failure.” I still intend to do that.
Don’t feel bad for Susan Collins. She can head to a comfortable retirement with a nicely padded bank account. The worst that will happen is she’ll be haunted by the ghosts of the American women who died because they couldn’t get abortion care in time.
After Tuesday’s Democratic shellacking — and at the time of writing — Paul LePage might be the only Republican in the entire country to have flipped a seat in the House of Representatives. If Paul LePage is your upside, things aren’t going well for you.
If LePage is my congressional delegate, I will quite obviously not be thrilled. LePage supports terrible policies and I just plain don’t like him. His campaign leaned into homophobia in its mailings (of which I received several), repeatedly reusing an image of his electoral rival, Matt Dunlap, with an LGBT Pride flag. That’s it. That’s the whole attack. That a guy held a Pride flag because I guess LePage and his voters think supporting gay people is an inherently negative thing.
On the other hand, I almost feel bad for LePage. (Almost.) First of all, he’s at risk of having me as a constituent, and we all know I’m extremely annoying. Second, he’s 78 years old and not a particularly vigorous 78, either. He’ll be the oldest freshman congressman in American history. He barely looked like he wanted to run his campaign in the first place.
You can say a lot about LePage’s governorship of Maine, but at least the man looked like he was having a good time.
As of Thursday morning, he was clinging on by fewer than 2,700 votes in a district that Trump won by nine points in 2024. LePage could be relaxing on a beach in Florida right now. Instead, he has to keep pretending to live in an apartment above a barbershop in Augusta.
Also. While a couple dozen congressional races remain uncalled, at the time of this column’s submission, the count is at least 237 Democrats to 147 Republicans in the House of Representatives. (218 seats are needed for control.)
Not only will Paul LePage be in a minority — surely a terrifying prospect for the man who once expressed fear of the menace of “D-Money, Smoothie and Shifty” — but it promises to be a tiny, reviled minority, bound inextricably to a president who pretty much every average person dislikes.
It’s like LePage found a magical cursed monkey’s paw at Marden’s, wished to be a congressman, and the paw may grant his wish in a terrible way.

title: Obituary: Barbara Louise (McLaughlin) Pelletier
text:
GARDINER – Barbara Louise (McLaughlin) Pelletier, 92, of Gardiner, Maine, passed away peacefully in her sleep at her daughter’s home on Oct. 29, 2026, with all four of her children close by.
Born June 12, 1934, in Gardiner, Barbara was the third of four children and the only daughter of Charles “Charlie” Sr. and Freda McLaughlin. As a girl she pumped gas and kept the books at her father’s store and gas station. She graduated from Gardiner Area High School in 1952.
It was at the store that Barbara first noticed a quiet, shy young man named Louis Pelletier. She had a crush on him and made sure he knew it, flirting with him over all the other fellows who hung around the station. They married on July 2, 1954, beginning nearly 69 years together. They raised four children, Mark, Julie, and Tammy, born within five years, and Tim, who came along 13 years later, when Barbara was 40.
Barbara stayed home with the children, babysitting for other families as well, until Mark, Julie, and Tammy were in school full-time. She then worked in the office at Hazzard Shoe in Augusta, where Louis was a foreman on the shop floor. After Tim was born, she resumed her role as a stay-at-home mom, and once Tim was older, she worked as administrative assistant to the president of Gardiner Savings. She often said, “Being a mother is the hardest job you’ll ever love.”
The house Louis built was always her “Home Sweet Home,” and she delighted in decorating it for every holiday and filling it with family. A woman of deep faith who had always wanted to be a teacher, she loved teaching Sunday school at St. Joseph’s Church in Gardiner and was a faithful member of her Bible study group.
Barbara loved sewing and knitting, music and dancing, and reading stories of family and faith, and she never tired of joking about her love of “beer,” the kind made from root. A fast walker, even in her final years she would proudly say, “I’m a great walker!” She loved hiking and the outdoors, and she and Louis often took the kids camping. She enjoyed games of every kind, and well into her later years she could still “give a whipping” to her kids and grandkids at bocce ball and croquet. With her grandchildren she was gentle and playful, always ready to sing, read, or turn a moment into a lesson. Positive and kind, she was devoted above all to God, her family, and her friends.
After Louis’s passing in 2023, Barbara moved in with her daughter Julie, next door to her son Mark. There, Julie lovingly cared for her, and the two were constant companions.
Barbara is survived by her son Mark and his wife Sheila, daughter Julie, daughter Tammy and her partner Kevin, son Tim and his wife Bethany; grandchildren Sarah, Matt, Chris, Emmi, Kevin, Jaime, Sydney, and Logan; six great-grandchildren; and many nieces and nephews.
She was predeceased by her husband Louis; and her brothers Bernard, Charles Jr., and Philip.
Visiting hours celebrating Barbara’s life will be held on Wednesday, Nov. 11, from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. at Staples Funeral Home, 53 Brunswick Ave., Gardiner, Maine. A Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated at 10:30 a.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12, at St. Joseph’s Catholic Church, Gardiner. Burial will follow at the New Maine Veterans Cemetery, Mount Vernon Road, Augusta.
Condolences, memories and photos may be shared with the family by visiting the Staples Funeral Home website http://www.StaplesFuneralHome.com
Louis built a home for Barbara here on Earth, and we take comfort knowing she has now gone to the home he built for her in Heaven, together again with her husband and with her best friend, Jesus, as she always called Him.

title: Marveling at Maine from afar
text:
In his Nov. 5 column (“Susan Collins will be remembered for her service – and her shortcomings”), Steve Collins makes an important point: Sen. Susan Collins has a lot to explain. I think what Maine voters said by their votes is that they didn’t buy the explanations Sen. Collins has offered to date — and were tired of waiting for her to step away from President Trump.
As one who has marveled from afar at how Collins seemed, for years, to convince folks that she was carrying on the legacy of a truly great senator, Margaret Chase Smith, I kept hoping Collins would show the courage Sen. Smith displayed in her “Declaration of Conscience “speech. But all Mainers ever got were declarations of concern.
This election, voters sent a clear message to Sen. Collins: Enough. Our democracy is all the better because of that message. My thanks to Mainers.
Stephen Gladstone
Cleveland, Ohio

title: Woman allegedly killed by husband texted sister she was ‘not good’ days before her body was found
text:
QUITMAN, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A Texas man charged in his wife’s murder allegedly shot her in the head and left her in the bathroom for several days, according to newly released arrest documents.
Deputies with the Wood County Sheriff’s Office arrested Weldon Powell on Wednesday for the murder of his wife, Brittany Powell.
According to the probable cause affidavit, Brittany Powell’s brother-in-law called Wood County dispatch on Wednesday with a welfare concern. He and his wife, Brittany Powell’s sister, had not heard from her in three days, which he said was unusual.
A deputy met with the brother-in-law at the Powells’ home in Quitman. The brother-in-law said the last contact he and his wife had with Brittany Powell was three days prior when she told them about a physical altercation between herself and her husband. Her sister asked her if she was safe, and she texted back that she “was not good.” She told them she would call them as soon as she could.
Now, days later, the couple were concerned Brittany Powell was in danger. Her brother-in-law told the deputy that neither she nor her husband had shown up for work in three days, which was unusual for both of them.
According to the affidavit, he also told the deputy that he had Brittany Powell on his Life360 app on his phone, and the last time he saw her location was three days ago. The location at that time was Lake Quitman, so he went there Wednesday around noon to try to find her but was unsuccessful.
The brother-in-law told the deputy he tried again at 2:30 p.m. to contact the Powells. He said Weldon Powell answered his phone that time and told him he was out running errands while his wife was at home, according to the affidavit. The brother-in-law drove by the store but did not see Weldon Powell or his truck, so he went to the couple’s home.
When the brother-in-law got to the home, he says Weldon Powell was not there. He knocked on the door and called out to Brittany Powell but got no response. He then called Weldon Powell again and was told again that his wife was at the house.
The brother-in-law told Weldon Powell that he was about to call the police out of concern for Brittany Powell, and he said that Weldon Powell acted as if he did not care either way. However, he never answered any further calls from the brother-in-law after that.
Wood County dispatchers pinged the Powells’ phones around 6 p.m., and Brittany Powell’s phone pinged at Lake Quitman.
About 45 minutes later, the couple’s landlord called dispatch and said he had stopped by the house. He became concerned about the pets being left alone and went inside to check on them. It was then that he found Brittany Powell’s body in the bathroom, the affidavit said.
The landlord called 911 then said Weldon Powell pulled up to the home but sped off at high speed when he saw the landlord was there. He told deputies when they arrived that he saw Weldon Powell head toward the front gate of Holiday Villages, and they found him there and took him into custody.
The affidavit said that Brittany Powell had been shot in the temple. Deputies said they observed marks of blood on the floor leading into the bathroom where she was found that indicated she had been dragged there from an outside back door, as if she had been shot elsewhere and then brought into the house.
The affidavit alleges Weldon Powell then placed his wife in the bathroom, surrounded with ice, and left her there for several days.
The suspect is being held in the Wood County Jail on $1,000,000 bond.

title: Israel’s president officially gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government
text:
Israel’s president officially gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government
Israeli President Isaac Herzog gave opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government on Sunday evening.
Previous Israeli election coverage above
After the formal announcement, Eisenkot, who ran as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rival, now has to launch complicated negotiations with potential coalition partners. He has six weeks to form a government.
At the ceremony in Jerusalem, Eisenkot said he wanted a leadership that people can trust, that will act in the interests of the public and that represents all parts of society.
The Oct. 27 election gave neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor Eisenkot a clear majority in parliament. Among the kingmakers — and most politically fraught potential allies — are the Arab-led parties. They made historic gains in the election and have been a target of Netanyahu and his allies.
Eisenkot said Sunday that the conditions for parties joining his governing coalition are support for Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, for its declaration of independence, for military or national service, and recognizing the Hamas militant group as a terrorist organization.
While the announcement doesn't guarantee that Eisenkot will be the next prime minister, Herzog’s decision is another blow to Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority in the election.
Here’s a closer look at what lies ahead:
There was no clear winner
In Israel, people vote for parties, which form alliances. A coalition needs to have a majority of at least 61 seats in the 120-member assembly, known as the Knesset, to form a government.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot secured a majority in the election. Netanyahu’s coalition plunged from a peak of 68 seats to just 53. The opposition bloc, led by Eisenkot, won 48 seats, and Arab-led parties secured the other 19.
But after his consultations last week, Herzog decided that Eisenkot has the best chance of cobbling together a coalition. That is because the Arab-led parties said they were ready to support him.
It remains unclear, however, whether Eisenkot is willing or able to bring them into a future coalition. After three years of wars in Gaza and across the Middle East, cooperating with Arab-led parties is politically difficult.
Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister
Eisenkot has three options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties — something several members of his bloc do not support — or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community.
Eisenkot, a former army chief, and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the long-standing draft exemptions enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox.
After Herzog announced Saturday that he would tap Eisenkot, the candidate vowed to form a government as quickly as possible.
But doing so will almost certainly require compromises or broken promises.
Netanyahu presses unsubstantiated claims against Arab voters
Netanyahu has repeatedly claimed the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, which rallied their supporters to vote in large numbers. But he has offered little evidence to support the claims.
Netanyahu is expected to continue his pressure tactics against Eisenkot, saying any alliance with the Arab parties would be an act of betrayal.
Israel’s Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country’s Central Elections Commission — and Herzog — say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing is found, it did not have a significant impact on the result.
Netanyahu called for a “national unity” government with Eisenkot on Saturday night. But it remains unclear whether the two rivals could agree on a power-sharing agreement, and these coalitions are fragile and often collapse.
Support from Arab-led parties faces opposition within Eisenkot’s bloc
Eisenkot has the option of forming a coalition with the support of the two Arab-led parties, which won an unprecedented 19 seats in the highest Arab election turnout. Only one Arab party, Ra’am, has ever joined a governing coalition, in 2021. Ra’am has said it will support Eisenkot, but the party does not have enough seats on its own to push Eisenkot into the majority.
Breaking with decades of precedent, the second Arab-led party, the Joint List, said it will support Eisenkot from outside the coalition to end Netanyahu’s grip on power.
That cooperation is fraught for both sides. For the Joint List, it would mean backing a government unlikely to end Israel’s wars or curb settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. For Eisenkot and other opposition parties, it would mean aligning with parties that not only criticize Israel’s policies but reject its identity as a Jewish state.
Eisenkot has laid out a series of conditions for any Arab party to join his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and declaring the Palestinian militant group Hamas a terrorist organization.
One of Eisenkot’s partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beytenu party, already has said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties.
Cooperation with ultra-Orthodox falters at anger over military exemptions
Eisenkot also says that any party that joins him must support mandatory military service or civil service. It remains unclear whether the ultra-Orthodox religious parties are prepared to compromise.
These religious parties, which were part of Netanyahu’s outgoing coalition, want to preserve their military exemptions, which they say are needed to preserve their devout lifestyle. But the exemptions have grown especially controversial among the broader public during the past three years of war.
Anticipating its position as a swing vote, the ultra-Orthodox party United Torah Judaism has left the door open to cooperating with Eisenkot.
What’s expected this week in Israel
Eisenkot will officially receive the mandate to build a coalition during a ceremony on Sunday. It comes after two days of meetings last week between Herzog and the political parties.
Eisenkot has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible two-week extension from the president. If he is unable to form a government, Netanyahu could then be given a chance put together a coalition. If Netanyahu is also unable to do so, the country will return to elections early next spring.
Israel’s new members of Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday evening. Netanyahu and his Cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity, with limited powers, until a coalition is formed.

title: Staff at the US center for AI safety are reporting to the White House, raising independence concerns
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — With public anxiety growing over mounting reports about out-of-control artificial intelligence agents, the tiny U.S. government division charged with assessing the safety of new AI offerings lacks a permanent leader and has stopped publishing its research.
Officials with the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, or CAISSI, an independent division of the Commerce Department, recently were asked to informally report to an office of the White House. That’s according to two former government officials with knowledge of the ongoing conversations who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to avoid repercussions for current staffers.
The new arrangement concerns some critics, who worry that the executive branch might be politicizing decisions that could affect everything from cybersecurity to bioweapons and that the center’s findings could be altered or muted in deference to the tech industry, which has been largely entrusted to police itself.
“These are really powerful institutions that can drastically improve our lives, or the alternative. And the hope is that you can put in nonpartisan or bipartisan technocratic experts to enact policy in a way that best serves the American public,” said Caroline Siegel Singh, an AI and emerging technology program manager for the Federation of American Scientists.
Others argue that bringing AI safety officials closer to the orbit of President Donald Trump, who has taken an outwardly hands-off approach to the issue, could give the division more prominence — and perhaps more funding.
The center, which has experienced departures and until recently was called the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation, is allocated $10 million per year. That’s about one-eighth the annual budget of its counterpart in the United Kingdom, which is far less celebrated for its frontier technologies.
In April, the division’s director was hired and then fired within days. His replacement lasted a few months before he resigned, and the center has been without a permanent leader ever since, although the head of its parent institute doubles as its acting director.
In August, Congress started asking why the center suddenly stopped making public its reports about how safely certain AI systems were performing. San Francisco giant OpenAI also had chimed in by then, asking policymakers to throw more money and support behind the division.
The White House didn’t respond to specific questions about CAISSI. But it said in a statement that Trump had formally established his new Super Intelligence Force — the president’s preferred term for artificial intelligence. Trump has commissioned a report on risks from his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, and will ensure “continued U.S. leadership on SI for the benefit of the American people,” the White House said.
An industry that polices itself
The federal government often takes an active role in deciding what is safe for the public.
Take the automobile industry, for example. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration sits crash test dummies in cars and then runs them into walls to measure how human bodies are affected by vehicle collisions. Government researchers then analyze the crash test data, share it with the public and prescribe national standards to improve vehicle safety, all with the mission of saving lives and lowering economic costs from crashes.
With AI models, safety testing looks very different.
Under then-President Joe Biden, leading AI companies voluntarily agreed to promote “safe, secure, and transparent development” of their models by sharing details with the newly created division of the Commerce Department and following the administration’s guidelines for tests and transparency reports.
In September, following alarming reports of AI systems eluding their makers’ control, Trump asked leading AI companies to undertake “tremendous self-policing” as part of a voluntary safety pact, but his administration hasn’t said how it will monitor the AI companies’ implementation.
The technology is advancing so rapidly that many models are now deployed instead as AI agents that work without human prompting and can plan out myriad steps in real-world environments, such as in a recent case in which an AI agent sent a false tip to Philadelphia police about an unsolved homicide case.
As AI capabilities have grown, the government’s capacity to independently check these systems hasn’t kept pace. There still is no standard process for testing how safely AI agents are acting in the real world, even in simple cases such as when AI agents book a flight, said Sayash Kapoor, an incoming assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley School of Information.
“Our previous methods would just look at the final answer, the final check, whether the flight was correctly booked. And in this case, it might seem as if the task was solved correctly,” said Kapoor, the co-author of a new paper examining agent evaluations. “But unless you’re looking at the entire set of steps that an agent took, you won’t be able to tell that the agent made a huge mistake.”
Trump has prioritized dominance in AI
When Trump started his second term, he initially empowered venture capitalists David Sacks and Sriram Krishnan as his AI czar and senior AI policy advisor, respectively. Their expertise was in leading tech investments, not the technical evaluation of AI models.
Both stepped down earlier this year but Sacks now serves on Trump’s technology advisory council. And after a relatively unknown Anthropic engineer resigned, warning about the dangers of AI development, Trump made a series of policy changes.
Trump empowered National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to lead his new Super Intelligence Force, which the president said would keep the U.S. dominant in AI development.
Clayton’s appointment to the force, along with the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, Emil Michael, shows how the administration is pushing to frame decisions around model safety as a national security matter that needs executive discretion and secrecy, overshadowing AI’s risks to consumer protection, privacy, and civil rights, said Amos Toh, a senior counsel at the Brennan Center for Justice.
Even as Silicon Valley companies have disclosed their models’ involvement in troubling cyberattacks this year, CAISSI has kept a low profile when it comes to testing for AI safety.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also have been promoting the work of independent evaluation firms to help vet their companies’ safety practices, but the AI giants can limit their access and dispense with their evaluations.
“There’s this unclear mission for government evaluators if the largest AI companies are also being encouraged to set up their own internal evaluation systems and/or hire external evaluators,” said Logan Koepke, a senior project director at the civil rights and technology nonprofit Upturn. “Like, what role does government testing actually play in that scenario?”
Letting the labs police their own models and failing to clarify the role of government in AI safety testing weakens independent checks on AI systems that can cause real-world harms, Toh said.
“At the end of the day, all of these decisions are of immense public consequence and should be explained and rationalized in the public eye,” he said. “And that’s not happening.”

title: Powerball jackpot hits $1 billion. Here's everything to know, including when's the next drawing
Dad of 20-year-old co-pilot in Florida Learjet crash says her final radio calls showed ‘she’s tough’
text:
(AP) - The father of the 20-year-old co-pilot killed alongside eight others in a Florida Learjet crash said Friday he has repeatedly listened to her final radio transmissions, searching for answers and finding pride in how she handled the crisis.
Allan Filgueiras, a pilot who helped teach Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras to fly, said he marveled at how “she’s tough” even as the plane plunged straight toward the ground Sunday.
“I wanted to be by her side. Inside the plane, to help,” he said at a news conference, often holding back tears.
“She showed me what it is to be a hero,” he said, “because once you see that coming, a lot of the big boys — military or whatever — they can’t handle. And she was the one over there to the last minute fighting.”
Nathalia Filgueiras can first be heard calmly telling air traffic control about ice buildup on the plane as it flew into a thunderstorm. Turbulence tossed it up and down by 700 feet (200 meters), but the situation quickly escalated as the aircraft fell at breathtaking speed. “Declare an emergency 722-Bravo-Delta. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute!” she said.
Her father and aviation safety experts have praised her composure as she called out updates while knowing the plane’s fate was sealed. The captain, 55-year-old Jeff Gregory, is believed to have been at the controls.
“For the family — it’s like having the heart torn from my chest,” Allan Filgueiras said in Spanish. “I have to find a way to go on living.”
Young co-pilot’s family and instructor say she earned her job on merit
The family has challenged online criticism questioning whether she had enough experience to be in the cockpit of a high-performance business jet. She had more than 1,300 hours of experience and completed extensive training to earn her commercial pilot’s license and Learjet certification.
Her father’s attorney, Stuart Grossman, said the news conference aimed to “preserve not just her memory, but her reputation.”
“She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years,” Grossman said, noting there were no immediate plans for any lawsuit.
The National Transportation Safety Board has not yet determined what caused the crash. The Learjet accelerated beyond its design limits as it fell, and pieces of its tail were found miles away from the crash site, which is a deep crater on the edge of a road. Investigators were still searching the area Friday after finding part of an engine a day earlier. The cockpit recorder remains missing.
Allan Filgueiras said he helped teach her how to fly after taking her aloft for the first time at age 12. Once she got a job as a pilot, she told him she couldn’t believe she was getting paid to do something she loved.
“It was her happiest moment, to fly,” he said.
Mentor says her professionalism showed in final calls
Her mentor and instructor, Chris Kirk, said she earned her position through dedication and perseverance by putting in hard work and long hours.
During her Learjet 60 check ride in March, the examiner was so impressed he thought she had more than 5,000 hours of experience — nearly four times the amount of flight time she had logged.
Kirk said her professionalism was evident in those final radio transmissions, which gave the NTSB important information. Many members of the military special forces who Kirk worked with probably couldn’t keep their wits in a similar situation.
“This was an incredible human being,” Kirk said, “who did a job that very few people would have been able to do under a duress that’s unimaginable.”
Retired airline pilot John Cox said earlier this week that his career began similarly to Nathalia Filgueiras’, as he started flying professionally at age 19. He said she had done well to earn a Learjet co-pilot’s seat.
“To be in the right seat of a Lear 60, she had to impress somebody, because that’s a good ride. I mean, that’s great. I know she loved it,” said Cox, who now runs Safety Operating Systems, an aviation consulting company.
The other crash victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children, relatives said. The family’s nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed. The other two victims were Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, who owned the Arca Boutique Hotel in Honduras.

title: Fowler scores early to lead UMaine hockey to win over UMass
text:
ORONO – University of Maine hockey captain Owen Fowler knew how important it was for his Black Bears to carve out a win over the University of Massachusetts on Saturday night to snap their three-game losing streak.
So the graduate student left wing took matters into his own hands, scoring just 19 seconds into the game and producing a game-high nine shots on goal to lead the Black Bears to an impressive 2-0 win over the 19th-ranked Minutemen.
UMass had won Friday night’s game 2-1 despite being outshot 47-22.
UMaine had a 44-16 advantage in shots on Saturday night and dominated every facet of the game, but UMass freshman goalie Ethan Eskit turned in another gem to keep his team in the game, finishing with 42 saves.
Senior left wing and Robert Morris (PA) transfer Tanner Klimpke gave the Black Bears some well-deserved breathing room by scoring his fifth goal of the season 7:21 into the third period.
Senior Albin Boija stopped all 16 shots he faced to post his second shutout of the season and 12th of his career. He didn’t face many high-percentage chances but was rock solid between the pipes and made the saves he needed to make.
UMaine improved to 5-5 overall and 1-3 in Hockey East while UMass fell to 5-5-1 and 2-1, respectively.
Fowler’s second goal of the season came off a Max Scott rebound.
Scott came around from behind the net and had Eskit kick out his wraparound attempt and his rebound try. But the puck rolled over to Fowler, who camped out to the goalie’s right and he shoveled the rebound behind him.
“You couldn’t ask for a better start,” said Fowler. “It felt great to get the boys going. That’s something we were looking for the last couple of games which was a good start. And to get that crowd going was a lot of fun.”
“We have definitely been preaching [getting to] net fronts and stuff like that,” he added. “When you come off the goal line and throw it low, anything can happen…lot of sticks, lot of feet. It can kind of kick anywhere and, on that one, it luckily came to me.”
“That was awesome,” said UMaine coach Ben Barr. “It would have been nice to get another one or two before the third period.”
“[Fowler] has a really good pulse to what is going on,” added Barr. “That was a huge goal. Just to get a lead for the first time on the weekend.”
Junior defenseman Isa Parekh also picked up an assist along with Scott.
UMaine had a 19-3 shot advantage in the first period and a 13-6 edge in the second but it was still a one-goal game entering the third.
Klimpke then extended the lead when he took a pass from Sam Alfano down the right wing, bore down on Eskit and squeezed a short backhander past him inside the near post.
“[Alfano] made a great pass to me, I saw a little opening next to [Eskit’s] hip there,” said Klimpke. “He wasn’t quite tight on his post so I just tried to sneak it in there and it ended up working out.”
“That was a big one. Sometimes that’s how it goes,” said Barr. “You have how many point-blank looks and get nothing all weekend and then you get one of those.”
“But you keep shooting and crashing the net and eventually something breaks. We were fortunate on the second one,” he added.
Jaden Lipinski also earned an assist along with Alfano.
UMaine bottled the Minutemen up in the UMass zone with its aggressive forecheck and won most of the puck battles all over the ice. The defense corps made good, simple break-out passes and also skated the puck out of the zone to minimize UMass’ possession in the UMaine end. And the forwards came back to help out in the defensive zone.
“The first period was okay but we definitely shut them down the next two periods,” said Fowler. “They [generated] nothing, honestly. Just high flips and wishing for lucky bounces.”
“We kind of picked up where we left off on Friday night with our work ethic,” said Barr. “We found a way to get two tonight which we couldn’t do last night.
“To a man, the guys worked extremely hard all weekend. It’s fun to be out there with them,” added the UMaine coach. “We just have to find a way to execute better [offensively].”
UMaine will next travel to Vermont for games on Friday and Saturday nights to take on the surprising league-leading Catamounts, who are 5-3-1 overall, 4-1-1 in Hockey East.
UMass will play a home-and-home series with Boston College (2-5-2, 1-2-1).

title: Amoeba infections leave 5 with permanent vision loss, 1 dead in this state
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - The Louisiana Department of Health has identified 10 Acanthamoeba infections since 2024, including one fatal brain infection this year. The state epidemiologist said contact lens wearers should remove their lenses before showering, swimming or using a hot tub
Theresa Sokol, state epidemiologist for the Louisiana Department of Health, said Acanthamoeba is found in many environments.
What Acanthamoeba is
“Acanthamoeba are what are referred to as a free-living amoeba,” Sokol said. “These are single-celled organisms that live in the environment. They’re in soil, they’re in dust, and they’re in fresh and salt water.”
Sokol said the organisms also can be found in swimming pools, drinking water systems, and HVAC systems.
“Pretty much everyone is going to be exposed to Acanthamoeba during their lifetime,” Sokol said. “The good news is that most people exposed to Acanthamoeba aren’t going to get sick, but for a few people it can cause serious infections of the sinuses, of the brain, and sometimes of the skin and the eyes as well.”
Cases reported in Louisiana
Sokol said eight of the 10 infections since 2024 were eye infections. Seven of those eight people wore contact lenses, and five cases resulted in permanent vision loss.
“It’s a severe infection, even though it typically doesn’t spread to other parts of the body or result in death,” Sokol said.
The other two patients were reported this year, Sokol said. One had a sinus infection and the other had a brain infection. The patient with the brain infection died. Sokol said both patients had underlying medical conditions.
Sokol said the department is not releasing further details about the patients, including where they lived.
“We want to protect the privacy of the patients that have been infected,” Sokol said. “So we don’t share any more detailed information than that.”
She said the patients were located throughout the state. Sokol said the amoeba can live in tap water in any drinking water system in Louisiana.
“The amoeba can live in tap water anywhere in Louisiana or in the United States because it really takes a very, very high level of chlorination in order to kill these amoeba,” Sokol said. “It’s not a level that would be practical for use in drinking water systems.”
What contact lens wearers should do
Sokol said eye infections linked to contact lens use often occur in people who are healthy. She said some of those people did not follow the best contact lens hygiene or wore their lenses while swimming or showering.
“Contact lenses can absorb and hold water,” Sokol said. “If the lenses come into contact with tap water or swimming pools or some other water where the amoeba live, then those amoeba can sort of latch onto or get trapped beneath the lens, which is directly against the cornea. That’s where the infection happens.”
Sokol said contact lens wearers should:
- Wash their hands with soap and water and dry them thoroughly before handling lenses.
- Remove lenses before showering, using a hot tub or swimming.
- Clean and rinse lenses with the proper solution every time they are removed.
- Store lenses properly.
“You need to dry them thoroughly,” Sokol said of hands. “You don’t want to have your hands wet while you are handling them.”
She said leftover water on the hands can get into a lens.
“That’s the water that can then get into your contact lens perhaps and be absorbed or latch onto it and then just remain there,” Sokol said. “That’s what we’re trying to avoid.”
Sokol said getting water in the eyes while not wearing contact lenses has not been shown to be a risk for infection. She said a person who has had trauma to the eye or recent eye surgery might potentially have an opening. She said most infections are identified among people who wear contact lenses.
Symptoms, diagnosis and treatment
Sokol said symptoms of Acanthamoeba eye infections can look like those of other common eye infections. They include eye pain, redness, blurred vision, sensitivity to light, and excessive watering.
“It’s really best anytime you get any of those symptoms to just check with your healthcare provider,” Sokol said. “There are prescription treatments that are available.”
“The earlier you seek care, the more likely to have a positive outcome,” she said.
Sokol said symptoms could appear “several days or up to several weeks after exposure.” She said it can be hard to know when someone was exposed.
Sokol said the amoeba sometimes can be seen under a microscope. She said reference laboratories can run tests that identify the amoeba’s genetic material. The specimen depends on the type of infection, she said. A brain infection might require a brain biopsy, and an eye infection might be tested with fluid from the eye.
She said skin and sinus infections caused by Acanthamoeba often are treatable but can spread to other parts of the body, which makes them harder to treat.
“The brain infection that is caused by Acanthamoeba is oftentimes difficult to diagnose,” Sokol said. “If the diagnosis happens at a later stage, then sometimes that increases the risk that a patient may not survive that infection. However, several patients with that infection have been successfully treated in the past.”
Nasal rinsing, medical devices and tap water
Sokol said using tap water for nasal irrigation, or cleaning nasal irrigation devices with tap water, is a known risk factor for sinus and brain infections caused by Acanthamoeba.
“Tap water should not be used for nasal or sinus irrigation,” Sokol said. “It really can pose a risk of severe disease.”
Sokol said nasal irrigation devices can be used safely with water that is labeled sterile or distilled. Boiled and cooled tap water also can be used, she said.
She said people who use other medical devices that use water, such as a CPAP machine, should follow the manufacturer’s instructions and use safe water.
Sokol said sinus and brain infections occur mostly among people with weakened immune systems. She said those conditions include HIV, AIDS, a history of an organ transplant, cancer, and diabetes, among others.
“People who have a condition that weakens their immune system need to be especially aware of using the safe types of water in nasal irrigation devices or other medical equipment,” Sokol said.
Sokol said people can still shower with tap water. She said infection is not associated with swallowing or drinking tap water.
“There’s no need to be concerned,” Sokol said. “That’s not how Acanthamoeba infections happen.”

title: Deportation flight of Iranians from US scuttled at last minute, attorney says
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — A U.S. deportation flight of Iranian nationals bound for Iran by way of Pakistan was abruptly canceled Sunday morning, according to an attorney who spoke to some of the detainees slated for repatriation.
At least eight Iranians were loaded onto a plane Sunday morning in Mesa, Arizona, for a deportation flight headed to the country of Georgia, then on to Pakistan, according to Ali Rahnama, an attorney with the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund who filed emergency motions on behalf of some of the Iranian detainees. The flight was canceled without explanation, he said.
Court documents unsealed days ago in a civil lawsuit filed by the fund showed the Trump administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians to Iran, even as the war there drags on, via an unnamed third country. The lawsuit was filed in July and alleges that the U.S. government illegally shared confidential information about Iranians seeking asylum in the U.S. with Iranian officials.
There were three deportation flights to Iran between September 2025 and January 2026, with over 100 Iranian nationals deported. But the administration’s confirmation of the new plans amid the war that began in February highlights its resolve in carrying out its hardline immigration crackdown, which has involved ramping up removals, including to places that critics say could endanger the lives of the returnees.
Homeland Security refuses comment
In response to questions Sunday from The Associated Press, the press office of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security provided a statement attributed to an unnamed spokesperson that said Immigration and Customs Enforcement does not comment on “prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details,” nor would the agency confirm future removal operations.
“As promised, the Trump Administration is employing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history,” the statement said.
The administration did not specify in the October court records when the deportations would be carried out. But in the past week, roughly a dozen Iranian nationals in immigration detention said they were notified that they were scheduled for an upcoming deportation flight to Pakistan and then to Iran, according to numerous attorneys who have since confirmed those plans with DHS.
Advocacy group says detainees have been contacted by Iranian officials
According to Rahnama, the eight detainees who boarded the flight on Sunday were visited by a senior official with the Iranian Interests Section — an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani Embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs — and were told that the Iranian government would transport them from Pakistan to Iran.
In the litigation brought by the Iranian immigrant advocacy group, at least a dozen Iranian detainees have said they’ve been contacted by Iranian officials who had knowledge of sensitive information on their asylum claims.
U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes, a nominee of President Joe Biden, has not ruled on the claims but ordered the U.S. government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country, and five days’ written notice before any such deportation is carried out.
In a court filing Sunday, the defense fund laid out what it had learned about plans for a removal flight Sunday and argued that the administration may have violated the judge’s directive to give advance notice of deportation plans.
Later Sunday, the government filed court documents in the case, but they were sealed and inaccessible to the public.
Group says individuals could face persecution
The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund has called for a halt to the removal flights, saying in a news release that they would “reportedly mark the first deportation of Iranians to Iran since the U.S.-Iran war began.”
The group’s executive director, Yasmin Chubin, said in a statement Sunday that it was difficult to comprehend why the U.S. would forcibly deport Iranians, including asylum seekers, to Iran, amid ongoing military hostilities.
The consequences of removal, Chubin said, “could be irreversible and individuals may face persecution, torture, or death.”
At least one person who had been part of the scuttled flight volunteered to go back to Iran after nearly two years of detention, Rahnama said, out of desperation to leave what he described as inhumane imprisonment. It’s not clear how many other of the deportees may have volunteered to leave.
____
Associated Press reporter Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia, contributed to this report.

title: Novel Jazz Septet at the Opera House
text:
An evening with the Novel Jazz Septet is so much more than a musical show. Steeped in the stories and the history surrounding both Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn, the band brings the audience into a time and place that informed some of the most iconic and influential music of the 20th century and helps listeners understand the forces that shaped Ellington’s and Strayhorn’s contributions to the jazz world. The septet will bring their compelling program to the Opera House at Boothbay Harbor on Friday, Aug. 21, at 7:30 p.m. And, the show will be recorded for a new CD, so the enthusiasm and engagement of the room will be captured as an added element of the experience.
Band member Barney Balch finds the experience as mesmerizing today as he did 22 years ago when the group first assembled. “It all started in a performance that we were doing an informal thing, and someone called out an Ellington tune that none of us had ever heard of before. And I said, ‘Sheesh, you know, between the seven of us playing here, there’s about two centuries of collective jazz knowledge, and none of us have ever heard of this tune. I wonder how many tunes Duke Ellington wrote?’ and the answer to that is, thousands.”
Balch’s fascination is sustained by the extraordinary access that he has had to precious, and rarely seen, compositions. “Ellington started writing in the mid-20s and, and he died in ‘74 and he was just writing constantly. So I thought, ‘I wonder where all these are?’ And I found out about what's called the Ellington Archives, at the Smithsonian Museum of American History, where they have the originals, the penciled manuscripts–lead sheets, they're called; there are 400 book boxes of these that had been in a garage someplace, and had sustained some water damage. So that's when they consulted with the Smithsonian, and the Smithsonian said, ‘Well, we'll take it!’” Balch reflects on the momentous experience of being in the presence of archival gems: “The first time I held the penciled copy of Mood Indigo, my hands were shaking. There's nothing like it and it's really fun.”
Balch shares that Strayhorn, who was quite a bit younger than Ellington, and tragically died very young, also composing at that time, and “There are lots of backstories about how those guys met, and our shows basically deal with both the tunes and the stories. There's a story behind every piece and it's my jazz iceberg, I call it. We've been chipping away at this, as I said, for 22 years and haven't even made a dent.”
Asked about how the collaboration process works with the septet, Balch says, “We start by looking through the collection of tunes that we've been thinking of doing. They have to be down ranged from typically being written for 18-piece orchestras, down to seven pieces. So that's a challenge. After we do a first arrangement, we all get together, and it's probably one of the most fun sessions of the year. We play these things, try them out, and then we sit around and say, ‘Geez, you know, this would sound really cool as a samba. And let's pick up the tempo.’ So we're not necessarily reproducing these songs exactly as they were written in 1928 or 1936. We're dusting them off and bringing them up harmonically and rhythmically. And there will be times where we make a change to one of these tunes and we all just go, ‘Whoa!’”
With regard to the storytelling that places this music squarely in its tumultuous history of absent civil rights, Balch says, “There are a lot of stories tied up in that, and I really try to bring both of those out in our shows–the song as well as the backstory. Because it's just so compelling and we have a lot we can learn. There’s a lot the audience can still learn about music; how it has responded to social issues has never been more relevant than right now in so many ways.”
Advance discounted tickets, $20, are available from the box office at 86 Townsend Ave., Boothbay Harbor or by calling 207-633-5159. The bar will have cold drinks for sale, cash only.

title: Maine Republicans must reconstruct anew
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sam Patten worked for Maine’s last three Republican senators, including Susan Collins’ first electoral campaigns, is a former managing editor of the Maine Wire and is the author of “Dangerous Company: The Misadventures of a Foreign Agent.”
From her first run for elected office 32 years ago to last Tuesday’s “blue wave,” Sen. Susan Collins was often confronted with — and usually prevailed over — circumstances that could be called unfair.
When Collins ran for Maine governor in 1994, a right-wing activist challenged her eligibility, arguing she wasn’t really from Maine (having defeated that spurious claim in court, later that year Collins lost the general election to Angus King, a man born and raised in Virginia).
The principal complaint against Collins this year was that she was a stooge of President Donald Trump, which her record will show was not actually the case.
Even though I made a case for her opponent in my last column for this paper, watching Collins lose this week I couldn’t help but be struck by the magnitude of effort it took for her to persist in politics this whole time. Could Collins, the national press asked in the weeks running up to Tuesday, “defy gravity” yet again?
Born into a cold climate with a sense of scarcity hard-wired in at the earliest of ages, most Mainers well understand that life isn’t fair. When all the confetti is swept from the floor and the righteous gloating wears itself out, some may eventually come to miss Collins. Only time will truly tell.
Without the last standing Republican senator in the Northeast, another truth will become more quickly apparent in Maine: The state’s GOP can no longer expect to run on life support.
After eight years without a Republican governor, or majority in either chamber of the Legislature, the rationale for backers of the party coffers to keep giving has been waning for some time. Without Collins to support, it is now gone altogether.
Beyond the seismic loss of her Senate seat, the Republican ranks in Augusta also shriveled — especially in the House, where the minority lost a dozen seats. Democrats, who have been largely unopposed in state government for some time, can now change the Constitution at will. For those who believe in limited government, that is a terrifying thought.
For too long, Maine’s Republican Party has sustained itself with external aid (analogous, in a way, to the U.S. Agency for International Development which Elon Musk’s boys triumphantly shuttered last year).
There was once the Bush family foothold in Kennebunkport and, more recently, there was the Trump administration, to which Republicans in the State House repeatedly turned for help on a host of issues over the past two years.
Former governor and now congressman-elect Paul LePage left behind his own set of strap-hangers as the party apparatus. It is likely that the most junior member of a minority faction in he U.S. House will have no ability to keep them fed any longer.
What is left of the Republican Party in Maine will have to stand on its own feet. But how?
Shouting into the void like madmen aggrieved by the world’s decline is probably not a winning strategy. Successive, discrete wins, on the other hand, dot the only viable path out of the wilderness.
When the Gov. Hannah Pingree administration takes office early next year, it will be staring down the barrels of a grim financial reality. Maine state government is perilously over-leveraged. Its appetites swelled by COVID-19 money after 2020, it must now adapt to austerity. It must learn to live as most Mainers do.
Wild-eyed visions of a green energy paradise, for instance, are simply unsustainable. So too is the state-supported ecosystem of nonprofits that has become accustomed to cranking out diktats disguised as policy papers.
During the debates, Sen. Collins countered attacks by Troy Jackson, now senator-elect, by pointing out how the high cost of living in Maine is the result of Augusta’s policies on everything from energy to taxes and regulations on the drowning businesses that have yet to flee the state.
But as Collins’ loss has shown us, that was not the argument for a U.S. senator to make.
Now even further diminished, Maine Republicans must pick their battles wisely and find what fissures may exist in the post-midterms mega-party of power. Single-issue campaigns offer some promise, but they must be winning issues with broad popular support. Conservatives can’t afford another failed referendum drive.
Just as importantly, Maine Republicans must find new financial backers. The right ones will follow the right issues: improving our beleaguered business environment, fixing the depleted quality of education in the classroom as opposed to getting hung up on who goes to what bathroom and taking aim at bloated — and in some already identified instances, fraudulent — state spending.
Rome wasn’t built in a day. A political party that effectively champions the rights and needs of those who aren’t celebrating right now won’t be either. But a focused effort to construct one from the ground up is long past due.
Is this possible? Only time will truly tell.

title: 3 people sent to hospital after shooting at Winston-Salem State University
text:
2 charged in deadly shooting at Winston-Salem State during homecoming weekend
A 19-year-old man is dead, a 22-year-old woman was injured, and two men are facing charges after a shooting on the campus of Winston-Salem State University, according to Winston-Salem, North Carolina, police.
“Our condolences go out to the families, to the friends, and anyone who witnessed this,” officials said Sunday.
Video above: Winston-Salem police hold Sunday morning press conference following shooting
Just after 9:45 p.m. Saturday, officers responded to the 600 block of South Martin Luther King Jr. Drive after hearing gunshots in the area.
Police found 19-year-old Peyton Patterson with a gunshot wound and began lifesaving measures. EMS personnel also provided aid, but Patterson died from his injuries.
The circumstances surrounding Patterson's death remain under investigation. Detectives have determined that the shooting was an isolated incident, and Patterson's next of kin has been notified.
22-year-old Alyssa Ellerbee was also found with a gunshot wound. She was taken to a local hospital, where she was treated and released. Police have not released any information about if Ellerbee is a WSSU student at this time.
Police charged 20-year-old Ziyaire Spinks with general murder, assault with a deadly weapon with intent to kill or inflict serious injury, and felony possession of a firearm on educational property.
18-year-old Cequan Brower was also charged with affray in connection with the incident. Neither of the suspects were students, according to police.
During a news conference, officers said the victims and suspects were in two separate groups when an argument broke out, leading to the shooting that killed Patterson and injured Ellerbee.
Spinks is being held without bond. Brower is being held on a $50,000 bond. Police said both Spinks and Brower will appear in court on Monday. They also have not released their photos at this time due to the investigation being ongoing.
Second shooting happened less than an hour later
Police said the second shooting occurred at 10:22 p.m. on the university's campus. Police said as officers were investigating an earlier incident nearby they also heard gunshots in the area.
Police found 21-year-old Najir Pearsall, who taken to the hospital and was listed in critical but stable condition. Officers said they also located Makyiah Ward, 20, who had been shot and was also taken to the hospital. She was listed in stable condition at this time. Police said they identified and later found a vehicle related to the incident.
Police said the circumstances around the shooting are still under investigation, and no arrests have been made. They also have not said if Pearsall or Ward are students at WSSU.
Chancellor Bonita J. Brown issued a statement Sunday morning, calling the shootings “senseless violence.” She assured students, faculty and parents that the campus was secure and that additional law enforcement would remain while the investigation continues.
